VISITOR (in penitentiary)—What brought you to this place, my friend ?" • Convict—" Siteezing ?" Visitor—" Sneezing ?" Convict—" Yis, sor ; it woke the gintleman up, an' he nabbed me." WALKING down St. James's-street, Lord Chelms- ford was accosted by a stranger, who exclaimed, " Mr. Birch, I believe." "If you believe that, sir, you'll believe , anything," replied the ex. Chancellor as he .passed on. HUSBAND—" My dear, that is a long motto you are working." Wife—" Yea, John." He reads on it:—" While the lamp holds on to burn, the vilest sinner may return." Is it to be hung in the ves- tibule of the church, my dear ?" "No, John; I'll hang it ou the chandelier in the hall." A PAISLEY man unconsciously got himself into . trouble one evening. His wife asked him whither he was going. "I am going to sally forth," he replied. "Let me catch you going with Sally' Forth, and there'll be a first-class opportunity for your fire company to throw themselves on a set of obituary resolutions." HERR SCHMIDT is an absent-minded German who gives lessons on the cornet. One of the pupils asked him—" At what o'clock do you want Me to come to your house to-morrow to take my lesson, Professor?" "Oh, veil, choost come when you got ready, put pe sure you vash on time, for I don't vant to be kept waiting." SARCASTICUS and his wife don't agree very :well. The other morning he discovered that she had appropriated his only necktie. Sarcasticus— " What in thunder are you wearing my cravat for ?" Mrs. S.—" Because I haven't any of my own." Sarcasticus (gloomily)—" Oh, I see I It is the only tie there is between us." -

• SOME of Luttrell's Irish stories (says Sydney Smith) were most amusing. One—" Is your master at home, Paddy ?" "No, your honour." "Why, I saw him go in five minutes ago." " Faith, your honour, he's not exactly at home, he's only there in the backyard a-shooting rats -with cannon, your honour, for his devarsion." MORGAN JOHN O'CoNNELL, nephew of the agitator, had (says Harrison) the ready wit of his country in a remarkable degree. We, were walking by the Wey one day when an Oxford graduate, a Mr. White, who had a taste for botany, plucked a flower ( Balsamum impatiens) from the river, remarking that "it was a veil rare plant." "it is an out-of-the-/Vey one, at any rage," was

the reply. PARTY SPIRIT in Dublin was at one tune attended by continual duels. It was upon one of these occasions that Giffard, the editor of the Dublin Journal, being called out, appeared on the prou nd. with his spectacles on. This was objected to by his adversary's second, and he was desired to take them off, which he did, exclaiming, "By my soul, this is too bad. I could not see to shoot my own father without them !" CHARLES KEMELE told the story of how one day, he was followed up Sackville-street, Dublin, by two beggar women, between whom the follow- ing dialogue passed, evidently with a view to his edification :—" Och, but he's an illgant man, is Misther Charles Kemble !" "An', 'deed, so was his brudher, Misther John, thin—a moighty foine man! and to see his demanour, puttin' his hand in his pocket and givin' me sixpence, bate all the world !" RECENTLY a French newspaper announced that a banker's country house had been robbed in the night, "hut fortunately the thieves, in their hurry, had failed to open the second drawer on the right- hand side of the escritoire, in which was a large sum of money in bank-notes." Two or three days later the editor received the following note : " Mr. Editor, I cannot sufficiently thank you for the information given in your excellent paper. It was in every respect exact, as I found on going last night for the second time to the house of M.Z. T'ne notes were there, and are now in my posses- sion. No signature. You will understand my scruples." "WILL you be kind enough to • take that sack off the seat ? ' said a countryman, who got in a train. "No, sir, I don't propose to do anything of the sort," replied the traveller, who was sitting on the other side of the seat. "Do you say that you are going to let that sack stay right there?" "Yes, gr, I do." "In case you don't remove that sack, I shall be under the painful necessity of calling the guard." "You can call in the guard, the engineer, and the brakeman if you want to. Perhaps you had better stop at the next station and telegraph the general manager himself about it." "The guard will put you out of the train." "I don't care if he does. lam not going to take that sack from the place where it is. The indignant passenger went along the train, and soon returned with the guard. "So you refuse to remove the sack, do you? "asked the guard. "I do." Great sensation. "Why do you persist in refusing to remove the sack?" "Because it's not mine." "Why didn't you say so at once ? " "Because no- body asked me." GREELEY'S IMAGINATION. Stories about Horace Greeley are always interesting," remarked Charles M. Walker, in conversation. " The other day I met one of the proprietors of the Knights- town Banner, who gave me two that have never been in print. He worked in the New York Tribune office ten years during Mr. Greeley's time, and had many anecdotes of that great editor. It was Mr. Grealey's custom on Sunday forenoon to isliterid Dia Chapin's chtirch, after which he would saunter -crOsist to the Tribune office and look through the exchanges. One remarkably cold Sun- day he came down to the office, after church. The janitor had neglected to build any fires. Mr. 'Greeley went into the editoral room and, his feet feeling cold, he took off his shoes and hung his feet in the register. Presently the foreman came down -on some errand of business. • It was freezing cold, and there was a cold draught rushing through the register, where Mr. Greeley sat immersed in ex- changes, wholly oblivious of all sublunary discom- forts. " ' Why, Mr. Greeley,' exclaimed the fore- man 'what in the world are you doing? There's no ire there, and you'll take your death of cold.' "'D-- it," said the philosopher, pettishly, why did you tell me? I was warming myself very nicely." A CRUEL Affirm—Alike commendable for its subtlety and inoffensive humour was the pleasantry with which young Philip Yorke (afterwards Lord Harslwicke) answered Sir Lyttleton Powys's banter on the Western Circuit. An amiable and upright, but far from brilliant judge, Sir Lyttleton had a few pet phrases—amongst them "I humbly con- ceive," and "Look, doyou see—"which he sprinkled over his judgments and colloquial talk with ridiculous profuseness. Surprised at Yorke's sud- den rise intolucrative practice, this most gentleman- like worthy was pleased to account for the unusual success by maintaining that young Mr. Yorke must have written a law book which had brought him early into favour with the inferior branch of the pro- fession. "Mr. Yorke," said the venerable justice, while the barristers were sitting over their wipe at a "judge's dinner," "I cannot well account for your having so much business, considering the short time you have been at bar; I humbly con- ceive you must have published something ; for, look you, do you see, there is scarcely a cause in Court but you are employed in it, on one side or the other. I should therefore be glad to know, Mr. Yorke, do you see, whether this be the case." Playfully denying that he possessed any celebrity as a writer on legal matters Yorke, with an assumption of candour, admitted that he had some thoughts of lightening the labours of law students by turning Coke upon Littleton into verse. Indeed, he confessed he had already begun the work of versification. Not seeing the nature of the reply, Sir Lyttleton Powys treated the droll fancy as a serious project, and insisted that the author should give a specimen of the style of his contemplated work. Whereupon the young barrister—not pausing to remind a company of lawyers of the the words of the original—" Tenant in fee simple is he which bath lands or tenements to hold to him and to his heirs for ever"—recited the lines— "He that holdeth his lands in fee Need neither to quake nor quiver, I humbly conceive: for look, do you see, They are his and his heirs for ever." The mimicry of the voice being not less perfect than the verbal imitation, Yorke 's hearers (says Jeaffreson) were convulsed with laughter. "You have no piano, I see." " No, sir, I haven't." "But dont you think you ought to have one ?" "Not any." "But consider, if you had one your daughter would play it, and—'' "Yes, that's what I'm afraid of.

div.head: QUESTION.
div.p: QUESTION.
BY A. 11. CROSFIELD.

. The following is a full report of the speech made by Mr. A. 11. Crosfield, at Stockton Heath; last week in supporting a vote Of confidence in Mr. Latham the Liberal candidate for Knutsford : 1 gatt:er from the remarks we have just heard that he asks your support on the grounds that he is in favour of those various mea- sures and reforms which will be the subject of Liberal legislation if we win, and because he is an advocate of Home Rule. We have heard it said in a good many quarters lately that we are trying to put Home Rule into the back ground. That is rather a bold statement. I fancy most of us thought Home Rule had been kept very much to the fore the last six years. It is not our interests to put it in the back ground, but, as Liberals, have pretty well made up their minds on the Irish question, they are naturally beginning to think about other things as well. We have to prepare ourselves for many atiother problem that springs up and forces itself upon our attention, the product of our increasingly complex social relations and the enormous increase in our population, our commerce and our wealth. Ido nut refer only to

div.head: NEWCASTLE PROGRAMME
div.p: THE NEWCASTLE PROGRAMME

which naturally forms the basis for most of our local programme. That in itself affords material for years of energetic work by the progressiveTparty ; but besides the subjects for more immediate legis- lation which it includes you will have.others to deal with later on, one way or another, whether by acceptance, refusal, or compromise—such questions as the Currency, Female Suffage, Parliamentary Regulation of the hours of labour in this trade or the other trade, and alteration in the incidence and method of Taxation. The very names of such ques- tions suggest a crowd of conflicting interests and considerations. How much attention have you given, have the bulk of members of Parliament given to them? The absorption of Parliamentary time is only half the evil. It is a bad and unhealthy state of affairs in which the public attention is pre- occupied year after year by this endless contro- versy, largely to the exclusion of what comes within the proper sphere of our interests and poli- tical activity. That is bad, but it is not the worst. As a writer of, I think, unmistakably Unionist pro- clivities truly says in the " Contemporary " for this month :—" It is in the last degree unstatesmanlike and a source of extreme danger to the Empire to allow the Home Rule question to remain unsettled longer than can be avoided. It is a sort of open' wound or sore in the constitution." Even in time of peace he calls it " A GRAVE INCONVENIENCE " _

as well he may, for it threatens to stultlfy Parliament- ary and Party Government, and certainly interferes with the impartial consideration of every English question of importance. And in time of war! If you are determined to treat the Irish as Hottentots,unfit for the management of their own affairs ; if you refuse to recognise their capacity or Nationality, you must make up your minds to deal with them permanently as enemies. Why should we so deal with them? Why coerce and not conciliate? It costs us millions a year and prepares for us an active enemy at our own doors, waiting their opportunity, should we ever again be engaged in some great struggle • sufficient to tax seriously our resources. Such a struggle may be as far as we are concerned—we hope it is—a remote contingency; but still, even England cannot be sure of never being dragged into another serious war, ' and the question is therefore entitled to consideration, above all, by those who are so anxious, honestly anxious no doubt, about the security of the Empire. Supposing their were such a war' what, I should like to know, would their Paper Union ,be worth then? The word union is misapplied. The TO'ry Policy is not a policy of Unionism but of disunionism. It is the Tories and Unionists who threaten us with bitter feelings and estrangement between the two nations, just as their leaders aro deliber- ately trying to stir up those feelings between two sec- tions of the Irish themselves. That brings me to what is, I believe,
A SERIOUS STUMBLING BLOCIC

in the way of many who would otherwise be inclined to favor a settlement of the Irish question. Separation is played out ; they put their money on that horse at the start, but apparently it was only to make the run- ning for another called Ulster, and now they hope to win on that. I do not think they will. I think the electorate are shrewd enough to see that Ulsteria has a good deal in common with Hysteria, and as much a bogey as Separa tin was. You are asked to believe that under Home Rule the Catholics would oppressthe Pro- testants of Ulster, and the rest of Ireland. All history points the other way. Who has ever heard of a Protes- tant, as such, illused by Catholics? Yet many of them live In the south and -West of Ireland surrounded by Catholics and outnumbered 100 to 1. Surely it is a strong point in favor of my contention that from these very districts you have some of the staunchest and ablest Protestant Home Rulers. Protestants in these districts are not treated as enemies or in any way ill- treated by their Catholic neighbours. No ;it is left to Belfast Orangemen to show that kind of contemptible intolerance. And to what is it due? It is due to the old spirit of ascendancy that has outlived the times of , the English garrison and pervades those who are not content to be on terms of equality with their neigh- bours. There is nothing in this cry, in these apprehen- sions of religious oppression. If the worst came to the worst and if any such attempt was made, do you think the English Parliament or English people would permit it? But there is no real grounds for these fears. If there was, would you find shrewd Irish Protestants deliberately committing social and political suicide ? If

Ulster was be badly treated, would those whose for- tunes are wholly bound up with that part of the coun- try, support our policy, as not a few of them are doing? When the opposition of Ulster is spoken of, do not let us forget that Ulster actually returns 17 Home Rulers out of 33 representatives, a proportion which will belittle if at all altered at tha next election ; and recollect, too, that the Orangemen of Ulster have treated us to some
I BIM TALL TALE

on other occasions. I will give you one or two extracts bearing on that point. First of all, here is what Mr. Chamberlain says about Ulster's present attitude: "If," he says, "Home Rule is to be established in Ireland. you will have to reckon with the men of Ulster. They move slowly, but they move surely. They are not easily led into excitement, rebellion, or resistance ; but, believe me, if these men take up the sword, they will not lay it down till they have accomplished their object." Compare with this, the phraseology employed by and about the same north-east corner of Ulster in 1869,when the Irish Church was disestablished. Here is what the leading organ in the Press said on the 13th July, of that year :—" No statesman can any longer gffect to ignore or disguise the state of feeling of the Protes- tants" (i.e., be it observed, of the Orangemen) " of Ulster. The proceedings yesterday were stamped with the features characteristic of that remarkable race. The steady determination, the indomitable will, the orderly organisation vrkich characterise the men of Ulster, was everywhere apparent." Then you, have the Grand Master of the Orangemen of Donegal .declaring in the same year that as regards disestablishment of the Irish Church, which the Ulster men were resolved to resist "It behoves all who love their country, and country- men of every denomination,all who love their God, to take warning and exert themselves earnestly while it is , yet time to avert these calamities, and the fearful scenes of bloodshed and carnage in a civil war." This language was used 23 years ago, but the concession did not produce disturbance of any kind whatever. I will give you another instance .in which not concession, but ' the refusal to concede a reasonable demand, in a case remarkably analagous to that of Ireland, produced very serious disturbances indeed. When Canada asked for self-governmlnt 60 years ago, the conditions were re- markably like those existing in Ireland. Removable magistrates, boycotting, coercion, and the demand for a free Parliamentary and a responsible Executive were all in
CANADA 60 YEARS AGO

as they are in Ireland to-day. You had too, an aslend- ant minority and a petition from them to Parliament, which, in substance, I have no doubt, the resolution about to be passed by Ulster Orangemen will strikingly resemble. Here it is :—" By theendearing recollections of a common origin and a powerful sentiment of com- mon danger, we are prepared to resist to the utmost the efforts of a party which under the speciaus guise of popu- lar institutions would sever wisdom from power,respect from intelligence, and consign us to unendurable bond- age." Lord Stanley said in the English Parliament— " the concession of an elective legislative Council would remove the only which to the tyrannical power of the dominant majority—:a majority, he would re- mark, in numbers only. for in wealth, in education, in enterprise, it was greatly inferior to the minority of settlers of British descent. One thing was certain, that if the British settlers found themselves deprived of the protection of the Government here, they would protect themselves. He would venture to say that in six months after the institution of an Elective Legislative Council, the British population of Lower Canada would have determined that the protection of the mother county being withdrawn from them they must take measures for protecting themselves." Let us see things as they are, We recognise the opposition of a minority in Ulster, but we are not going to overestimate its im- portance. There are probably at the outside 100,000 Protestants in Ulster opposed to Horne Rule, and, says the" Manchester Guardian," cool observers on the spot say there are probably not 300 men belonging to the party that are prepared to die in the last ditch. We can understand the opposition of this section of Ulster, and it does not at all follaw that because iit s opposed to Home Rule it will there- fore suffer by it. Home Rule cannot fail in the end to be a benefit to the whole country. All of us I fancy, have at one time or another in our lives had

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JUNE 25, 1892.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JUNE 25, 1892.

to submit for our good, to what we have not relished, and may have resisted passively or even actively. So it is in politics. Our Tory fiiends must remembr some doses they have had to swallow quite as unpalatable to them as Home Rule is to the Orangemen. Take the reform of 1832. They opposed it tooth and nail. Would any of thew dare to get up here and say the country is the worse for it? I hope we are too wide-awake to be deceived by the cry of any faction seeking to balk the final solution of this longstanding difficulty and encour- aged and stimulated by the leaders of our opponents. I have detained you much longer perhaps than I should have done ; but one feels that the moment and the issues before us, are of grave and deep importance. This will be no slight and trivial incident in party warfare. The country's decision will affect Ireland's future to an incal- culable extent. Yes,and not only Ireland's,but England's future ; even perhaps to some extent the opinions and policy of continental nations and indeed tire whole civilized world. I trust that in the approaching fight, Mr. Latham will have your active, cordial and conscien- tious support, and that every one of us here and in Warrington will work together with a will to carry to a ' successful issue this great cause of prudence and tolera- tion and justice.

whose lips sh-ould smile, even when they pretended to scold him. Silvia did not seek to detain him when he announced his -intention of returning to London. She knew him too well for that. He would be restless and ill at ease until he had gone back. Besides, the winter was close at hand, and Silvia remembered vividly how the long, dreary months of cold had depressed and worried her during her first winter in the north, and did not wish to subject Teddy to the same ordeal. , would not bear it with patience, she was quite certain of that! She herself was so happy that nothing outside of lter own life seemed to signify in the least. After the night of sorrow, a sun of gladness and rejoicing had dawned; and in its glorious beams her nature ripened and expanded, as a bud expands into a blossom, a flower ripens into a fruit. - She loved Teddy, but she was ashamed to confess how little she would miss him. • All that was necessary to her now was her husband's love. It turned winter into summer, night into day. And Teddy was not always so deferential as he (night to have been to Sir Lancelot, she fancied! The little man could not quite forgive the treat- ment she had received at her husband's hands,- and took small pains to hide his feelings. Of course, since Jack was getting better, and they had shaken hands all round; it was not in Mr.. Wynne to be a persistently surly and unforgiving member of the party, but his manner was decidedly cool over the hand-shaking part of the business. Altogether it was exceedingly well for him to go; and he proceeded with his arrangements, un- checked. His leave-taking at the Widdringtons' cottage was amusingly characteristic. He put on his smartest garments, and wore a very grand air, sustained -by an inward consciousness of supreme merit; unappreciated certainly in those wilds, but recognised by a fashionable woman whose delicately penned lines he wore next his heart. He brought a gay shawl for old Nanny, and a pretty gown piece as a wedding present to Bell; and felt magnanimous in the extreme as he gave the latter to the laughing,- but not grateful, girl. "I am only sorry for one thing, Bell, my beauty," he said, patronisingly, "I should have liked to see you dressed in it, and to have danced at your wedding. If you would only defer that interesting ceremony until the spring, there might be some chance of my witnessing it, but I suppose the big fellow—how do you name him? Oh, yes, thank you, Dick Daglish, that's it—l expect he is impatient? And 'pon my life I don't wonder at it; for though there is no one better acquainted with all the reigning beauties of the past half-dozen seasons than myself, I have never yet Seen one fit to compare—but I must not make you vain, child, so I shall hold my peace. And you will remember .me sometimes, and wish to see me again?" He was growing sentimental, and Bell knew by past experience that sentiment in his case was to be avoided.. She appealed therefore with promptness to her grandmother. "Mr. Wynne is off te Lunnon, Granny," she said quickly, "Come te say good-bye te ye, he is! An' he's fetched ye another shawl, for the winter." The old woman smirked and bridled, as though a great compliment had been paid to her. "Ay, ay, the gentry ha' taken to runnin' efter us bonny fisher lasses noo ! But they're all tarred wi' one brush, gentle an' simple, an' a pair o' wicked eyes 'll make every man Jack o' them as mad as a march hare. But ma certes ! What can a young lass do wi' such a crood e' sweethearts? An' yet there's niver a you o' them can hold a candle to Willie, if he'd but gettin' the gear !" "Hand yer fond clash, an' mind what a body's sayin'., Granny! You inun be efter thankin' the young gentleman for his kindness, an' him Lady Callerley's brother; forbye bein' canny and free spoken hirnsen" Leddy Callerley ? Ay, she had a good heart te marry into a family that was cursed through all its males fm' .generation to generation! Aw've knawn fower Leddy Callerleys. Which on them do you mean ?" "Ye must just excuse her, sir, for she's gaen clean daft Since--since -wor Bill was drowned," apologised Bell, "there's no gettin' a sensible word oot On her, poor aad creetur. An' she's nigh on a hunnerd, mind ye that !" The old woman caught the last words, and they seemed to pierce through her dulled and wandering _senses. She darted an angry look at Bell, and shook her withered fist in her face. "A hunnerd? nigh on a hunnerd dost Amu say, thou leein' slut, thou ? Aw wes a hunnerd more than a year ago, ma canny gentleman! An' aw can see to thread a needle without spectacles yet— what de ye think o' that? Ma memory's as good as ever too, though aw say it as shouldn't. Aw telled the little lady to ask Madam, though ! Aw was none gannin' te flee i' Sir Lancelot's face an! tell her what lie chose to hide. But there was no love lost between Madam an' her, as it needed no witch to see." Teddy wondered a little what mischief the old creature had been up to. Her face grow diaboli- cally alive as she spoke, and all the weakness and hid:4-614y fled for the nonce. Still in its embers glokrecl an unholy fire. But Bell understood perfectly. It made her Emd and remorseful to think of all the misery Lady Call efley had endured, through her grandmother's impish malice,. and Madam's wickedness together. "You will be married before I come back," re- marked Teddy, as he held Bell's hand in parting. She bowed her head for answer. "An' mebbe yogi bring a bonny bride with you also, Mr. Wynne?" "Who k4tows ? Stranger things have happened," answered Ole little dandy significantly, tapping his heart, whereon reposed the billet doux of his fair mentor, and thinking tenderly of various love episodes in the past. "Ay ay, get a eat o' thee own kind !" broke in ICK:iny, now wide awake. Whereupon Bell and her quondam adorer laughed, au i said farewell !
Ouirrrn LIM TEDDY IS CONSOLED.

Mr. Wynne was not sorry' to get back to town and its distractions. After the first novelty of , country life had worn off, he had pined for his com- panions, at least had pined for them as much as it was possible for ono of his light and gay tempera- ment to do. The clubs, the theatres, Ranelagh or Vauxhall Gardens,- the fashionable crowds all these were as the breath of life to him. He was the true product of an artificial age, and trifles filled his world. In a week he had almost forgotten his visit to Seaton Callerley, and had quite got over the shock to his vanity which Bell's indifference had produced. As he sat in Lady Ormskirk's pretty drawing-room in Queen Anne Square, Bloomsbury, he appeared perfectly at home, and perfectly happy. With the consummate impudence that was a part of his nature he, so soon as he had made his peace with the fair proprietress of the place, walked round, commenting on the various chang.es that had taken place in the arrangement of the room during his absence; criticising Lady ()rms.. kirk's latest caprice in the way of dragon china or jewelled bon-bon box; teasing, Macaroni, her dog; giving advice as to the proper light for cer- tain pictures to be hung in, in fact, playing his original role of spoiled favourite. He ignored any unpleasantness in the past; took it for granted that she was charmed to see him again, and by his coolness and his assurance bridged over what might otherwise have been an exceedingly awkward meeting. The pretty widow seemed quite contented with this state of things. "Ah yes, my dear Lady Ormskirk, there is no place, after all, like London !" said Teddy, en- thusiastically, "a trip such as you take in the autumn, to Bath or Tunbridge Wells, may be advisable to recruit, and to drink the waters, after the fatigues of the season; but the eountry, the genuine country, you cannot form any con- ception of what it is like. The roughness, the deprivation of the most ordinary comforts and of all the elegancies which have become from force of habit necessaries. 'Pon my soul, Ph.ilhis, Ido not , know how I have survived the ordeal !" - .

"And yet Silvia hints that you managed to amuse yourself exceedingly well amongst the rustics. Oh, Teddy, you provoking boy, it is too humiliating to have to confess that it has been dreadfully dull without you. I have had the spleen, the megrims, the vapotu.s, and all the other evils that feminine flesh is prone to, since you went away. Having no one to scold or look ifter has, I verily believe, had a bad effect upon my spirits !" "I expected as much," responded Mr. Wynne, calmly, you acknowledge then that I have a beneficial influenceoafter all, though it remained to be proven by my absence. An antidote to the spleen is worth having, even in my shape, is it not ?" .
"Why did you stay 342 long 1 I never meant to

keep up my displeasure for ne-arly a year, although you certainly behaved shamefully to that poor Miss Scraggins, and caused a breach between us which will never be healed." " Indeed ! Do not expect me to say that I am sorry, my dear lady. You see I hope to be with you a great deal now! and really, that angular form, with its accentuated elbows stuck out be- hind like the limbs of a grasshopper, and its pock-marked nose, would be too terrible to con- template as an accessory in an interior graced with so charming and so opposite a principal figure as Lady Ormskirk." " Now, Teddy, no flattery !" laughed the lively widow, in no ways displeased, however, With the compliment. She was conscious of looking her best in a flowered satin gown, with orange ribbons and point lace copied from one with which a certain actress had bewitched the town in Goldsmith's

_ comedy "She Stoops to Conquer," at that time. Lady Ormskirk was only four years the senior of her young relative, a seniority giving her a ma- ternal jurigdiction over his actions and the de- lightful privilege of scolding and petting him al- ternately; but a seniority which did not alto- gether preclude- certain passages of a playfully coquettish nature, liable to the charge of flirtation from a spectator's point of view. "So you . really missed me, dear?" asked the little man in a soft caressing voice, not without

charm to his listener. When Teddy chose to be nice, no one had more winning ways; and Lady Ormskirk often con- fessed this, with a sigh of regret that such pleas- ant traits should be wasted over her dear scape-

grace. "Missed you? Have I not indeed ?" mused the lady, playing with the ears of her toy spaniel, Macaroni, who resented the liberty with a growl, after the manner of spoilt favourites. "Then why, dear Phillis, why on earth did you send me away, or at least why did you with- draw the light of your smile, so that the world grew too cold and dark for your humble adorer !" "Humble adorer, indeed!. This is the first time I have heard you lay claim to that title, Teddy I" broke in the widow, in a quick and yet a nervous manner, which amused 'Teddy immensely, be- cause he read it so easily. "Not at all," lie retorted, " you have known it perfectly well for a long time past. Now tell me, would you not have been frightfully jealous and disgusted if I had gone in for wealth and boni- ness in the person of Miss Letitia Scragg,ins ?" "It would have been a good match in a worldly sense," murmured Lady Ormskirk. "That is no answer! Phillis, put that wretched little cur down immediately, or I shall be temp- ted to throw it out of the window; you have never looked at me once, since rbegan to talk to, you seriously, and you know how I admire those black orbs of yours, excepting only when they scorch me up with their displeasure. By the way, you black eyed women have the devil's own tem- pers 9 • there, excuse me, Phillis—so they tell me. Is that statement true, dear coz. ? And supposing I, whom with all faults you profess to care for and to miss when absent—suppose I should fancy that in a black-eyed beauty I had found the woman who would suit me best and make the happiness of my life, would you honestly advise me to marry her, and risk the temper ?" Then at last the dark eyes referred to were raised to his, and though they were by way of being angry, Teddy gleaned from them nothing but encouragement. "Really Teddy, you are too absurd! I like your impudence !" " Exactly! Then do not you think it would be advisable to secure that same impudence to your- self for evermore, my pretty boz ? Come, Phillis, be honest, and confess that you and I suit each other to perfection; confess that there is more fun in quarrelling with me than in sentimental- ising with the rest of your adorers—confess that, the world is a blank without me, and that you would rather marry me yourself than allow any- one else to do so !" "You seem to take it for granted that I am in love with you ! I do declare that you are the most conceited young man it has ever been my luck to meet," said Lady Ormskirk, with a flash

of her old spirit. "My dear Phiflis, philosophy has taught me one thing at least, namely, that if one does not appreciate one's own good qualities, it is quite certain that no one else will do so. But all this is beside the question. Since you want humbug— after the manner of your sex, to whom I was fool- ish enough to hold you superior—here goes; and 'pon my soul I shall try to pitch it strong, making you answerable for the lies needed to win you. At lovers' perjuries they say Jove laughs, which will certainly keep that great Olympian continually on the broad grin, a state of affairs not quite com- patible with his god-like dignity. However, that is neither here nor there ! Lady Ormskirk, fairest and sweetest of women, behold on bended knees before you, your humble and despairing lover, who begs that at least you will deign to , answer him kindly—after the dictates of your own fine and generous nature—and if you must needs refuse him, do it so as at least to hurt his vanity in as slight degree as possible! He is all too conscious of his own unworthiness, but even angels stoop to pity sometimes and— "Oh stop, Teddy, do stop, you silly fantastic 4oy, or I shall have to close my ears," and suit- ing the action to the word, the merry widow pre- tended to cover them. But Teddy was full of resources. He kept up a show of dumb play, knelt and kissed the hem of her skirt; pretended to weep piteously; and altogether behaved in such a ridiculous fashion that Macaroni—evidently under the impression that mischief to his mistress was intended—frisked round him in a circle bark- ing and yelping vigorously. The scene was so ludicrous that Lady Ormskirk subsided into the depths of a chair, and peals of silvery laughter rang out from her pretty lips, adding to the , con- fusion and general hubbub. "Now, now, my dear Phillis, you really must not give way to these hysterical emotions ! ' said Teddy rising, and, carefully, dusting the knees of his silk stockings; after which he perched himself upon the arm of Lady Ormskirk's chair and with a huge fan of ostrich feathers commenced fanning her quickly, and uttering soothing little speeches as to a petted child, until the poor lady scarce knew whether to box his ears or to laugh more loudly than ever. Then at last, when she 'grew calmer, Teddy asked with preternatural gravity for an answer to his question. "But it is so ridiculous! I should be the laughing stock of the fashionable world, the talk of the town! You do not mean it seriously, Teddy ?" Teddy had by this time managed to insinuate his arm around her plump waist, and for answer he kissed her rosy mouth. "A fig for the fashionable world, and another for the talk of the town ! You will not keep me waiting long, dear one ?" - Lady Ormskirk's laughing eyes were very soft and melting now. She had really been in love will). Teddy all along, as the rogue had very shrewdly guessed; only the seeming absurdity of the passion, and his apparent indifference had pre- vented her acknowledging it, even to herself. - "Was ever woman in this fashion won ?" she asked, half in scorn of her own weakness. "I am older than you, Teddy, and you will soon tire of me !" "Of such infinite variety as Lady Ormskirk possesses, who could tire? My dear Phillis, that is why you will suit me so admirably. You are half a dozen women in one. Every mood and every caprice reveals some fresh charm. I shall be the most devoted of husbands, I can assure you 1" " Ah me, that seems too much to ask, too good to be true! But since you have guessed that I care for you, I suppose there is small use in pro- testing against this state of things. I must e'en close my eyes to your shortcomings and my ears to other people's tales. Teddy, be true to me, dear, and I will make you a good and loving wife !" Once again Teddy kissed her. "I will be true," he promised, and of a certainty he kept the vow better than most men keep those they take at the altar. "You will expect me to minister to your vanity and think you irresistible ?" said Phillis mis- chievously. "Nay, you have proved that most unmistake- ably b_y loving me," retorted her lover at once. "Lady Ormskirk would never have cared for an unattractive person, so has certainly justified my good opinion of myself! And then you know, dear, you will never be bored, and that is a great deal to look forward to, is it not ?" Lady. Ormskirk assented laughingly, and the engagement was sealed by another kiss. After all, there was no manner of doubt that they suited each other admirably. Silvia was intensely amused when she heard of the approaching mar- riage. But she was glad of it also. If any one on earth could manage to keep Teddy in order, it would undoubtedly be Phillis Ormskirk. So Teddy was consoled and his wings were slipped by inatsimony, tEe made as ixood a hm:
bafid as he had proinised d Licif Orinskfric escaped boredom.

div.head: PLUCKY AND CLEVER CAPTURE.
div.p: A PLUCKY AND CLEVER CAPTURE.

The only prisoner made by the English Reserve at Waterloo was a French general, whose capture was due to the cool head and stout heart of a young brigade-major anxious for an adventure. During the battle several regiments of cavalry and infantry were kept in reserve under a heavy fire from the French guns. Great was.the havoc, and neither men nor horses relished the passive attitude to which they were condemned. While a group of young officers in front of the left wing of the re- serve were discussing the situation, their attention was attracted to a French general and his staff, all on horseback, who were looking through their glasses at the Englishmen. One of the group was Captain Halkett, a young brigade-major, mounted on a thoroughbred. Suddenly he exalaimed, "I'll lay anyone £5 that I will bring that French general over here dead or alive. Who'll take my bet ?" "Done—done—done" shouted several officers. The captain examined his saddle-girths and his pistols. Then shouting" Good-bye," and putting spurs to his horse he dashed at a furious pace across the plain between the British and the French lines. His comrades followed him with their glasses,not speak- ing a word. The Frenchmen opposite seemed puz- zled. Believing that the Englishman's • horse had bolted and that the rider had lost control over him, they opened their ranks to let the runaway through. Halkett steered his steed so as to graze the mounted general on the right side. At that in- stant he put his arm around the Frenchman's waist, lifted him bodily out of the saddle, and throwing him over his own horse's neck, turned sharp and made for the English lines. When the general's staff realised the meaning of the bold rider they dashed after him. But he had a good start, and not a Frenchman dared to fire for fear of hitting the general. Half a squad of English Dragoons, seeing Halkett chased by a dozen French officers, charged them. They opened their ranks to let Halkett through, closed them up again the moment he was in the rear, and then forced the Frenchmen to turn swiftly and seek shelter under their own guns. Amidst the maddest cheering, Halkett stopped in front of the British lines with the general half dead, but securely clasped in his strong arms. He jumped from his horse, apologised to his prisoner for the unceremonious way in which he had been handled, and, in reply tc the congratulations of his comrades, said simply, "Praise my horse, not me." The cap- tured general was treated with the utmost cour- tesy; horses and servants were placed at his dis- posal, and he was sent under esoort to Brussels.— "Twixt Old Times and New." A SPENDTHRIFT ELECTION.

There was no chance of poor men getting to Par- liament in the olden days. In the last century, fortunes were sometimes staked upon a single com- bat. It is stated that the two great contests for Hampskire in 1790 and 1806 cost the Ministerial candidates £25,000 apiece on each occasion, while their opponents' expenses were proportionately. large. At the tamous election in Northampton in 1768 the opponents were the Earls of Halifax, Northampton, and Spencer, and the candidates they pitted against each other were Sir George Osborne, Sir George Bridges Rodney, and the Hon. Thomas Howe. Of this contest Mr. Grego writes as follows in his "History of Parliamentary Elections":—The can- didates were of small account in the conflict; their patrons bore the brunt, of the battle. The canvas- sing commenced long before the polling : this was extended over 14 days. . . . According to the poll book the legitimate number of electors, some 930, was exceeded by 288, but c(,)nfusion of persons , is accounted for by the promiscuous hospitalities of three noble mansions being at the mercy of the crowd for weeks. . . . . During the six weeks the scrutiny lasted 60 covers were daily spread at Spencer House, St. James's, for those concerned in the case. The results were no less eccentric: the number of votes being finally found equal, the election Was referred to chance and decided by a toss, which Lord Spencer won, and nominated a man out in India. The cost of this escapade then had to be counted. It is said Lord Spencer ex- pended £lOO,OOO, and his antagonists are credited with having wasted £150,000 each. . . . Earl Spencer came off lightest,and appears to have been in no way involved; Lord Halifax was ruined ; Lord Northampton cut down his trees, sold his furniture at Compton Winyates, went abroad for the rest of his days, and died in Switzerland.

div.head: "CHARMS OF VAGRANCY."
div.p: THE "CHARMS OF VAGRANCY."

At the meeting of the Warrington Board of Guar- diens, last week, a brief but interesting discussion arose on the ways of the vagrant. The Chairman (Mr. R. Heaton) mentioned that he had attended the meeting of the North-Western Poor Law Confer- ence at which one of the subjects of discussion was that of vagrancy. He added that a good deal had been said and done with vagrancy. The mild system had been tried and the hard system had been tried, and now they were going to try some other system. Still the number of vagrants seemed to go on increasing. flie Clerk (Mr. J. C. Sutton) said that when a person had once acquired a taste for the charms of vagrancy he rarely lost it. He had heard lately of an elderly man of some intelligence turning into a grocer's shop in Warrington to beg a piece of string. The shopkeeper said to him, "Why don't you look out for some work? " Work! "the tramp replied "do you remember the Queen's visit to Manches- ter?" The shopkeeper said he did, and the man then added—" Until then I worked, but I went to see the Queen and the Royal Family at Manchester and I have never worked since. I have been on the road ever since, but like everything else it is coming to nothing now.' The Clerk further remarked that when the public ceased to put their hands in their pockets vagrancy would cease, but not till then. In illustration of this he mentioned that at a certain point there were two roads leading to London of about equal distance, but on me of them a charitable gentleman lived who made a point of giving every tramp who called a drink of beer and some bread and cheese, and as a consequence of this all the tramps went by this road, and there wasn't one on the other. The Chairman said that he had known at least ten instant!es of men who worked till the time of the cotton famine an'd were good hands in the mills, but who from that time to this had done nothing but travel the country as beggars. He met one of them only the other day, and, when asked if he was hard up, the man replied that he was not—be had just been at Southport and by means of the "dying dodge "had raised about .C 2.
ALLEGED ABDUCTION AT ST. HELENS.

A young married gipsy named Nathan Boswell, was brought before Dr. Twyford and Aid. Bishop at St. Helens, on Monday, and charged with having abducted Ann Nora Boswell, daughter of Phcemx Boswell, the head of a tribe of gipsies who have been camping in Dunriding-lane, the girl being, as stated in the information, under the age of eighteen years. Chief Constable Wood stated that the father I took out a warrant on Friday. The girl had made a statement, which he handed to the magistrates. He added that he was afraid they would not be able to get a copy of the register of her birth. She had produced a certificate granted by the Manchester police showing she was nineteen years of age. Prisoner was her cousin.— The father was called, and said his complaint was that his daughter ran away with a married man, neglected her parents, and made away with the goods she took.— The Clerk : That is your complaint against your daughter, not against the prisoner.—Witness: One is as bad as the other. She was sixteen on the 29th of last April. She has had her age put wrong in her certificate. —Witness could not produce a copy of the register !,o show her age, and as the girl produced a certificate in which her age was put down as nineteen the prisoner was discharged.—The girl went away evidently well pleased with the result of the proceedings.

THE CURSE OF THE CALLERLEYS.
BY LILLIAS WASSERMAN, Author of "Some Fisher Folk," "Judith," "Where the North Wind Blows," dc., &c.

CHAPTER LL GOOD-BYES. It was a sad day for Jack Breamish when he was pronounced to he sufficiently recovered to leave Seaton Callerley, and to join his regiment. Sad in one sense, and yet he was-glad to go, glad to have something definite to do, glad to begin a new life, and do his best to forget the old one in
• active duties. His adieus were brief, as a soldier's ought to be. The last view he had of Silvia Callerley was one that haunted him with strange pathos in after
years. She was leaning against her husband, with one hand passed lovingly through his arm; while she iyitved her handkerchief to Cousin Jack, going down

the avenue. She was in safe keeping. That was well. What harm could ever reach her now that she had taken her proper place in her husband's heart? Though the pain of parting was sore, these and kindred thoughts comforted Jack, and helped him

on his solitary journey. There was, after all, no one to miss him, save perhaps little Lance; who sobbed and cried and clung about his neck, and utterley refused consola- tion ; even when it took the form of a brand new riding whip and a liver and white spaniel puppy. Poor Jack! Ile was sorry for the lad, but he was a little glad for his own sake, all the same. It would have been very sad to think that his absence made no difference to anyone. Even the _ _ .

i"(;;;-oia child is better than nothing. So Jack left the North Country with a full heart and a tear on his cheek, lie was a very Soft- hearted young fellow, but that did not prevent him from becoming a splendid soldier. There were other good-byes said in those days. As Dorothy Breamiah said in her excited mood, the, autumn was indeed passing quickly, and soon, too soon alas, would the winter, the long, bleak,
-- - , sullen, lingering winter of the North, arriie. Stormy and wild were the heavens, with flam- ing sunsets lighting up the flying squadrons of the

ski. The birds took to migrating south in immense flocks. High overhead flew the wild geese, while wild ducks, widgeon, and teal kept flying on a less elevated. level. All was hurry and excitement. Sand-pipers and gulls ran alang the sand, or skimmed close to the surface of the water. From far across the ocean came feathered visitors to pay brief visits to this rugged shore. Long ago the swallows had followed the sunshine to brighter lands. All this restlessness and motion affected Mr. Wynne's nerves, and made him think longingly of town and its distractions. Since the return of Dick Daglish he was scarcely able to get a word alone with Bell. The big man regarded his visits to the cottage with anything but a favourable eye, and took no pains to hide this fact. He was sure enough of his.sweetheart ; but there was no reason why' this little dandy should be philandering about her for ,ever, distaacting her attentiqn from its proper recipient, and sunning himself in her smiles. It mattered not that she oftener laughed at* than with ihe young gentleman. Dick had been parted from her so much that now he was jealous of her every look and word. And though Teddy was certainly much smitten with the beauty of the fisher lasi, there was on the whole more of romance than of reality about his passion. He could not exist without an object for his devotion, without someone to show off his airs and graces before, someone to dazzle and to fascin- ate. He reverted to that natural order of things which the unfortunate preponderance of the feminine sex has reversed. In primitive states it is the male creature that has to do the dazzling and the fascinating; for which reason it is gifted with the brightest plumage, the noblest form, the sweetest song. The dowdy female is the re-content to admire and to love. Teddy on his part would have been quite satisfied with the natural order of things. He admired himself so much that the shortest way to his heart was most decidedly through his vanity. Quite satisfied that is, except in one particular. No dowdy female for him! He had too highly tivated -an eye for feminine beauty to be con- tented with plainness. That Bell found more amusement in his vagaries than admiration for his personal attributes, had always been a, sore point with him. And now she seemed neither to have eyes nor ears for anyone save this stalwart, black-eyed lover of hers—confound his size, and his good looks Just at the time when Teddy was fuming and fretting under the stings of mortified vanity, came a letter from his lawyers loft arming him of some good fortune which had befalr.en him. So far as his finances were concery ed, Teddy was as tenacious of life as the p :overbial cat. When things were at their worst with him, some stroke of luck was certain to accrue' seine turn of the wheel would be sure to bring him up to the top

again. This was the ease at present. Some house pro- perty from which he had not as yet parted com- pany, simply because it was so old and dilapidated that it would fetch little or nothing in the market, and upon which even the money-lender whom Teddy affected refused to advance anything; had suddenly become valuable and had risen in the market tremendously. The site of two of these wretched hovels had been chosen for a new theatre, and through the others' a street then in process of construction, was necessary to pass. Mr. Wynne's lawyers had done their best for him, and the sum paid for the property would set him on his legs again, even after paying off all his creditors. This lucky windfall clenched Teddy's wavering determination. He must go to town himself, and at once, to complete certain business transactions. The country suddenly became exceedingly distaste- ful to him. If anything had been wanting to induce him to return to London, a little note enclosed i* a letter to Lady Callerley. would have done the deed. It was from the one woman who had always stood his friend until the last unlucky matrimonial attempt of his had Proved a failure; when she had quarrelled with him,. and forbidden him to enter her presence. This had been a decided blow to Teddy, because after his sister, Lady Ormskirk had been his refuge in affliction, his true friend and loving counsellor, and withut her hospitable house to fly to, town had become unbearable. Besides this, Phillis Ormskirk was a beauty and a hello, and to be an aeknowleked favourite of hers was a sort of passport to fashionable society. It is certain that there must have been some charm about Teddy Wynne, Tore than the first impression of him warranted people in supposing, because people did get so extremely fond of, even while they were perpetually. lauglung_at_ lirn. A fund of unfailing high spirits, good limnour, fun,, and a kind heart, make an irresistible combin-: ation, even without much common sense to back them. Scarce a week had passed after their quarrel before . Lady Ormskirk regretted her hasty mood, -and she felt ,so insufferably chill without her dear scape-grace. that had it not been for pride, and a little soreness at the thought of the readiness with which he seemed to aequicsce in his displeasure, she much inevitably have extended the olive branch. When he left town without attempting a recon- ciliation, or without saying farewell, she was bitterly disappointed, and felt inclined to accept Lady Callerley's invitation, and to follow him down to the country. Had she not been conscious of a certain little ,weakness on her own part for the culprit, a weakness for which she felt great self- contempt, she would certainly have done this. The role of mentor is not always a safe one for a woman to play towards one of the opposite sex. When months rolled on without a word from Teddy, and Silvia's letters seemed to hint that he was enjoying himself extremely well in the North Country, Lady Ormskirk felt very unhappy indeed. Even the waters of Bath, whither she went for her autumn sojourn, did not prove efficacious as those of the fabled Lethe. Her opportunity appeared now to occur, when the news of Teddy's good fortune reached her, and on the impulse of the moment she enclosed him a note of congratulation, which, woman-like, she feared was too kind, as soon as it had gone irrevocably. Hearts are caught at the rebound, they say, and it is certain that Teddy's felt wondrous soft, as he read Phillis Ormskirk's tender lines. A vision rose before him. The vision of a pretty woman, exquisitely dressed in the latest style; a woman,• who_se dark eyes should look admiringly at him, and
