div.head: iENUTSFORD .PARLIAMENTARX
div.p: iENUTSFORD .PARLIAMENTARX
SION. , LIBERAL :MEETING AT DABESBURY. On Tuesday ovening Mr. A. M.. Latham addressed ,Ipublic meeting in the Board School, Daresbury, Captain Rodger presided. There was a fair attend-

;wee. The CRAIRIEtaI, in his opening remarks, said that although the father of the present candidate had been defeated three times, the Liberal Association thought that the electorate ought to be given the chance of exer- eising a choice. (Applause.) Mr. LATIUM said that he belonged to the party which Was in favour of giving a large measure ofareform to ,I;Le agricultural labourer and fezmer. They were also In favour of giving a large measure oflocal self-govern- !tent. It was hardly proper that they should beagoverned In small matters from Westminster, or even Chester.; and in regard to the election of Poor Law Guardians, he was of opinion that the rich man should not have one !eta more than the poor man. Further, heshould like these elections to be conducted hyballot, and have "one lhan one vote:" ,He was perfectly certain that were the People given the power to geevern themselves, they Would not misuse that power. (Hear, hear.) The Liberal partpwas willing and aenious to trustthe people, and allow them to govern themselves, but the Con- servative party were unwilling to trust the people, and whenever they introduced a Bill a 'clause was usually inserted which rendered the provisions practic- ally inoperative. The Conservative members never Considered the people who sent them to the House of. Commons, but they always thought of their nsighbours —the rich men and landlords. He was of opinion that tee representative should not consider a certain class of his constituents, but should act in accordance with the wishes of thermajority of them. an regard twallotments the speaker said that the Liberal party aimed at giving the laboarer the privilege of having the same .length of notice as the farmer, who had a large holding, was entitled to. Not only did the Liberal party wish to benefit the lot of the farmer, but they wanted a better Small Holdings Act, and in this they would include not only the farmer, but those who held the smallest of allot- Ments. He would also give the Parish Councils the Management of the public footpaths. It was cften the casein rural districts that peoplepreferred to journey by the footpaths, for the scenery :was more picturesque. Several instances had come under his observation in Which the magistrates at the Quarter Sessions had closed such footpaths on the application of landlords, because no one had opposed such closing. If Parish Councils were established, attention would be paid to such Matters. The Liberal party were also pre- pared to legislate so that the farmer should have Proper security with a view of allowing farmers to work their own land profitably. so long as they did not wil- fully impoverish it. It was also manifestly unjust that When a man had lived on a farm for 64 years, on being served with notice to quit he should only be given-one- Sixth of the value of the improvements which he had effected. (Applause.) In 1875, the Tory party passed an Agricultural Holdings Act, but in this a clause was inserted empowering landlords to contract improvements out of the Act, zed, of course, every landlord availed himself of the clause. In 1883, the Liberal Government Passed an Agricalltural Holdings A-ct, and he was fain to admit that there were many mistakes in that measure, but they were due to the representation of Tory mem- bers. Mr. Gladstone was bound to accept the statement of the phalanx of Conservatives representing agricul- tural constituenees that farmers did not want a thorough- • going Agricultural Holdings Act, Nineyears had passed by since that Act was framed, and he felt convinced that farmers were beginning to see that what was contained Unit did not meet with what they required. Mr. Eger- ton, the Conservative candidate, was not likely to vote • for any reforms which might arise in this direction, and he asked the audience to return him ,(the speaker) to • Parliament as their representative, and as one who 'was likely to support reforms which were required. Speaking in regard to the "dodge of the inherent capabilities of the soil," Mr. Latham said that if the farmer was responsible for the improvement to any farm he ought to be compensated forit. Dealing with the notice which was required to be served for a clairh for improvements, the speaker considered that two months was far too long a period to serve. A system of Arbitration by official valuers was also required, and he was of opinion that the County Council or a Board of Agriculture should be appointed to appoint officers 'whose duty it would be to arbitrate between landlords " and tenant, and who should be paid a fixed salary, or by fees, the latter to be equally divided between the landlord and tenant. Continuing, he said that a tenant 'ought to have a perfect right to invest as much money ,as he wished on the land. He also contended that com- ,Pensation should be given for feeding stuffs con- -sumed by cattle and horses. Mr. Latham also advocated ,the largest Measure of free trade possible. if Protection Was introduced everything would be more -expensive. {Applause.) Mr. BURGESS, who was one of the audience, said that farmers preferred to have agreements in preference to an -Agricultural Hddings Act. Further, if the system which -Mr. Latham advocated were adopted, the land would be -eaten out. Mr. LATHAM, in reply, said that the system which he had advocated had been embodied in his father's agree- 'tnent with his tenants. He came into his property in 1856, and sold it in 1888. It was then •in a far better condition than when he came into possession. That did Cot look as if the land had been eaten out. In regard to agreements, it was possible that the farmers in Dares- bury had good landlords, but there were bad landlords, ,and it was in this direction that the Liberals wished to legislate. He asked the farmers to think or those who were groaning under the yoke of bad landlords. Mr. JENKINS said that Mr. Latham in his address said that he would encourage farmers in all possible ways to ,Inake the best use of the land, and to increase wherever he could the yielcl per acre. He wished Mr. Latham would explain more fully what he meant by the expres- sion. Mr. LATHAM said he would give the farmer full security 'or the capital which he had invested on the land. ..He would also wish to have enacted the same penalties on manure manufacturers' for adulterating manure as the Illan who watered milk Mr. Jexxins : Owing to pressure of circumstances iiamiy landlords are unable to do what they would like .or their tenants. Through agricultural depression ten, 414 ts SnlKe often unable to farm their land 0 obtain, the
oalfmelessrers
(r Ii

results they would like. Would you approve of such a development of our agricultural bureau, which is r, comparatively new thing, and which I would remi'Jd you is an institution commenced by the Conserva:sive Government? Would you support the loan of such a reasonable amount of money as would relieve brAli land- lord and tenant from a possible dilemma of that kind, and thus encourage the tenant by means of additional capital, lent by the Government at a small rate of inter- est, to do better with his farm Mr. LATHAM : The remedy for what you say would be to give something like what was passed for Ireland —an Ashbourne Act, to enable the tenant to purchase his holding. The credit of the Cheshire farmer was pledged so that the Irish tenant farmer should buy his holding. By the system the rent was reduced for 49 years, and at the end of that time the holding became his property. The result was the Irish farmer, having less rent to pay, was able to send stuff te the English markets, and thus compete with the English farmer, who supplied the meney to do this thing. He would be perfectly willing, if it could be done, to support a measure of the kind referred to, to enible the English tenant farmer to buy his bolding. If it was good for the Irish tenant farmer to buy his lad, he did not see why the Conservative party should re2use it to the Eng- lish farmer. (Applause-) A vote of thanks was tendered to the Chairman for presiding, and the meeting then en&ed. MOORE. 'Mr. LATRAII addressed a public meeting at Moore the same evening. There was a fait attendance, and Cap- tain Rodger again presided, Mr. LiVrEIAM dealt with the 3me Rule question, and said that if the English wished to rule themselves the Trishought to be entitled to rile themselves. (Applause.) It had been asseetedthat if Eorne Rule was granted the 'Catholics would oppress the !Protestant minority. That argument was absurd. Atthe present time, in Catholic [ districts, Protestants were net persecuted. The con- verse was the casein Ulster. There the Corporation paid £B,ooo,per annum for wages, but of this amount -slily £3OO was paid to °Catholics. It was extremely difficult for a Catholic to,obtain a situation in the employ Of the Corporation. It had been stated that Ulster wonld rebel in the event of the granting of Home Role. That statement would not held water. The majority of the membersin Ulster were in favour of Home Rule, and .if the Belfast votes were deducted. there would be a large majority of Ulster people in favour of Home Rule. He did not think it right that a minority should govern Ireland. (Cheers.) Miss Derron, inothe course of an excellent speech, moved the adoption of the following resolution::—:+4 That this meeting considers Mr. Latham a fit and proper person to represent this division, and pledges itself to use its best endeavours to return him to Parliament." The resolution was seconded by Mr. tAtAcu, and sup- ported by Mr. PRICE, Warrington, secretary of the Navvies' Union. In supporting the adoption of the resolution, Mr. Price referred to the meeting of the War- rington Church Society, which was held on Monday evening, and said that one of the speakers had asserted that the Church of-England in Wales was as active as the Church of England. He denied that, and he was only sorry that he was not present at the meeting. It was not fair that tithes should be devoted to the mainten- ance of a church which was not attended by the people. En submitted that some of the tithes should be devoted to the denominations the services of which were well attended. The resolution was carried unanimously.' LIBERAL MEETING AT WHITLEY. A meeting in support of Mr. A. M. Latham, the Libe- ral candidate for the Knutsford Division of Cheshire,was held last evening week, in the Board School, Whitley. Mr. Charles Edward Rumney presided, and on the plat- form were—Captain Rodger, Preston Brook.; Mr. Bro- derick, Wilmslow ; Mr. Brenerd, Mr. Fairfax, Sec. The candidate, being introduced by the chairman, addressed the meeting at some length, after which Mr. Brenerd spoke on the Home Rule question. The resolution in support of Mr. Latham's candidature was put to the meeting by Captain Rodger, and seconded by Mr.,Bro- derick. The resolution was tarried unanimously, those against and these who did not wish to show their politics leaving the room. PRESTON BROOK. A Liberal meeting was held in the Preston Brook Schoolroom, on Saturday evening, in supportof .Mr. Latham, the Liberal candidate for the Knutsford :Divi- sion. There was a good attendance, and the chair was occupied by Captain Rodger. The Chairman said it would not be required of him to state the reason of their coming there that night. He considered that that meeting consisted of Liberals who would support a man who was descended from a well-known -Liberal who at one time contested that division. They sincerely trusted that they would shortly be able to .return his son, who would carry out the ideas that his father promulgated: (Hear, hear.) Mr. Latham then gave an effective ad- dress on political questions. In the course of it he said he thought that if the landowners pulled down cottages, [ then they should build new ones in their places, and proper ones, too. There were cottages with,,a, family of seven or eight, and only two bedrooms. .(Shame.) Some of the landlords at one time made their tenants vote according to them. But by the present system of a secret ballot, everyone could vote according to his own censcience.—Mr. LUKE Joszs said that he had great pleasure in moving the following resolution: "That this meeting considers Mr. Latham a fit and proper person to represent the Knutsford division, and pledges itself to use its best endeavours to return him."—Mr- W. SPEED seconded the proposition.—ln reply to questions, Mr. LATHAM said that he and Mr. Brunner were of the same mind with regard to Trades• Unionism. He had thorough sympathy with all Trades Unionists. (Applause.) With regard to the hours of labour, he pledged himselt to vote for an eight-hours day far miners, but he would leave it to themselves to settle with regard to other trades. (Applause.) He would vote for a direct veto with regard to publiahouses, but as to the closing on Sunday he also left that to themselves. (Applause.) As to the pension scheme, he thought that they could not improve upon their friendly societies. He would vote for free education entirely. (Applause.) The resolution was then put to the meeting, and carried without a dissentient.

HATTON. A Liberal meeting was held at the Hatton School-room, on Monday evening in support ofthe candidature of Mr. A. L. Latham, the candidate ter the ,Knutsford 'Division. There was a good attendance, and the chair was occu- pied by Mr. J. Done, in the absence of Captain ttodger.— Mr. LATHAM said that the chairrnan had referred in the kindest possible manner to his late father. He could never hope to be as far advanced in politics as he was. lie trusted that they would not find in him any bad 1 political views. He thought they would agree with him that the Liberal party had done more for the working- man than the Conservatives. He thought that he could speak with experience on the farmers' and labourers' questions, as for a certain portion of his life he had lived on a large farm, and had mingled with those workmen upon it. He could tell them a thing ‘which had hap- pened not a thousand miles from Hatton. A certain farmer had had a farm for 64 years. He had tilled ;it and invested all his money in it, and then passed it to his son, who attended to it for 19 years. But the old landlord died, and his son on looking over his tenant's well-kept land, thought the tenant could afford, to pay a higher rent for it. He went to the tenant and, asked for a higher rent, but he replied that the land had been brought to its present state of efficiency by his, money and work. However, he eventually agreed to pay a higher rent,:and the landlord thereupon requested him to give him a written agreement. The tenant refused to do this, and he was turned off his farm. He (the speaker) considered that the tenant had a perfect right in refusing to sign an agreement. This was a thing that he would strive to put a stop to. He would advoc- ate a new act, whichewould embody some of the best clauses in the present Act and leave out the worst. (Applause.)—A vote of thanks having been passed to the Chairman, the meeting was brought to a close. '

MEETING Al' STRETTON. On Thursday evening a meeting in support of the can- didature of Mr. Latham, for the Knutsford Division was held in the National Schools, Stretton. Captain Rodger presided, and there was a moderate attendance, amongst those present being Mrs. LathanarMr. Roger Bate, C.C., and Mr. J. Darbyshire. The CHAIRMAN said he expected about all the land- lords of Cheshire would be at the large meeting at North- wich that night,and probably all of them had subscribed to the testimonial that was being given to Mr. Smith- Barry. What that testimonial was for he could not tell, because he did not suppose there was one man present who called himself an Englishman who would think a testimonial due to a man, who, there could not be a doubt, _went out of his way to turn cotta,gers, not to speak of farmers, out of their holdings. There could not be the smallest doubt that Mr. Smith-Barry went out of his avas. to do that. The fact of the testimonial being presented, should make Liberals all the more de- termined to uphold a man like Mr. Latham who was dead against any such tyranny and all such wrong-doing. They believed, and that was the reason that Mr. Latham was before them, that all men ought to be put on the same footing. They wanted to do away with all inequality. (Hear, hear.) A wave of Liberalism seemed to be pass- ing over the country, and the Conservatives themselves seemed to have lost heart so much that they had done the injustice to arrange that the borough elections could not take place on a Saturday which was essentially the day of the working-men. (Hear, hear.) Mr. LATHAM, who was well received, speaking in favour of the people of rural districts having a more direct voice in the management of sanitary and other affairs, he alluded to an inquest that had been held at the other side of the country, and said the jury had brought in a verdict that the death of the unfprtunate people was due to some irritant poison, and the coroner —a man for whom he had the greatest respect and who would not speak before he had thoroughly studied the matter—said he had not the slightest doubt that death was due to drinking impure water. He (Mr. Latham) said it was a shame that cottager s of England, and of Cheshire in particular, should be obliged to drink water which contained such im- purities as would cause their death. He belonged to the party that wished to give the people power to manage their own affairs, and among other things to look after the water that IWAS supplied to their dwelliogs, which

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JUNE 25, 1892
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JUNE 25, 1892

wits, perhaps, of even greater importance than good dwellings. (Hear, hear.) Speaking of the present member for the division, Mr. Latham pointed out that he had voted against the second reading of the Bill to give them small holdings, and that he voted against elections of Guardians being by ballot. If there was one thing that was a cruel sham it was the, present method of voting for 'Guardians. It was impossible for a workingman to give his vete as he would wish, be- cause he knew It would be known how he had given that vote, and that it was possible if he gave that vote against the wishes of his landlord he might lose his employment or his house. The Liberal party gave them the Ballot Act, and the Conservatives said they were not against it, • yet if they were not afraid of it why did they say the election of guar- dians should not be by ballot? (Hear, hear.) He was in favour of farmers getting the full value of their un- exhaustedimprovements on leaving their holdings, and was against landlords having the rower to turn a tenant out because, forsodth, he might differ from the land- lord in politicos, or because he went to chapel instead of to the church to Whickthe landlord belonged. He had heard‘rumours of a case which occurred in Cheahire where a tenant farmer had 'oeen expected to go out with theyeornany and because he refused he had to quit his bolding. (Hear., hear.) Mr. Roger Late, C.C., said he had had the honour ,of standing en the same platform as the present candidates' father, and he believed that in the late Mr. 'Latham they had one of the foremost political minds that that county ever possessed. Liberalism was greatly indebted to-the late Mr. latham for its advocacy at a period when Liberalism was not so highly thought of as it is now. He was pleased that the son was standing for that constituency, and he believed the address they had listened to auguredwell for the future.' il3 thought. they might well believe that Mr. Latham would wadr in the footsteps of his 'father and vote for measures for the well-being of thegreatest number. (Hear, hear.) Mr. Bate then in an interesting address commented up- on the, benefits that had been derived from Liberal legis- lation during the past 40 years, and upon the opposition that bud been made to reforms by Conservative repre- sentatives of Cheshire. In answer to Mr. John Derbyshire, Mr. Latham after- wards mentioned some particulars in which the Agricul- tural Holdings Act might be amended. Mr. Derbyshire also asked the candidate if he was in favour of making the laws of the laud accord as much as possible wit& the law of God. Mr. Latham replied that he should like to see sill legislations accord with the law of God. A-vote of thanks to the chairman brought themeeting to aclose.

THE NEWTON DIVISION. MR. NEILL'S CANDIDATURE. :An important meeting in connection with the Liberal campaign in the Newton division was held in the Primitive Methodist Schoolroom, Earles- town, on Saturday evening. There was:a large at- tendance of workers from ell parts of the consti- tuency. Mr. G. W. Rawlins presided, supported by Mr. W. Neill (the candidate), Mr. W. Mather, M.P., Mr. S. Taylor, and other gentlemen. The Chairman said they were met as workers in pre- paration for the coming figlat, and Mr. Mather had been kind enough to come down to encourage them in their work. Very encouraging weports were being received from nearly every part of the division, because it was recognised that Mr. Neill, their candidate, well repre- sented a cause which war now the popular cause in the country, and the belief was growing stronger and stronger in the division that by combined efforts and energy the Liberals. would not only be able to win the , seat but would return Mr. Neill by such a majority as would cause the Conservatives to hesitate before they would attempt te again bring Mr. Legh forward. (Ap- plause.) Mr. Neill, who had a .flottering reception, said he would not occupy much of their time, as Mr. Mather, M.P., who, as President of the Lancashire Liberal Feder- ation Council took such a deep interest in that consti- tuency and in every other-constituency in Lancashire, had kindly come down to address them. When he (Mr. Neill) came to that division he told them that if the seat could be won by hard work on his part it would be won, and he believed when the contest was over no one would be able to say that he had gone back upon his word. (Hear, hear.) ZPersonally it was a small matter to him —a matter of some tittle sacrifice—the .fighting of that division, but to them as Liberals it was a very great matter, and if they only.drew their whole hearts into the work the seat would be won for the great Liberal cause. The Liberal leaders might have thought that Newton division was .hopelessly sunk in Toryism and ignorance ; but at the .fight which was close at hand they were going to alter that impression. (Applause.) Mr. Mather, M.P., who was loudly cheered on rising, commenced by congratulating the Liberals of that division on their excellent candidate and chairman. Their organisation—accomplished during the last few weeks—was eo satisfactory that it was quite unneces- sary for an outsider like him to come amongst them.— (Laughter.) Every man present was himself a leader, if that he could lead his fellow-men ; and he believed they were all determined to prove that fact by a success- ful issue of the -coming contest.---(l.pplause.) The Federal Council, of which he happened to be chairman, had thoroughly gone into the matter, and they counted a certain victory in the Newton division.4--(Loud ap- plause.) The Tories had attacked seats where large Liberal majorities had been attained at previous elections, and Liberals were now attacking constitu- encies in the great county of Lancashire and else- where which had been held by Tories by majorities of 1,200, 1,600, 2,000, and even 3,000. These the Federal Council counted on winning back again to the Liberal cause, and returning candidates like Mr. Neill to the House of Commons—men who were pledged to carry out the Liberal reforms for which the country was waiting. In comparing the Newton division with many others, he considered they were in a very happy state. It was true the Liberals had not been victorious there in previous contests, but even in. 18,86 the majority against them was only'about 700, since which time many things had hap- pened, and he did•not remember a time when he could look forward with-such hope to the-earnest devotion of the Liberal party as at the present. (Applause.) All that could possibly be-urged against Home Rule had now I been said, and the-Liberal party were now confident as ' , to the result of the determined struggle they were about to enter upon. Let -them view the opposition in its latest phase. (Laughter.) Only the previous day the long-promised great Ulster Convention was held,. and when one looked at the result and remembered the words that had been used during the last year or two—when they remembered the great promises as to what Ulster was going to do and when they thought of so much that had been said about the foul designs Mr. Gladstone had upon the integrity of the British Empire—(laughter),— when they remembered all this, and saw how innocently the great Convention had ended, they could only express surprise at the mistaken notions of the Protestants of Ulster. Having read all the speeches delivered at the Convention, and the principal leading articles thereon, he had come through the ordeal more than ever satisfied with the position he had long since taken up with regard to Home Rule, and more than ever satisfied with the righteous cause Mr. Gladstone. had taken up on behalf of that country. (Applause.) nnder Home Rule, which he (Mr. Mather) preferred to

call" a scheme for the better government of Ireland," 1 there was -nething upon which the Ulster Convention were justified in saying that in future there was not to be one flag and one throne.—(llear, hear.) A Parlia- ment in Dublin would be subservient to the Imperial Parliament, it would be created by the Imperial Parlia- ment, and could be ended ley it; and as it could both create and annihilate, what more supreme power could be wanted ?--(Cheers.)—Under Mr. Gladstone's guidance Home Rule would be thoroughly and thoughtfully planned at Westminster, and when it was given to Ireland it wetuld be subject to its being taken away again if it was found that it was being used either unjustly against the people or against the interests of the Imperiml Parliament or the British Empire. He felt certain that the sensible people of Ulster would find that it was conceived in the interests of all, for the benefit of all, and !C.or the real benefit of Ireland ; and if it was accepted in such a spirit he had hopes that some of them mightyetlive to hear of another Ulster Convention, vOhen they would meet to celebrate the establishment of a local'. government which had done much for the peace and prosperity of the people of that nation. (Loud applause.) Upon the motion of Mr. Neill, seconded by Mr. S. Taylor (Eccieston), a hearty vote of thanks was accorded to Mr. Mather for his address. Mr. Mather briefly replied, and the proceedings, which were characterised with the utmost enthusiasm through- out, then terminated, Mr. Neill (the Liberal candidatc) took up his residence in the Newton division on Monday, and will apply him- self continuously to the campaign until the close.
OPEN AIR MEETING AT BARLESTOWN.

A large and enthusiastic meeting in support o. the candidature of Mr. Neill, was held on the market ground, on Wednesday evening. Mr. E. T. Evans presided, and he was supported on the plat- form by Mr. W. Neill, Mr. 3. A. Duncan, M.P. for Barrow, Mr. G. W. Rawlins, and others. The CHAIRMAN said he was glad to see so many present, as is was a sign of reviving life to the Liberal party. He thought they had been rather sleepy of late, but he was of opinion their oppo- nents would find out that they were awakening, and that they should be like the giant "refreshed." (Hear, hear.) He thought he might tell Mr. Neill that they were not arm-chair politicians, they were all ready to work hard any time, and he believed they had got an excellent candidate in Mr. Neill, and that he meant to win. (Hear, hear, and applause.) He de- served ts win, and he believed they would win all along the line, and would not stoop to any mean tricks to do so. (Hear, hear.) He believed the other side were quaking in their shoes, and had been doing so for some time, or why should the Prime Minister stoop so low, to avoid defeat,as to raise before the peeple of this country the bogey of religious intolerance—(hear. hear)—and class hatred among the people of Ulster? It was too late in this 19th century for that sort of thing to have any weight with the people of this country, and he hoped they in that division would do all in their power to relieve Lord Salisbury of the Premiership in the next Parliampnt, by returning Mr. Neill, who was pledged to support and place in power the good and grand Old Man. (Applause.) Mr. W. DAVIES then proposed "that this meeting expresses its entire faith in the policy of Mr. Gladstone for the better Government of Ireland ; its approval of the reforms proposed it the Newcastle programme, and that it pledges itself to use every legitimate means to return Mr. Neill to the next Parliament as the Liberal member for the Newton division." The Conservatives, he said were going about sending out leaflets, saying they had given the people free education, but he asked those who had children, if they had free education. (" No.") The bill was carried lof a majority of Liberals, and he believed their present member, Mr. Legh, voted against it. If they lived a few years longer, they would have the Tories going about saying they had passed Home Rule. (Langhter.) He asked the miners' in that part, if they could conscientiously support Mr. Legh. It appeared he was going to represent the mine owners, and not the miners. They, as working-men, wanted someone to represent them, and he maintained if they carried out that resolution, and returned Mr. Neill to Parliament they would have a man of that description. (Applause.) Mr. J. Cordingly seconded the resolution, and Mr. J. A. Duncan, M. P. for Barrow speaking in sup- port of it said they were not fighting anywhere in this election upon grounds of personal criticism; they were fighting upon grounds of everlasting principle. Their resolution commenced by asking their support at the poll, in the first place for their grand old leader, and in the second place for the policy, he represents. (Hear, hear.) It was not merely a name they were advocating, but were asking their support for Mr. Gladstone because. he truly represented the policy of the party. The Con- servatives promise, if they are returned to power, which he hoped they would not be, to introduce their Irish Local Gp,,ernment Bill, which he called the brand of National inferiority. The Conservative Government knew very well that whatever might happen in the Newton Division of Lancashire at any rate all through the country it was certain that the result would be a large majority in favour of Home Rule. (Hear, hear.) The Home Rule scheme for Ireland, was just as much a democratic measure as one man one vote of the New- castle programme. One man one vote was a reform that he had twice, in the House of Commons had an op- portunity of voting for, and had they only seen the division list they would have opened their eyes, as to which party was on the side of progress, and which party was dead against progress. If they had one man one vote then they had the road open to a simple form of registration of votes. If they had the abolition of the ratepaying qualifications and the reduction of resid- ence to three months, at the most, if they had a simple form by which a man could carry his vote about from one constituency to another, the difference to him in a constituency like his, would be between 2,000 and 3,000 votes, which were votes of working-men. As soon as the Irish question was settled, and a variety of other matters were disposed of and reformed, there tvould come before them a large number of social questions. some of which were classed together under the name of labour problems. These labour problems were to his mind matters of chief importance to this country in the future. How were they to reach a true decision about those questions unless they got a full expression of opinion from that class of .men whom it most affects. If they were going to come to a just decision about them, they must get hold of the real honest expression of the working-men, and this question of putting every work- ing-man on the register was of supreme importance to them. (Hear, hear.) If they worked with all their will until the polling day, they in the Newton Division would gain a v:ictory, amongst the great victories which were going to come. (Applause.) The resolution was then put and carried without dissent. Mr. NEILL, in rising to return thanks, was en- thusiastically received. He thanked them for the enthu- siastic way in which they had passed the vote of confi- dence, a vote which he hoped it would be his good for- tune to deserve, not only in the near future, but in many years spent in their service. (Applause.) He was sure many ardent Liberals had been working and doing their best to get steam up to carry the election, and if that work was kept up, he had no doubt as to the result. (Applause.) He had endeavoured to find out what policy Mr. Legh was in favour of, and to see the measures he advocates, and compare it with the

Liberal programme, of which he (the speaker) was an ardent advocate. He had seen Mr. Legh's election ad- dress, la which he said "my views upon the principal political questions of the day are well known to you," and that was all. (Laughter.) Mr. Legh's political views might be well known to, his hearers,but they were not well known to him (Mr. Legh). Speaking of the Ulster Convention, he said although he had the most serious apprehensions, he was pleased at the way the matter had passed off, be- cause it had shown him that the people of Ulster were what he always said they were, hard headed solid men of business, not fools or firebrands, not to be led astray into folly, iniquity and wickedness such as was suggested by Lord Salisbury. They had shown in the wonderful way they organised that demonstration, that they had the wonderful power of self-Government. There were no doubt some fiery utterances at that con- vention, but the net result was that the resolutions were all mere or less of a passive nature. All the Ulster con- vention had done, was to record their objection to being placed under the feet of those who ought to be their brothers, but whom they had come to regard as their enimies. If there was any fear on the part of Ulster or any desire to be separated from the rest of Ireland, and be joined to this country, although he for one should strongly object to it, still, he thought it would be a reasonable demand, if there was such fear; but Ulster had been asked over and over again to desire some scheme of their own, and be separated from the rest of Ireland, and they had always indignantly refused any such suggestion. If Home Rule was passed they would see Ulster, so far from fighting or rebelling, against the Imperial Parliament or the Parliament in Dublin, set to work like clear hard headed men as they were, to en- deavour to obtain in the local Parliament in Dublin so much of the power and administration of the country, as they could. (Hear, hear.) He asked them to make up their minds and send back Mr. Gladstone to perform this act of justice to Ireland, and with his useful reforms to endeavour to keep this country, what she has been in the past, the envy of the whole world. (Applause.) Mr. G. W. RewLins then proposed a vote of thanks to the Chairman and after its adoption the meeting sepa- rated.
THE REPRESENTATION OF WIDNES.

-- LIBERAL MEETING IN THE DRILL HALL. Last night week Widnes Drill Hall was crowded 1 to its utmost limits by an enthusiastic meeting of the supporters of Mr. H. Wade Deacon, the Liberal candidate for Widnes Division. Gostiage's band played selections of music previous to the com- mencement of the proceedings. Mr. T. S. Timmis J.P. presided and amongst those on the platform besides the candidate were, the Right Hon. H. Campbell Bannerman, M.P., very Rev. Dean Fine- gan, Rev. Father Clarke, Major Wareing, Messrs. S. K. Muspratt, IL S. Timmis, S. Deacon, Dr. O'Seeffe, S. Owen, J. Jackson, S. Sadler, Whitfield,S. Calvert, T. Sadler, A. G-ossage, H. B. Shores, (secretary.) The Chairman said the electors had a most moment- ous issue to decide at this election. It was, whether they would perm;t Mr. Gladstone to crown a long and brilliant career by giving Ireland justice and peace, or whether they would give the Tories another lease of power, so that Lord Salisbury could give them the 20 years of Coercion which he had advocated. (Cries of "no " and applause.) Is to the candidates they had on the Liberal side their good friend Mr. Deacon who had lived amongst them the whole of his life, and whose comings in and goings out were well known to them. (Applause.) Ever since early manhood he had taken an active and prominent part in the government of the town in numerous offices. (Applause.) He was besides sound in politics. On the other side was a gentleman from London and nobody knew anything about him except what he said and what his friends said—and very little they had said. (Laughter.) As to the reason why he had deserted Clapham it might be true that he had expressed a desire not to come forward again for that constituency and it was his (the Chairman's) belief that: the people cif Clapham jumped at that. (Loud laughter.) They did not want him—(renewed laughter) —and in a few weeks they in Widnes Division would tell him that they did not want him. (Applause.) Mr. Deacon, who had an enthusiastic reception, moved "That this meeting expresses confidence in the leaders of the Liberal party and believes that under their guid- ance the question of Home Rule for Ireland will be finally settled in the new Parliament." (Applause.) They in Widnes, Mr. Deacon said, would send a representative to help in carrying out this glorious Work. He believed that he would gain some votes in the outside districts, but he relied upon the men of Widnes to send him to Parliament. (Cheers.) Those was a price at which he would not have victory. He had lived amongst them all his life, and lived amongst friends,and he would dur- ing this contest leave no word of his to rankle in the heart of any man after the election was over. (Ap- plause.) He would not abuse either his opponent or his agent. (Loud applause.) He regretted that on that platform at the last Conservative meeting a gentleman made use of expressions which he should not have used considering his position. It was an instance of" We have no case so abuse your opponent's agent." (Applause.) They would have nothing of that sort on his (Mr. Dea- con's) platform; neither he nor his supporters if his in- fluence could prevent it, would descend to personal abuse. (Applause.) Mr.Oilliatt was to them a politician and his public life was open to criticism as much as his (Mr. Deacon's) public life was open to him. (Applause.) A man could not sit for six long years in Parliament with- out making some speeches, and giving.some votes with- out making some record and it was their (the Liberals) bounden duty to lay before the electors if they thought it necessary. (Applause.) Mr. Deacon then dealt with general political questions, and declared himself in favour of the extension of the Factory and Workshop Act, and of the right of workmen to combine, believing it to be in b the interest of trade that the 'combination of both em- ployers and employed should be as strong as possible. In his opinion labour ought to be directly represented in Parliament, and he strongly advocated payment of mem- bers. In conclusion he effectively exposed the fallacy of the cry that was being raised in Ireland in opposition to Home Rule. (Cheers.) Major Wareing seconded the motion, which was sup- ported by The Right Hon. Campell Bannerman, M.P., who in support of the resolution, said in a few days they wool have the opportunity ,of giving effect to their opinions at the poll. They had maintained for many years that nothwithstanding the majority against them in the Rouse of Commons, the country was with them, the Liberals. (Cheers.) They had maintained that the last election was little short of a fraud upon the people ; that the issue put before them was a false issue as it was put by those who gained the majority ; that pledges were given that were never intended to be redeemed, and that had not been redeemed ; and that the greatest misrepresentation was used as the motives and the policy of the Liberals in public affairs. The Newcastle programme was a settlement, on essentially Liberal principals, of the topics of the day and of the require- ments and circumstances of the day. (Cheers.) The first thing they sought to do was to improve the ma. chinery of the representation of the people. They were engaged in a long and continotis struggle. It was not in Ulster alone that there was a decaying privilege and a decaying ascendancy that it was thought to keep upon
trd litesteSest ERZAD

its legs when it should be knocked down, 1.1" lk ay to opp,se these privileges was not to fly at then), lgr Ii ot all to see that they were properly equipp-o and arm- ed for the contest, and they would not he pr'>, e:iv equipped and artned, they would not be able t out forward their whole power. until they had made their electoral machinery what it should be. They wanted a complete reform of the registration laws. Let them have one man one vote, and let it be recognised that the power of voting was given, not to the property a man possessed. but. to the opinions he held on public ques- tions. Let them also increase the power of a free choice of candidates by paying members of Parliment. The question of religious .equality had been practically settl- ed so far as this empire was concerned, because by their action with regard to the colonies, and by their action with regard to the Church of Ireland, they had practi- cally laid it down as a rule that it was not incumbent iupon the State to maintain a Church in connection with it under all circumstances and in all places, but that ( ach individual instance was to be judged upon its own merits. In regard to the question of the control of public houses, to that question they applied the main principle of Liberal policy, which was," Trust in the people "—(cheers)— because the foundaticn of their opinion upon that subject was that the best judges on the question of licensing—the best judges on the impor- tant question of whether a public house was or was not wanted in a particular street, were the people who lived in that street. (Cheers.) Something should be done, and on a large scale, to improve the condition of the workers in the community—of the wage-earning classes, upon whose industry depended not only on the pros- perity of the nation, and the increase of the wealth of the country, bnt the very maintenance of society itself. (Cheers.) Neither by Act of Parliment nor otherwise could they lay down any specific number of hours ap- plicable to all trades and employments, but surely the public opinion of the country, and the goo/ sense of the country. should arrive at some conclusion that should give relief to those who complained of excessive hours of labour. (Cheers.) Referring to Ireland, he asked on what possible ground could the Irish wish to be separated from the empire which they had .largely helped to make. There was no real and effective desire in Ireland for anything but a continuance of a close connection with the empire. (Cheers.) The resolution was then carried. MR. DEACON AT GARSTON.

The Reading Room, Garston, was crowded on Wednes- day evening by an enthusiastic gathering of the sup- porters of Mr. H. Wade-Deacon, the Liberal candidate. Mr. W. B. Bowring presided, and was supported by Messrs. A. P. Thomas, LL.D., T. S. Timmis, Holbrook Gaskell, jun., J. Handley, George Timmis, A. Bathgate, J. Shield, J. B. Wimble, R. Craig, T. Neil, H. B. Shores (election agent), Captain Brown, lee. The Chairman said they would be called upon to exer- cise the franchise—one of the most sacred duties that devolved upon the inhabitants of a free country. He had not a word to say against the Conservative candi- date personally. They wished that contest to be con- ducted on the most genteel and pleasant lines. (Hear, hear.) They, however,believed that the other candidate was advocating a cause that would lead to the dismem- berment of the empire. (Applause.) On the other hand, they had as their candidate a gentleman who was thoroughly in accord with the proposal to grant to Ire- land a measure of Home Rule which we had granted to our colonies, which had been proved in various countries to be a blessing, and which if granted would bring about true union and peace and happiness to that country and to this. (Applause.) Mr. Bowring criti- cised the action of the Government in so fixing the dis- solution that the work-people could not record their votes on a Saturday. In that division they had an ex- cellent candidate and a great cause, and he had not the , slightest doubt that the country generally would give a ' large majority to the greatest statesman of the cen- tury. (Applause.) Mr. Deacon, who was enthusiastically received, said that large meeting was a reply to the statement that Garston was Tory. He hoped every elector would re- cord his vote, for they had a large majority to wipe away. Mr. Gilliat had been speaking in that place, and in the course of his speech said the Liberals might be put into power if it were not f.:r foreign affairs. Well, it was true Lord Salisbury had, to his credit, forsaken the Jingo policy, but they might ask Mr. Gilliat why it was Lord Salisbury had handed over Heligoland to the Ger- mans. Mr. Gilliat also talked about what Lord Salis- bury had done fcr the army and navy, but was it not notorious that the army was not in a satisfactory con- dition? rhere had been a commission which had re- commended reforms in the army, but they had not been carried oat,nor would they until they had men they could trust at the head of affairs. (flear,hea,r.) The Irish ques- tion was the great question after all. Mr. Gilliat charged them with trying to cover up that question, but he (Mr. Deacon) would ask the electors whether he had not al- ways kept it to the forefront. (Applause.) The great is- sue at the coming election was whether they would trust Ireland with self-government, or they would go on with perpetual coercion. What was wanted was to give the Irish people more freedom. and let public opinion have its full weight. (Applause.) Mr. Deacon concluded by proposing a vote of confidence in the Liberal leaders.— Mr. W. Bathgate seconded the motion, which was sup- ported by Mr. A. P. Thomas, LL.D., of Liverpool.— The other speakers included Mr.Timmis,Captain Brown, Mr. Handley, and Mr. Craig. MR. DEACON AT DITTON. On Thursday night, Mr. H. Wade Deacon, J.P., C.C.. the Liberal candidate for the Widnes Division, held a meeting at Ditton in support of his candidature. Mr. Sadler presieled.—Mr. Deacon proposed—" That this meeting expresses its confidence in the leaders of the Liberal party,and believes that under their guidance the question of Home Rule for Ireland will be finally settled in tho new Parliament." He spoke in support of the re- solution,and alluding to the Irish Local Government Bill introduced by the Government, he said that the Govern ment never intended to pass it. Referring to the tem- perance question, he said he was strongly in favour of the direct veto and the power being given to the people to control the issuing of licenses, and he was as strongly opposed to compensation being given to publicans for the loss of their licenses. (Applause.)—The motion was seconded by Dr. O'Keeffe, supported by Mr. Hugh Farrie of Liverpool, and carried.
NEWTON-IN-MAKERiTELD TECHNICAL DAY SCHOLARSHIP. .

The report of the examiner on the examination held on the 26th, 27th, and 31st May and Ist June, at the Viaduct Institute, in connection with the above scholarship has now been received, and is to the effect that Jesse H. Harrison has been success- ful in obtaining it. The scholarship was open to pupils of either sex between the ages of 14 and 21 years, but when the examination in connection with the competition was held, Jesse Harrison was the only candidate who put in an appearance. The papers given were not of an easy nature, and in order for the , lad who is only 16 years of age to obtain the scholarship, ,he had to obtain a certain percentage of marks. The report of the examiner, who is from the Lancashire and Cheshire Union of Institutes, shows that the percentage has been exceeded and the work very well done. The fortunate scholar, is the son of Mr. Benjamin Harrison of Earle-street, Earlestown, and is at present employed as an apprentice fitter at the L. and N. W. Co.'s Wagon Works. The scholarship is of the value of £3O per annum tenable for two years, and its acceptance necessit- ates the giving up of his employment for the time being and entering some Technical School, which we under- stand it is tke intention of Master Harrison to do.

SUFFOCATED BY SEWER GAS AT WIDNES. The adjourned inquiry has been held into the cause of death of Richard Chester, (50). of James et., Widnes, and Richard Jones, (30), Church View, who was suffocated in a sewer on Widnes Marsh, belonging to Hutchinson's Trustees, on Wednes- day in Whit week. At the previous inquiry the jury could not agree on a verdict,and the inquest was ad- journed,the deputy coroner (Mr.F.A. Jones) threat- ening to commit them to the Assizes if they did not then return a verdict. Mr. Routledge was present on behalf of the trustees. Mr. J. 0. Swift, solicitor,appeared for the United Alkali Company,who are interested in similar drains which require periodically to be cleaned out. Inspector Pattinson represented the police. The evi- dence given on the last occasion was repeated and a number of additional witnesses were called, who de- posed that Chester had great experience in the work of cleaning drains and was foreman of the men' although while he was only paid 21s a week, several of those under him received 235. a week, Mr. Routledge explained that this was because they had worked longer for the firm. It was further stated that there were ropes the men could use for their own safety when in the sewers. On the morning in question the men were not working in the sewer but had gone in to fasten the rope to the irag.—A witness named John Bates deposed that he had been gassed in the sewer a week previous to the accid- ent. After the Coroner had summed up, the jury were left to consider their verdict in private and at the end of 20 minutes, Mr. Ireland, the foreman, announced that the jury had unanimously found that the deceased men were accidentally poisoned by.sulphurettal hydro- gen gas, and they suggested that in future extra care ought to be taken in cleaning out these sewers and that belts with ropes attached ought to be supplied to the men engaged in the work.

TRIP OF WARRINGTON UNION GUARDIANS AND OFFICIALS.

The sixth annual excursion promoted by the Guardians and Officials of the Warrington Union took place on Monday, when a party of about sixty paid a -visit to Derby and Osmaston Manor, the Derbyshire seat of Sir A. B. Walker, Bart. A start was made from the Warrington Central station by the 6.10 train, Derby being reached about half-past eight. Outside the station wagonettes were waiting and in these the party were driven to the Kings Arms and County Hotel, where an excellent break- fast was served. About an hour after breakfast, the visitors had an oppoe':anity of looking round the old town of Derby. -smaston Manor is about eleven miles from Derby, e .a the drive there was of a very enjoyable charactc. , the only drawback being a heavy shower of rain which fell when about midway. Fortun- ately the party were able to shelter at a pretty wayside inn, and so escaped a drenching. On arriving at the house, the visitors were courteously received by Mr. Turner, butler and house steward, and Mr. Brownson, the estate agent. They were first shown over the house, and afterwards taken to inspect the gardens and park, and later on to the village of Osnaaston, The grounds and park cover some 3,500 acres. The house itself is most richly furnished. In it are splendid collections of birds, elk-deer heads, &c., many of the birds having been obtained by Mr. Pater Carlow Walker - in his travels abroad. An elephant's skull, &c., was viewed with much interest, Mr. Peter Walker having saved the life of a man who was being pursued by the elephant, which received its quietus from a well directed shot from Mr. Walker's rifle. In one of the rooms was also a fine painting of Sir A. B. Walker by W. Q. Orchardson, Q.A. Unfortunately owing to illness, Sir A. B. Walker is confined to his house at Gateacre, but Mr. Barclay Walker, one of the sons, accompanied the party. The luncheon was served in the racquet court, and this unexpected generosity of Sir A. B. Walker was thoroughly appreciated. Before leaving, Mr. J. C. SUTTON proposed the health of Sir Andrew and Lady Walker. (Applause.) It had been his privilege to know the Walker family for some years. He was very intimately acquainted with the late Mr. Peter Walker, the very worthy sire of Sir Andrew. He believed he sat with him for some years in the War- rington Town Council, and he had always highly esteemed the family. They would have been better, pleased if the health of Sir Andrew had been better, but he felt sure that with one voice and with sincerity they wished soon to hear of his restoration to health. (Ap- plause.)—The toast was heartily drunk.—The return journey to Derby was accomplished under very favour- able conditions, the weather being all one could desire. The County Families Hotel was reached shortly after six o'clock, and here dinner was partaken of.— Mr: BEATON (who again presided) proposed the toasts of the health of "The Queen" and "The Prince and Princess of Wales and the Royal.. Family."- Mr. SUTTON, in proposing the health of the Chairman gave instances to show that the position of chairman of a Board of Guardians was an honourable one, and much appreciated. He quoted the word Sof the late Duke of Devonshire, to the effect that of all the positions he had ever held—honorary or otherwise, chairman of Quarter Sessions or county magistrate, or his position in connec- tion with the Cabinet—there was none he valued so highly as that of chairman of the Board of Guardians of his own union. (Applause.) The toast was warmly received.—The CHAIRMAN suitably responded, and said he was willing to do whatever he could for anyone, even for a pauper or for a vagrant. As a citizen he felt that it was his duty to give what ability he had to public duties. '[his was a glorious country to live in, and al- though the Poor Law system had been attacked of late, and people said it was degrading, nothing had ever come under his experience, which extended over a period of 30 years, which could be thus characterized. The Chair- man concluded by proposing the health of the officers and committee—a toast which was very warmly re- ceived. To this Mr. SAMUEL SurroN (assistant clerk) responded, and alluded to the fact that Mr. J. C. Sutton was appointed clerk to the Board on the 19th June, 1872, and both he and his father commenced work on the following day, or exactly 20 years ago that day (Applause.)—Dr. PEACOCKE and Mr. BASIL SHEARER also responded, the last-named remarking that there were more Guardians present on that occasion than he had ever seen at any previous trip. (Hear, hear.)—Mr. WILLIAM HOUGHTON proposed the health of "The Visit- ing Frienis."—Mr. W. H. J. JENKINS and Alderman WRIGHT responded. The proceedings then terminated, and the return journey was safely made, Warrington being roached about 10 o'clock.
LONDON & NORTH-WESTERN RAIL-
WAY SPORTS AT SUTTON WEAVER.,

_ The 28th annual athletic festival in connection with the London and North-Western Railway Com- pany's servants, Liverpool,. took place on a field kindly lent by Miss Savage, at Sutton Weaver. on Saturday afternoon. The event takes the form of a pinic, which has become so popular that about 2,500 persons journeyed from the city in three- special.trains. On their arrival they found that the committee had made every arrangement for their convenience, there being several large tents erected. The ground was admirably laid out for racing Ipurposes. The day, though fine, was cold, and an overcoat was a very welcome garment. The events resulted as follows : Tug of War (nine teams).—Winners, Mr. Wright's team Waterloo-street : runners up, Mr. Critchley's team. Crown-street,-120 Yards Handicap, flat race, for youths under 16, 1 Issac Whalley, 5 yards; 2, J. R. Carter, 1 ya,rd ; and 3.. S. Hughes, scratch.-440 Yards Handicap, fiat race (open to all railway servants in Ilverpool) :1. R. Ray, Lancashire and Yorkshire, 5 yards, ;2, G. H. Boothman, London and North- estern, 20 yards ;3, J. H. Hutchins, Shropshire Union. 13 yards.—The final heat in the 120 Yards Handicap, flat race was, 1, J.H. McGuinness. 4 yards; 2, A. E. Davies, 3, yards ; 3, P. Larkin, scratch.-150 Yards Handicap, flat race (for those 35 years of age and upwards), 1, P. Stirrup, 18 yards ; 2, T. Robinson' 20 yards ;3, J. Fair- brother, 25 yards,-200 Yards Handicap, flat race (for youths under 18) ; 1. J. M. Elliott, 8 yards ;2, R. W. Evans, 8, yards; 3, J.M: Scrymgeour, 10 yards.-100 Yards Handicap (for those 45 years of age and upwards) 1. J. Fairbrother, 14 yards ; 2. G. Forrest 15 yards ; 3 W.D. Wallace. 14 yards. Half-mile Handicap :I,W. G. Martin,4o yards ;2. W.H. Palins scratch •, 3. J. Raven,4o yards,-200 Yards Handicap, flat race : 1, J.P. Redhead, 80 yards ;2, W. Briscoe, 45 yards ;3, H. Renton, 23 yards.-440; yards Handicap : 1, J. H. McGuinness, 45 yards ;2, J. Larkin, 40 yards ; 3, J. Cullen, 45 yards.— One Mile Handicap :1, W. H. lalin, scratch ;2, J. Raven, 90 Yards ; 3, T. Breston' 40 yards,—Consolation Race: I,F. Townsend; 2, C. J.Sykes, 3, C. Davies.

div.head: MIL S. MORLEY AT ACCRINGTON.
div.p: MIL S. MORLEY AT ACCRINGTON.

-- Speaking at Accrington on Monday night, Mr. John Morley said that the delay of the dissolution, on the gound that the House of Lords would not otherwise have time to examine the legislation Befit up, was frivolous and provoking, and the excuses given for not having the poll on Saturday were the idlest that could he imagined. The coming election was a most critical one, becaus3 it would settle for some time what were to be the relations of the English and Irish democracy. The constituencies, however, were not now unprepared, as in 1886. They, had had six years' experi- ence of Tory -misrule, and he looked with confidence to. the result of the contest. Referring to the Belfast eon- ventign' he admitted that there were things to be said against Home Rule, and difficulties in the way of it, but such difficulties were not those which were described and relied upon at Belfast. He combated many of the argu- ments used there, and urged that nothing had been said to alter one jot or tittle of the convictions of those in favour of Home Rule. If the Conservatives should win the elections the Home Rule question would still be main- tained, followed by six more years of distraction in Ireland and the handicapping of the British Parliament.

stance, a principle which commends itself to common sense and common fairness ; but the Tories reject it, because they believe in the divine rights of property rather than the divine rights of humanity. Take also the proposal to pay members of Parliament. It is a natural outcome of the extension of the franchise ; and it is no more than what is done in almost every civilised country; yet the Tories elves° it because they know that it would give working-men a fair chance of being represented by their own class. The number of working-men members of Parliament is ridiculously small, and it will remain ridiculously small until members of Parliament are paid for their services. Then theLe is the question of restoring the land to the people; it is a vast criestion, for it involves. on all sides, far-reaching issues; but does any sane person believe that the Tories, as the great landowners, will strip themselves of the unjust privileges which they exercise ? Deliverance from the Land Monopoly as from the Drink Monopoly must come from the Liberal party. There must be local option to land as well as to licensing; and if the Addresses we commend to the attention of our readers are carefully considered it will be seen that "the way out "is clearly indicated as to these and other vital issues—not forgetting Home Rule, which is for the moment the most vital of all.

Licensing QUESTIONS relating to licensing hnd and Temperance have taken strong hold Temperance. upon the public mind; and it is therefore extremely desirable that all who are in- terested in the improvement of the masses, and have'votes to give, should know the views of Parlia- mentary Candidates. The matter was incidentally considered at a meeting of the Warrington Church Society, on Monday evening ; but no resolution upon the subject was adopted, the Rev. MORLEY STEVENSON remarking that he thought the tem- perance question might be left safe in the hands of the local temperance societies. As to this he is right; the Warrington Temperance Federation, recognising its responsibility at this juncture, has taken the matter up and put a series of questions to the candidates for the borough of Warrington, and the Newton, Altrincham, and Knutsford Divisions. These constituencies have been taken because, it is pointed out, "the Federation has amongst its members subscribers and voters in each of these Parliamentary Divisions." We give in another column the replies of the various candi- dates and the correspondence which has ensued ; and we desire to direct special attention to the subject, as we believe a far larger number of voters are deeply interested in these matters than is generally supposed. The four questions submitted are as follows :
1. Will you, if elected, support a measure giving the Ratepayers a direct popular veto on the issue or renewal of all Liquor Licenses ?
2. Will you oppose any attempt to grant com- pensation, from the Public Funds, to the holders of expired licenses who, in the public interest, may be refused fresh licenses ?
3. Will you support the English Sunday Closing Bill?

4. Will you support a Bill for the prevention of the sale of Intoxicating Liquors to children under the age of fG years ? It will be perceived that none of these questions can in any sense be said to be party questions; but it-is to the credit of the Liberal candidates ' that their replies are, on the whole, most satisfac- tory. Dr. HOUSTON, as might have been expected of him from the opinions he has expressed, has answered "Yes " to every question. His oppon- ent Mr. ROBERT PIERPOINT, had sent no reply whatever up to Monday evening—the limit of time fixed by the Federation. A. reminder of his failure brought a reply, on Wednesday, which is worth studying. It will be seen that he appears at last openly in the character of the friend of the publican rather than of the public. He does not say " Yes," to any one of the four questions. He regards Local Option as dictation. According to Mr. PIERPOINT, it is quite right that a few magistrates, such as he, should have licensing matters in their hands; but it will be dictation if the people exercise a voice in that which so vitally concerns them. As to compensation, Mr. PIERPOINT, though a lawyer, sets himself above the law, for he thinks the license-holder who fails to get his license renewed should be paid something, notwithstanding that the courts have declared that he has no just claim. He remarks that compensation was given to the owner of slaves when slavery was abolished. But there is no analogy between the two cases. If the slave- owner had received his slaves as a privilege from the State, a privilege good for twelve months only, not even Mr. PIERPOINT will say he would have been entitled to compensation if the State determined to withdraw its privilege after the expiration of the twelve months for which it was granted. So with regard to a license ;it is granted for twelve months, and, unless the license be taken away before the end of the twelve months, there should he no compensation if the privilege be'finally withdrawn. As to Sunday Closing, the Tory candidate will have none of it; and we put it to every elector who thinks England should follow the example set by Scotland, Ireland, and Wales whether Mr. ROBERT PIERPOINT is the right sort of man to represent Warrington. So wedded is he to the beer interest that he will not even promise to support the Bill for the Prevention of the Sale of Intoxicating Liquors to Children under the age of sixteen. The fact is, he makes a dead-set against licensing and temperance reform ; and it will be for licensing and temperance reform- ers to make a dead-set against him.

Mr. T. W. LEarr, the member for the Newton Division, frankly says that he finds himself "un- able to support the greater portion of the pro- gramme put forward by your Federation " ; while Mr. W. NEILL, the Liberal candidate for the Division and Mr. A. W. LATHAM, the Liberal candidate for the Knutsford Division, answer every question in the affirmative. Mr. A. DE TATTON EGERTON disposes of the matter by saying he will give: his views to the United Kingdom Alliance ; Mr. I. S. LEADAM refers the Federation to his address; while Mr. CONINGSBY DISRAELI puts himself out of court by failing to reply. I Under these circumstances, it is a matter of course for the Warrington Temperance Federation to appeal to the electors to give their votes only to those candidates who have sent favourable replies. This was tho resolution come to on Wednesday evening ; and it was further resolved that a manifesto to this effect should be issued within the next few days.

div.head: TREAT TO PRESCOT WORKTIOUSE INMATES.
div.p: TREAT TO PRESCOT WORKTIOUSE INMATES.

On Thursday afternoon about 300 inmates of the Prescot Union Workhouse were taken in convey- ances, kindly lent by the St. Helens and District Tramways Company and various waggonette pro- prietors, to St. Helens, a distance of four miles, where Mr, Lucas, of the Circus, entertained them free of charge to a performance of " Cinderella."
TO VC R AND GO."

While the question of old-age pensions is being discussed on every hand, a Parliamentary paper has been published which formulates and recom- mends a scheme of pensions for elementary teachers. It is not likely that anything will come of it just yet ; and it is perhaps as well that this is so. There is a growing feeling against pensioning any particular class, although it is not to be denied that teachers are more deserving of State aid than many who now receive it.

Let us" give three cheers, and one cheer more" for the success of the strike of the Bolton tram- way men. They are to have one day off every fortnight; it is not much, but it is what they fought for. What of busmen and tram-men in this and other parts of the country ? Are they not to benefit by the result ? The one day off in a fortnight should be granted now in every town throughout the kingdom. Let the men make their requests civilly and respectfully ; they are in the right; they have the support of the pub- lic, and they are sure to succeed in the end.

With regard to Home Rule, it has now been determined, in deference to a loudly expressed wish from all parts of tho country, that Irish representatives shall be retained at Westminster. Shutting them out would savour of separation, and nobody desires that. Our own view of the matter is that the difficulty will eventually be removed by granting " Home Rule all round." In that case each country would have its own Parlia- ment for its own domestic affairs, while sending representatives to the Imperial Parliament to deal with Imperial affairs.

The Tories, with the" measureless audacity " which John Bright once said was characteristic of them, are trying to make capital out of the fact that Mr. Gladstone has not committed himself to an Eight Hours Bill, as if Lord Salisbury was in favour of some such measure ! They know per- fectly well that both Lord Salisbury and Mr. Balfour declined to say word in favour of such a proposal when they were interviewed ; but, as usual, the Tories suppress the truth when it serves their purpose to do so.

The fact is it would be unwise for Parlia- ment to take action, until there is something like unanimity amongst the workers themselves as to what should be done. There is a wide diffe- rence of opinion amongst the miners ; and a recent ballot, at Nelson, shows that cotton opera- tors are also divided on the question. The largest number of votes was given in favour of " waiting for an internationair eight hours day." International action is certainly on right lines, for there will be no danger of slipping back if the hours of labour are made shorter on the continent as well as in England.

But as between Liberals and Conservatives, the best thing is to judge of the future by the past. It was the Liberal party that first gave workers a sure footing by legalising Trades Unions; and it is only a few months since the Liberals in the House of Commons sought to amend the law so as to get rid of indictments for conspiracy incase of picket- ing, &c. But they were defeated—by the Tories of course.

Further, let electors who are in doubt in this matter compare the replies of Tory candidates with those of Liberal candidates as to the ques- tions put by Railway Servants. They will then see how the wind blows. In Warrington, the Liberals are reprinting the answers of both candidates. After reading them, no railway man, or other workman, can refuse to vote for Dr. Houston if he is true to his own interests and the interests of his class.

The General Election is close upon us ; and the Tories are determined to win by foul means if they cannot win by fair. How miserably mean and contemptible to fix the date of dissolution so that no borough election can be held on a Saturday ! Shakespeare must have had a Tory in his mind when he spoke of " man, proud man, drest in a little brief authority " who— Plays such fantlastic hicks before high heaven As make the angels weep. However,it is something to be thankful for that the authority is likely to be brief ; and, to ensure that it shall be the case, let every elector who is put to any inconvenience through the poll not being on a Saturday, show what he thinks of the manceuvre by voting against the Tory party.

--- In Warrington the Mayor has already deter- mined that the election for the borough shall be 'on Tuesday week, the sth of July. Under the cir- cumstances this is perhaps the best he could do. Monday would not be a good day, seeing that it is one of the annual- holidays; for, although most of the excursions are held the previous Saturday, there are many people who extend their excursions until Monday night. It would be asking more than some would do to propose returning for the purpose of voting, although ardent Liberals would not hesitate about that. There must be no going away on the Tuesday, for the Liberal who should rail to poll would fail in his duty in the most important national crisis that this generation of politicians has known. Dr. Houston has shown himself in every way worthy of Warrington; let Liberals show themselves worthy of him. Besides—happy thought I—War- rington election will take place on Mrs. Houston's birthday; and what better birthday present could she have than be given the title that day of wife of the member for Warrington?

In the course of his peregrinations yesterday, Mr. Robert Pierpoint was introduced to an old inhabitant, who expressed the pleasure of meeting the Tory candidate,for,he said,be had "never seen him in his life before." Really, it would seem that it is Mr. Pierpoint who is the stranger. Now, if the old inhabitant had been a foreigner he might have come across Mr. Pierpoint sooner—say, in Malta or Africa.

The Tories are still at a loss to make out Mr. Robert Pierpoint's claim on the electors of War- rington. They cannot say what he has done, for he has done nothing. But, after diligent search, it has been discovered that his father gave—not the money for the Park or the School of Art— but for a small drinking fountain! And what if ho had given something really commensurate with his wealth? Does not Lord Bacon say—" They who derive their worth from their ancestors, re- semble potatoes, the most valuable part of which is under ground !" Besides, this is a case of very "small potatoes."

The members of the Warrington Sanitary Com- mittee seem to be figliting.shy of the boiler ques- tion. The bulk of them do not like to commit themselves to a glaring breach of tho regulations as to Corporation contracts. No business could be done on Wednesday night week, for there was not a sufficient number present to form a quorum. A large number stayed away again on Wednesday night. There were five only present out of a Committee often; but the five went to work and passed the minutes giving the contract to Messrs. Manlove, Alliott, and Co., three voting for and two against.

This moans that, despite the standing regula- lotion which requires that no contract shall be entered into for over 20 without tenders being advertised for, a Nottingham firm are to be given an order for a boiler, without competition, which will cost the ratepayers of Warrington over £6OO. If it can he shown that the boiler could not be made in Warrington, the ratepayers should at once be told the reason why. Failing this, it is to bo hoped the Town Council, at its next meeting, will refuse to pass the minutes ; and insist upon the boiler being tendered for in the usual way. There have been too many costly experiments at Longford to permit of another being entered upon in this irregular fashion.
