On Thursday evening, a youth named John Knight (16), Market-st., who was employed as a plumber's assistant at Messrs. Gaskell Deacon's works met with a terrible accident. The unfortu- nate boy was endeavouring to get a bucket of boil- ing water from a tank, when his foot slipped and he fell into the seething pot. He was dreadfully scalded about the upper part of the body and was at once conveyed in the horse ambulance to the Accident Hospital. 3011111 M Plt/TCHARD loops apatiaeles to salt all sights from a illing a pair.—Aldvt.
THE MYSTERIOUS POISONING OF A CHESHIRE FAMILY.

At Malpas, on Thursday, the inquest was resumed on the body of the child, Martha Jane Sudlow. The Coroner, Mr. Henry Churton, read the report of the analysis of the viscera by Mr. Edward Davies,analy- deal chemist, Liverpool, who stated that there was no evidence of the presence of mineral or vegetable poison, or that death was due to that cause. Nothing could be deduced from the appearance of viscera owing to decomposition. The Coroner was of opinion that the contaminated water supply pro- nounced by Mr. Davies to contain noxious sewage matter was the cause of all the mischief, and that the death of the child and the illness of the mother and the other child were due to the foul state of the water. There had been no official sanitary inspec- tion of the premises for the past six years. The jury found that death was due to irritant poison- ing, but of what description or how taken there was no evidence to prove.

div.head: RUNCORN FOOTBALL CLUB.
div.p: RUNCORN FOOTBALL CLUB.

ANNUAL MEETING. The annual meeting of the members of Runcorn Football Club, was held at Riley's Cafe, Bridge-st., on,Tuesday night, and there was a large attendance. In the absenc,l of Mr. P. Speakman, the president, Mr. A. Lightburn was voted to the chair.

div.head: BEASON'S RECORD.
div.p: THE BEASON'S RECORD.

Mr. J. E. Longshaw, the lion, sec. presented the annual report, which stated that the club teams had done remarkably well and could show a record which would be difficult to beat by any Rugby organisation, seeing that their matches had been with teams consid- ered first class. The first team played 38 matches, 30 of which were drawn and 5 lost. The team scored 40 goals, 68 tries, against 11 goals, 11 tries scored by their opponents, majority 29 goals 55 tries. The principal scorers were T. 11. Davies 44 tries ; Pendlebury 13, Crompton 8, Abrams 6, Riley 5, Massey 4, May 4, Hollingworth 3, liampson 3, Faulkner 4, Robinson 3, Lee 2, Reece, Gayter, and Antrobus one each. Crompton and May each dropped two goals. The A team played 26 matches, won 19, lost 4 and 3 were drawn. They scored 23 goals, 50 tries, against 4 goals, 11 tries; majority 19 goals, 39 tries. During the season tho club had the honour to be represented in the English team by Mr. Houghton, the full back. lt lwas most un- fortunate for their captain (Crompton) to meet with a serious accident on the field at a time when international honours were certain. The club was represented in the North v. South match by Messrs. Houghton and Riley' The club had been strongly represented ill all Cheshire matches, and tha Committee were sure their men in all these matches did their level hest to uphold the prestige of the county. They had a strong list of matches tor next season and the Committee hoped the teams would keep well together and make a strong effort to keep to the top of the tree. The report, which elicited frequent applausetwas unanimously adopted on the motion of Mr. E. Key, seconded by Mr. R. Moore.
TIIE FINANCES.

Mr. C. Pownall (the treasurer) read the financ....l state- ment, which showed the receipts as follows :—Balance from last season £2B 45., subscriptions from 169 honor- ary members £44 12s. 6d., 35 ordinary members £7, receipts at gate from 35 matches £552 6s. 11d., Runcorn Cricket Club rent £lO, miscellaneous receipts £2 12s. 6d, insurance company on account of claims £ll 103., Parrs Banking Company £74 12s. 11d., due to treasurer 15s. 9d., total £761 14s. 7d. The expenses included insurance to players £52, amount paid to players suffer- ing from accident £79 103., rent of ground and rooms £34 23., rates and taxes £4 6s. 9d., refreshments to home and visiting teams £63 lie. 2d., half gates £l3 14s. 3d., postages, telegrams, &c., £l2 175., honorariums, £2O 195., subscribers to Rugby Union and Cheshire Foot ball Union £2 is., printing, stationery, and advertising £49 12s. 5d., expesses on field £22, travel- ling expenses £222 17s. 9d., police and gatekeepers £3B 95., jerseys, pants, footballs, &c., £B9 133. 7d., referees £22 7s. 9d., miscellaneous payments £l4 2s. ld., cash in secretary's hands, £2O ; total, £761 14s. 7d. the treasurer pointed out that there was a falling off in the membership of 20. There had been a valuation of the assets taken, and after clearing off the liabilities there would be a balance In favour of the club of £42.—Mr. Key, one of the auditors, in criticising the accounts, referred to the fact that the Cardiff tour cost £7B 10s. 9d. This was a very large item, and it would bave been better for the finances of the club if it had been less. He considered that if any members of the club were entitled to a treat it was not the members of the Committee but the second team. (Applause.)—Mr. Goodwell said the South Wales tour cost .£2 12a. 9d. a head, and that the members of the Committee should undertake the trip when they had an idea that the finances were on the wrong aide did not appear to show that they took great interest in the Club.—Mr. Howard said he thought it was illegal for the members of the Committee to vote their own expenses. He asked how many went to Cardiff.—The Secretary replied six.— Mr. Howard : That means £2o.—Mr. Lewis said eight went. Other discussion ensued. and Mr. Carroll stated that the Committee had attended well to their duties and with due economy. Eventually the financial statement was adopted unanimously.

div.head: OFFICIALS.
div.p: OFFICIALS.

Mr. P. Speakman C.C., was re-elected President, amid loud applause, and Dr. McKenzie, Messrs. G. Whiteley, W. M. Sowerby, and W. Shore were added to the list of vice-presidents.—Mr. J. E. Langshaw, the secretary, and Mr. C. Pownall. the treasurer, were unanimously re-appointed to their posts at the respective salaries of £lO 10s. and £7 7s. After some discussion, Mr. John Ellison wa9 appointed assistant secretary at a salary of £2 2s. The qv ptaincy of the first team was again be- stowed upon Mr. J. H. Crompton, and Mr. T. R. Davies was made vice-captain, Mr. Faulkner declining to be placed in nomination because he would not play next season. . _

T. Antrobus was elected captain and J. Darbyshire sub-captain of the second team. T. Sherlock was ap- pointed umpire of the first team, and T. J. Stubbs was selected for a similar office to the second team. 31 nominations had been received for the 12 seats on the Committee, and the following were elected :—Messrs. W. Carroll (70 votes), W. Faulkner (63), J. Gatley (61), S. Lunt (52), H. Hughes (47), S. Houghton (47), J. Hollingsworth (42), P. Riley (41), W. H. Cawley (40), T. Moores (37), U. Robinson (34), H. Wright (33). A committee was appointed to draw up a set of rules for Ma guidance of the club.

Sir John Le.s, Bart., died at Itvde, on Sunday night, after a long illness, at the age of n. It is stated that a woman in Odessa, who had been deserted by her husband, killed her four children with an axe,
REPRESENTATION OF NORTHWICH
DIVISION.

MR. BRUNNER, M.P., AT NORTHWICH. On Monday night, a public meeting in support of the candidature of air. J. T. Brunner, M.P., was held at the Central Hall, Northwich. There was a crowded audience. Dr. D. B. Hewitt presided, and said it was destiable that a working-men's consti- tuency such as that was should be represented by a man who used the House of enetlllollS, not as a pleasant clutabut for the purpose of promoting real Liberal measures, and measures that were for the good of the working-men of this country. (Cheers.) Mr. Swift Mac Neill, M.P. for South Donegal, delivered a vigorous speech on the Irish question. Mr. J. W. Deakin moved : "That this meeting pledges itself to secure the triumphant return of J. T. Brunner, Esq., M.P., and views with gratification the early return of the Liberal party to power, when Home Rule in Ireland will be placed by Mr. Gladstone in the very first place in the Liberal programme." Mr. T. Hughes seconded the resolution, and it was unanimously carried, amid loud applause. Mr. J. T. Brunner, who was received with deafening cheers, said that meeting, looked like an ancommonly good beginning of the fight. (Cheers.) They ha been told that Mr. Balfour intormed the House of Commons that the hope was that the dissolution would come on Wednesday or Thursday of next week, when through the peculiar wording of the law it would be absolutely impossible to hold a borough election on a Saturday. In the same speech Mr. Balfour stated that the Lords were too busy to get through their work before Wednesday er Thursday. He should like to know how it was that so many of them could find time to come down to North- wich this week. (Laughter.) Mr. Whiteley blamed him for not voting for the Eight Hours Bill for miners. When he voted against that Bill he was in excellent com- pany, for Mr. Burt, Mr. Broadhurst, and Mr. Fenwick, the trusted representatives of the werking-nien, were in the same lobby with hint. (Cheers.) He did vote against the Bill, and unless it was amended he would vote against it again. Mr. Whiteley said nothing about eight hours in the brewing trade. (Laughter.) He said nothing about eight hours in the licensed victuallers' trade ; and he did say something about eight hours in the cotton trade. (Laughter.) He (Mr. Brunner) should vary much like to see the hours of labour of the people in public-houses reduced. (Hear, hear.) There was rig, class of people in this country who were more sweated and over-driven than servants in public-houses. But Mr. NVhiteley said there was too much competition in the cotton trade to allow the intro- duction of the eight hours system. (Laughter.) There was another phase of the eight hours question with which they were all familiar,but which Mr. Whiteley was extremely careful to remember to forget, and that was the question of the eight hours for shift men at Winning- ton and Sandbach. (Cheers.) He was told that his opponent—whom he had had the pleasure of meeting that day for the first time—he received him very kindly, and he had no fault whatever to find with him except that he was a Tory—(laughter) he was told that he was the most assiduous canvasser they had ever had to deal with in the Northwich Division. It was all very well to walk into a shop, or ;any place that was open to the public ; but he .had no right to enter any man's house unless he was invited to do so. (Cheers.) He had prepared a record of the most impor- tant votes he had given in the House of Commons since they last elected him. He had not had time to make it as complete as he should have liked, but it would be sufficient to enable canvassers in the interests of the Liberal party to answer every stupid and malicious thing that was said about him in the neighbourhood by Tory canvassers. There were some stupid and malicious things said about him to induce the electors to refrain from voting for him. One of them was—and it amused him considerably—that the number of men set out for holidays at Winnington was largely reduced, in order that he might have the honour of raising the number to the same figure as last year. There was absolutely no truth in that story. (Cheers.) Another tale was that he had treated a number of jovial ladies in New-st., to hot ruin and water. (Loud laughter.) They would only be too glad if it was true, but he was ton old al hand at electioneering to be caught like a fly on sugar paper in that fashion. (Laughter.) Another question Mr. Whiteley had touched upon was that of old age pensions. The scheme with which he (the speaker) land already dealt at Northwich and at Runcorn was one that had been promulgated by Mr. Chamberlain. Strange to say, this scheme, which had been recommended by Mr. Whiteley, had—so they were told—interested and met with the approval of some aged men in that neighbourhood. Now, if aged men took an interest in Mr. Chamberlain's Old Age Pen- sion Scheme, it was simply for the reason that Mr. Whiteley had not clearly explained it. The scheme was that at the age of 25 a man was to deposit in the hands of the Government a sum of £5, and until he reached the age of 65, he was to continue paying £1 a year. A scheme which was not to produce a penny of benefit to the man who entered it for 40 years was certainly not a scheme which taught to interest aged men. (Hear, hear.) His (Mr. Brunner's) gre t objection to the scheme, was that it provided no help at a time when the working-man most required , and that it would greatly hinder men from subscribing to friendly societies. A scheme which provided no help dur- ing a time of sickness was absolutely condemned by that very fact. 4 He therefore counselled them to stand by their friendly societies, and not to accept any such scheme as the old age pension scheme. (Cheers.) With reference to the Unionist demonstration on Thursday next, they knew the Duke of Westminster was to take the chair, and he hoped they would dis- appoint him in the idea that he was going to give him (Mr. Brunner) tit-for-tat for beating his son in 1837. (Laughter.) This imposing Unionist demonstration was managed by a list of noblemen and gentlemen, begin- ning with the Duke of Westminster and ending with Mr. R. G. Stanley-Banks. (Laughter.) So that they might say it was recommended by all sorts and conditions of men. (Laughter.) The object of this Unionist demonstration was to pre cent a testimonial to Mr. A. H. Smith-Barry- late of Marbury Hall It was years since Mr. Smith Barry lived in Northwich, and he wondered why they- were coming to Northwich to make the presentation. Was it owing to the fact that at the last general election he defeated the son of the Duke of Westminster ? They could not forgive him for that. (A Voice : " And you will beat Whiteley." Applause.) Why was Mr. Smith- Barry to be praised ? (A voice " For cruelty in Ireland.") Mr. Smith-Barry was one of a syndicate of gentlemen who, some five years ago, purchased the Ponsonby estate, in the county of Cork. That estate was cleared by means of evictions, and he (Mr. Brunner) had the inexpressible sorrow of witnessing those cruel evictions. en the whole of that country side there was no living person now except the miserable caretaker who was an outcast to whom no respectable wan or woman would speak. (A Voice : "God bless you."—Cheers.) Ile was content to rest his cause upon a contrast between Mr. Smith-flarry's work on the Ponsonhy estate and his work amonest them. On the Ponsonby estate they had fields which grew no food for the population,but were covered with sedges and thistles. Around Northwich, year after year they had fields well tilled and productive. Where Mr. Smith-Barry had been at work on the Ponsonby estate every house was untenanted, roofless, doorless, and windowless. Around him in Northwich he had seen grow up hundreds and hundreds of solid, substantial,happy comfortable homes. He asked them to contrast the two scenes, and decide at the coining election which of the two men was most deserving of their confidence. (Cheers.) MP. WHITELEY AT NORTHWICIL On laT ,iday evening, a meeting In support of the candid i a, are of Mr. George Whiteley was held n the Drill Hall, Northwich. The chair was occupied by Dr. Moreton. The hall was crowded. Mr. G. Whiteley, who was received with loud applause said they were approaching an election which was preg- nant with issues which would make or mar the sister kingdom of Ireland, and largely affect the welfare and prosperity of England. (Applause.) Where they going to hand the Irish over to the tender mercy of men who had threatened to make short work of the Ulster men, and who thought they were doing God service in exter- minating the Protestants ? Supposing an Irish Parlia- ment was established, the ruling statesmen would be the land leaguers,the plan of com poi gners and the boycotters, who had been connected with and had connived and winked at all crimes forbidden in the decalogue—murder iioendiarism, assaults on women and children, &c. He had canvassed many a hundred Gladstonians ii' the division, but when he had brought that fact ho. ta, t n, them he had not found one who could distinctly say he was in favour of Home Rule. (Applause.) Mr, Brunner dragged a red herring across the trail by drawing lurid pictures of the evil effects of the brewing and licensed victuallers' trade, describing that all the crime of the country was due to those interests, with almost all the taxation. WAS that a fair way to hi an election? Then lie endeavoured to connect him (his opponent) with those trades even in the face of his previous declar- ation of having no connection with them. Ile believed those industries to be as honest as the cotton industry. (Applause.) As a workina-man and a working-men's candidate—he (Mr. Whiteley) had expressed an opinion, not to catch votes, that he would be willing, if returned, to vote for an Eight Elmira Bill for the miners. 'fatire were no miners in that constituency, and it could not affect any votes ; but he believed that in an arduous and toilsome labour like that of the miners an Eight Home Bill was desirable. (Applause.) Mr. Brunner,in a speech made to the watermen at Runcorn, said he would have none of the old age pension scheme, and he (Mr. Whiteley) now asked them to judge between Mr. Brunner end himself, as to which was the most deserv- ing of the support of working,men ,the one who stood op- posed to the scheme,or he who was pledged to support it. Of what the future had in store they could not tell. In election matters, more than in others, they were aware .of the truth of the policy, "You must not prophesy until you know." Whether they would again see one of those pendulum-like motions repeated which they had i seen n elections in times past, they did not know, but they did know, whether in power or whether they were successful or unsuccessful, they would still hold to those pi incipies which, at the present time, they espoused ;

whether they were in government or whether in opposi- tion they would look forward to the time when those principles should again assert themselves as the right once, and they should march triumphantly from under any passing shadow. (Cheers.) Mr. Whiteley, then addressed a crowd of people who were unable to enter the hill, . . . . .

Mr. C. liar moved : That this rm‘eting is of opinion that Mr. George Whiteley is aSt and proper person to represent the Nortliwich Division in Parliament, and hereby pledgesitself to use all legitimate means to secure his return." (Applause.) Mr. Richard Beckett seconded. Mr. Hornby Lewis and Mr. T. Ward supported motion.
The motion was unanimously adopted with acclama- ion.

MR. BRUNNER AT MOULTON. A TORY DODGE. Addressing a crowded ineeing at Moulton, on Wed. nesday night, Mr. BRUNNMR, who was received with loud cheering, said he could not help referring to the un- fair manner in which Mr. Whiteley was contesting the seat in asking those who refused to give him their votes not to assist him (Mr. Brunner.) The Liberals had worked too hard and too long in obtaining them the power ef voting to ask them not to go to the poll. They wanted every man to go to the poll and give his vote, guided by his own opinion. They wanted the principle of the Ballot Act from the beginning to the end of the contest carried out in the very letter and spirit, and wished the law to be held in respect throughout. (Ap- plause.) He had two documents before him one sent out by the Liberals and the other by the Conservatives, and he was going to put it to them which party respected I the Ballot Act and which went against the spirit of it. In the Conservative circular there was a large form up- on which the receiver was asked to sign his name stat- ing for whorl he was going to vote. The following was an extract from the circular In making this request, there is no desire to infringe UT secrecy of the ballot, but it would materially assist us if we could know as soon as possible the amount of support we are to re- ceive." This circular was sent out to every voter without exception, and it asked (not in the spirit of the Ballot Act, whereby a man went into a closed partition, and there placed his mark by the name of the candidate he liked) them to do the very thing that the Liberals wasted to avoid when they passed the Ballot Act. In asking an independent man to write down for whom he was going to vote, where was the respect for law and order? The man who wrote that pamphlet had his tongue in his cheek when he had the pen in his hand. (A Voice : "They were wanting to make some bets, perhaps."—Laughter.) It would give great assistance, no doubt, to the election agent if the circular was signed by voters, stating to whom they were going to give their votes. He denounced the circular as an impudent evasion of the Ballot Act. (Loud applause.)

In connection with this mission special services were held in Runcorn Public Hall, on Sunday, and Mrs. Bax- ter of London, gave three admirable addresses. An open air service was also conducted in Devonshire Square by Mr. Cain, the evangelist.

Instead of opening at ten a.m and closing at one p.m on Saturdays, the hours at the Runcorn branch of Parr's Banking Co. will be open from 9am to 12 noon on and after the 2nd of July. It is believed that this alteration will be for the convenience and benefit of both customers and bank officials. dosawa PEITIHARD has the best stook of lasiles' silver and geld watches in the town.—Adct.

div.head: DEATH OF A RUNCORN LICENSED VICTUALLER.
div.p: DEATH OF A RUNCORN LICENSED VICTUALLER.

After a prolonged illness Mr. Hugh Tracey, of the Masonic Hotel, Devonshire-square, died at the early age of 31 years, much regretted by a wide circle of friends. He had been onanager of the hotel for three years cAr Messrs. Walker and Co., and he was a member of the Licensed Victuallers Association.

There were good congregations and an attrac- tive musical service was gone through by the choir under the leadership of Mr. Lancaster. Mr. Sivage was at the organ. div.head: JUBILEE OF A FRIENDLY SOCIETY AT VVIDNES.
div.p: JUBILEE OF A FRIENDLY SOCIETY AT VVIDNES.

The jubilee of the Hearts of Oak Benefit Society was celebrated at London on Monday, and the local members at Widnes recognised the event by holdiug a dinner at the Railway and Commercial Hotel. There was a good company present and appropriate toasts were honoured. It was stated that there were now 160,000 members in the society, and the reserve fund stood at £1,250,000.

WOUNDING A SISTER AT WIDNES. At Widnes Police Court, on Monday, Mary Hannon, of 7 Barn-st., was committed to the Quarter Sessions for trial on a charge of unlawfully wounding her sister Julia Miller. The parties lived together, and on the night of the 18th they had a quarrel about the change from a shilling given by the brother to fetch some beer of which they had all partaken. During the altercation the prisoner struck her sister on the head with a glass sugar basin, causing two wounds which penetrated to the bone. The brother informed the Court that the com- plainant threw a jug at the prisoner, and in his opinion they were as bad as each other.

SUCCESS OF • RUNCORN AMATEUR PROVOGRAPHER. Mr. C. Timmins, of Higher Runcorn, last week secured the first prize and medal of the Fairfield Camera Club. Recently Mr. Timmins made a cruise to Norway in the Steamship City of Richmond,and as mementos of a plea- sant and highly enjoyable voyage he has secured about 150 negatives of the romantic and magnificient scenery of that northern land. In the autumn it is Mr. Timmins intention to give a lecture on his trip, illustrated by his own lantern slides.

JOSE PH PRITCHA RD'S sale shop is 51,11igh-et.. his workshop 4, Bridge-st.—Advt. SONS OP TEMPERANCE AND THE ELECTION. The National Division of the Sons of Temperance, of which society there are numerous members in Runcorn district, has adopted a resolution which states that " believing that the legalised liquor traffic in strong drink is the great obstacle to religious, social, and national advancement, and recognising that legislation with a view to securing a sober community, is of greater importance than any other Political Party Question, and realising also that a moment of crisis has arrived, which demands a very special effort ; they, therefore—in view of the impending General Election—call upon every son of Temperance, to use his vote and influence only for such candidates, as will support the Sunday Closing of public houses, and are in favour of granting to the people in their respective localities, the Direct veto over the issue of licenses."

div.head: MR.. BILFOITR AT NORTHWICII.
div.p: MR.. BILFOITR AT NORTHWICII.

Mr. A. J. Balfour was the principal speaker at a meeting held on Thursday evening at Northwich for the purpose of presenting an address to Mr. A. H. Smith-Barry, M.P., in recognition of the part he took in connection with the Plan of Campaign struggle in Tipperary. The Dime of Westminster presided. Mr. Balfour's speech was largely eulogistic of Mr. Barry's action in regard to the founding of New Tipperary. He said that anybody who contemplated the facts would come to the conclusion that the game of law and order was not and never would be up in Ireland, and further , that the men who in cold blood could devise what he called the Tipperary conspiracy and watch unmoved the ruin that they wrought, were not the men who ought to be entrusted with the destinies of Ireland, and were not cipable of working Ireland on the linos of a free constitu- tion confined to that country. He appealed to the electors to hear no part in this iniquity, this gigantic betrayal ; and, in conclusion, said that whoever for poli- tical purposes threw in their lot with the boycotter, the dynamiter, the contriver of criminal conspiracies, and the ruiner of prosperous communities, the Unionist party 11 at any rats, would not bow the knee.

div.head: WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD.
div.p: WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD.

The monthly meeting was held at the Town Hall, on Tuesday afternoon. Mr. T. Sutton Timmia presided, and there were also present the Rev. Dean Finegan, Dr. O'Keeffee, Messrs. S. Wade Deacon, S. Quinn and G. H. Danby (clerk). The District Education Committee reported that (luting May (four weeks) there were seven applications for fees, which were recommended to be paid. 190 persons were summoned before the Committee for contravention of the Education Act, and 30 were prosecuted before the magistrates, 29 were convicted and one was sent to an industrial school.— On the recommendation of the School Management Committee, Miss Gardner was appointed head mistress of the senior girl's department of the West Bank School (vice Miss Clegg), at a salary of £94 per annum, rising according to the scale of the Board.—The Finance Committee recommended the payment of accounts antounting to £785 4s. 3d. The receipts for the month amounted to £549 14s. 63.—0 n the motion of the Committee it wag decided that the next meeting of the Board should be held on July sth instead of July 19th, and on August 30th instead of August 16th.—The Clerk read a letter from the Education Department en- closing a cheque for £346 12• i. 61., being the fee grant for the quarter ending May 31st.-111r. Deacon asked how this amount was made up and the Clerk replied that it was made on last years attendance—Dean Finegan said the grant was paid in four instalments, and if the Department had overpaid anything, or had not paid sufficient in the first three quarters it would he made all right in the last quarter of the year.—The Chairman said it was very satisfactory that the money was paid so promptly as in cases ware there was ti) School Board it might be awkward if the money were not recNved quickly.
THE PROPOSED TEMPETtA.NCE FEDERATION FOR RUNCORN.

The adourned meeting of tPmperanee representa- tive' for the purpose of considering the recommen- dations of the Committee appointed to draw up a. constitution and cods of rules for tke proposed Runcorn and District TeraperanCe Federation, was held on Tuesday eight in Union Hall. The Rev. Canon Maitland Wood presided and there were delegates present from every Temperance Society and Band of Hope in the town and district. It was resolved to form a federatiott under the title above mentioned, and that the objects should be to afford opportunity for united action of the revere( temperance societies in the town and district on matters affecting the Temperance reform ; which would include the following :—To consider matters relating to licenses and to tile such action at Licensing Sessions as may appear advisable; to take concerted action OR all temperance questions at the election of local administra- tive bodies ; to take action by petition, public meetings and otherwise in favour of licensing reform and temperance legislation generally; to render every assistance within its power to any affiliated society. The chief discussion of the evening took place on the following motion made by Mr. Somerville, of Weston, seconded by Mr. T. Heesom :—To take concerted action en temperance questions at every election of any mem- ber of Parliament. It was argued against this motion that it would be unwise to adopt it at the present time when the Federation was only in course of formation, and eventually consideration was deferred for a month : as was also the consideration of the constitution and rules. The following gentlemen were constituted a com- mittee to consider what action should be takes at the fortheonsing licensing sessions :—Tha Revs. J. Holden. A. W. Riley, C. Finch, and J. Pulford-Williarns ; Messrs. K W. Humphreys, G. Marshall, W. Millington, and T. Cooke (sec. pro. tem. to the Federation).

div.head: DEATH OF A LOCAL TRADESMAN.
div.p: DEATH OF A LOCAL TRADESMAN.

We have to record, with much regret, the death of Mr. Michael Sexton, one of the firm of Messrs. Sexton Brothers, provision merchants, of Winwick- road and Ball-st., Warrington, and Waterloo-road, Widnes. The deceased was a native of Ireland, and had been in )usiness with his two brothers, Messrs. James and Owen Sexton, for some ten years in War- rington. He had always enjoyed good health up to Whit-Sunday, when he complained of being ill, and took to bed. Dr. Fox, jun., in the absence of Dr. Fox, sell, who was away in Norway, was called in and on Tues- day he got up and started off for his Widnes establish- ment, but he felt so ill that he was compelled to come back and take to bed again. Tie was sub- sequently attended by Dr. Fox, sen., on his re- turn from Norway, Dr. Joseph and the eminent physi- cian Dr. Carter,of Liverpool, were also called in but Mr. Sexton died on Tuesday afternoon. The cause of death was inflammation of the bowels. div.head: PROPOSED NEW LINE TO LONDON.
div.p: THE PROPOSED NEW LINE TO LONDON.

Yesterday morning the Select Committee of the House of Lords presided over by Lord Basing resumed the con- sideration of the bill for power lo extend the M.S. and L. Railway to Railway to London. Mr. Littler, Q.C., continued his reply on behalf of the promoters. After a consultation in private the Chairman said The Com- mittee have determined to pass the preamble of the bill, but this will require a clause to be inserted to carry out what was stated in conversation just now, as to the preservation of open spaces. The conversationreferred to was to the effect that the committee would require that the cover for the tunnel at the London terminus 'should be retained in perpetuity as an open space. Tha tall has already been passed by Um House of Commons.

div.head: BEFORE THE MAGISTRA.TES.
div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRA.TES.

THEFT OF HAMPERS. At the Warrington Borough Police Court, on Monday, John Rhooney, Ship Canal labourer, 5, Ship-yard, was charged with stealing on Saturday night, in Bank-st., three hampers, the property of Thomas Lyons, fruiterer, Cloth Hali-vard. The prisoner took the hampers off the prosecutor's cart, despite the remonstrances of a man named Edward Igo, and threatened him for interfering. Sergeant Longbotham deposed to apprehending the pri- soner at home, and finding the three hampers in the home, hie sister stating that he had brought them home, saying that they would do for cradles. The defendant denied his guilt-, and was sent to jail for a month with hard labour. Myra Willis, wife of Robert Willis, 39, Scotland-road, was charged with stealing about the 13th inst., a sheet the property of James and Catherine Daly, longing-house keepers, Scotland-road. She was sent to prison for seven days. AUDACIOUS ROBBERY AND ASSAULT. Kate McDonald, wife of Patrick McDonald, a forge labourer, residing at 108 Pierpoint-st., was charged, at the Warrington police court on Monday, with stealing, from the house of John Mahony, forgeman, 106 Pier- point-st., on Saturday night, a Paisley shawl, value 55., • his property, also with assaulting, on the same occasion, Mary Mahony, his wife, and with wilfully damaging a window to the amount of ss. The prisoner pleaded not guilty to each charge. It appeared that she entered the house of Mahony, a next door neighbour, and after bor- rowing a comb from his wife wanted to borrow a shawl and quarrelled with her because she would not let her have it, and got hold of her by the hair, dragging her to the floor. She afterwards combed out a handful of loosened hair from her head which she now produced. Her husband put the woman out, and she smashed the window, then came back and smashed it again, and put her hand in and took the shawl out, severely hurting Mrs. Mahony's hand with some instrument she had in hers, and with which she struck the prosecutrix on her trying to prevent the theft.—The prisoner was sent to jail for a month with hard labour. THEFT OF A WATCH. William Harrison, last from Wigan, a married and respectable-looking man, was charged with stealing, on Wednesday morning, from the house of Mr. Edgar, painter, 58, Wellington-street, a lady's silver watch. It appeared that the prisoner, who is Mrs. Edgar's brother- in-law's brother, came to Warrington on Saturday, and stayed with complainant. On Wednesday morning he went out, telling Mrs. Edgar he was going for a walk, and a few minutes after she missed the watch, which had been hanging on the mantelshelf. She followed the prisoner and came up with him near the Theatre Tavern, and spoke to him about the watch. P.C. Chrirnes was near, and she told him; and as she was do- • jug so the prisoner dropped the watch into her hand, and ran away. The constable ran after him and over- took him. On the way to the Police Station he said he took the watch intending to pawn it to get a few shillings, and afterwards send the ticket, and if he could afford it, the money.—The prisoner cried like a child throughout the proceedings,pleadecl guilty,and professed gmat penitence, and the Bench, believing lie was con- trite, merely fined him 103. and costs (£1 95. in all) ; in default 14 days. THEFTS FROM THE MARKET. Elizabeth Worslev, a young woman daughter of a „ - puddler at Dallam Forge, living at 136, Winwick-road, . was charged at the Warrington Borough Police Court with stealing the previous morning, 10 yards of ribbon value Ss.. the property of James Holligan, a Manches- ter draper, who has a stall in the market, an anti- macassar and two toilet covers, the property of Philip Gansberg, and a pair of lady's gloves, value Is. 6d., thel property of James Glover.—D. S. Monaghan deposed to seeing the woman picking up the articles at the stalls in the market, and putting sense down, and afterwards' discovering on apprehending her that those stolen were in her basket.—The Chief Constable said five or six charges could be brought against her, but by law he could only bring three.—The Chaarman asked the pri- soner whether her father behaved well to her, and she replied sometimes.—lnspcctor Uphill, agent for the Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Children, said he had ascertained that her father had ill-treated her.— The priscmer's brother said she had lost her mother some time ago and had not been herself since. He could not ' understand her behavioun—She was fined 10s. and' costs ; in default 14 days' imprisonment. THE ASSAULT ON A CHILD. At the Warrington Police Court, on Thursday, before Alderman Chandley (chairman), Alderman Sutton, and Councillor James Fairclough, Luke Cranks, aged 72, living in Railway Square, and lately employed as a boiler tender, at Whitecross Works, was brought up on remand charged with committing, upon the 11th inst., a crieninal assault on Lucy Brown, aged 13. Mr. J. Lyon Whittle, Town Clerk, appeared for the prosecu- tion, on behalf of the Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Children, and Mr. A. Browne for the defence. Mr. Whittle said the girl was sent by her mother to a shoemaker's in Liverpool-road, and in returning was met by the prisoner who sent her for some beer. She brought it to him, at his request, to the Whitecross works, and he was caught soon after by Mr. Charnock, ene of the managers, in the commission of the offence. Mr. Whittle said at the sug,gestion of Mr. Browns, the solicitor for the defence, he left it to the magistrates to deeide whether, considering the prisoner's age, it would not meet the justice of the case to deal with it as one of common assault.—Mr. Charnock having given evidence, Mr. Browne pleaded guilty on the prisoner's behalf, but said he had been 51 years in Warrington and had always previously borne a good character, and said he could not account for his committing the offence, except in this way that there was no fool like an old fool. He had been hi custody a week, as he had not been able to find the large bail demanded in his case, and had also lost a good situation.—The Bench fined him £5; in default a month's imprisonment, the Chair- man remarking that it was most painful to them that they should have before them a man of his age charged with such an offence.—The fine was paid. ANOTHER ASSAULT ON A CYCLIST. At the Warrington Police Court, yesterday, John Mar- ratt, Fennell-street, was charged with assaulting Zenas Tomlinson, of Liverpool, in Knutsford-road, on Satur- day. The complainant said he was coming on a bicycle at the rate of about four miles an hour, through Kuuts- ford-road, on Saturday night. The defendant, a stranger to him, was 20 yards before him, and he rang his bell, a very loud one. The defendant deliberately stood in front of him, and threw him off. Instead of helping to pick him up, he struck him in the eyes, which were discoloured, and he broke his lamp, and collared him, and would have assaulted him again but for the crowd. He had to unscrew his machine and screw it up again, as the defendant knocked it out of shape. P.C. 9 said on his going up to the defendant, at the request of the com- plainant, the man said he had struck him and would strike him again, adding that lie had no right to keock him down. Marratt was under the influence of drink, and Tomlinson quite sober.—The defendant said he was going from Latchford to Warrington with a basket of pork pies, over 401bs weight, on his shoulder. He was crossing the road,and heard someone shout " Look out, Jack." la ith such a weight on his shoulder he could not turn:round, and did not know what to do, so stood still, and the complainant deliberately ran into him and knocked him down. He never heard the bell. He then struck the complainant,but he never told the pcliceman he would do it again.—Alderman Harrison said it was

div.p: time this sort of thing was put a stop to. There were some people who thought they were licensed to put any obstruction in the way of cyclists. The latter were not always free from blame, but people thought they had a right to elbow them off the road, and this sort of offence was a growing one.—The defendant was fined 40s. and costs (£3 in all) ; in default a month's imprisonment.

WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE: COURT.

SATURDAY.—Before Alderman 3urgess, (Chairman) 1 Councillor Voisey, and Mr. J. Geddes. CHARGE OF ASSAULT ON A SON.—James Kinsella, of Pierpoint-street, was charged with assaulting, on the previous night, his son Edward Kinsella, a lad.—P.C. Barlow deposed to finding the lad lying unconscious at home. He lay in that condition for forty minutes, and Dr. Adams had to be called in. When the boy recovered,he told witness that his father had caused him to become unconscious by seizing him by the throat. as he was running away from him—The lad now denied this statement, and said he fell with his throat against a brick in running from his father, and thus became in- sensible.—The defendant said the lad was in the habit of playing truant, and had been absent from home all day. He went in search of him at eleven o'clock at night, and saw him in Bewsey-road, and ran after him. He put out his hand to prevent him falling, and the lad being out of breath, and witness's hand coming in contact with his throat, he was thrown into a state of insensibility.—The case was dismissed. DRUNlC.—Michael Burke was fined ss. for being drunk, on the previous night. MONDAY.—Before Alderman Francomb (chairman)

and Harrison. DRUNK AND DISORDERLT.—Thomas Gleeson, labourer, Knutsford-road, on Sunday night, who had been throw- ing his arms about and stopping women in the road, ss. and costs.—John Leigh, in Haydock-st., on Sunday morning, ss. and costs.—Charles Smith was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Knutsford-road, on Saturday night, also with assaulting Hugh Kelly on the same eccasion.—P.C. 44 said the prisoner was drunk and creating a disturbance, with a crowd about him.—Hugh Kelly said Ise and five others were riding on bicycles into the town, and the prisoner deliberately walked into the middle of the road and said to him " I am going to go for you," or words to that effect. He also tried to hit witness's friend, Mr. Fatrickson, but he managed to turn out of his way. Then the prisoner got hold of wit- ness's lamp, and twisted it round, and the machine fell, and the prisoner on the top of it, but witness kept on his feet. Then he made up to witness and attempted to strike him, and rolled ever again.—The Chief Constable said another man came to him on Saturday night and complained of being pushed off his bicycle in the same road that night.—The prisoner was fined 40s. and costs. —Margaret Fallon, drunk and disorderly in Bridge-st., I on Saturday night, was discharged with a caution.— Joseph Warburton, in Winwick-st., and Bessie Taylor, in Wilderspool-road, on Saturday night, were fined ss. I and costs each.—Thomas Pannell, in Barnes-st., on Sun- I day night, ss. and costs.—John Williams, in Hamilton- St., on the 6th inst., 7s. 6d., including costs.—Winifredl IBarber, in Winwick-rd., on the 12:h inst.' ss. and costs. MORE JUVENILE THIETING.—Wm. Hollowell, son of Elizabeth, a widow, 20 Litton's Row, and James Thovaas Carey, son of Martin, 29 Rose and Crown-st , both lads, and previous offenders, were charged with stealing, at about a quarter past eight on Saturday night, a box value 6d., the property of Thomas Watt, of Everton, near Liverpool, from a stall in the market. Both pris- oners pleaded guilty and were detained in court till the other cases were disposed of, and then ordered to be kept in the cells till 8 o'clock, but prior to being released to have six strokes of the birch rod each. Fliewriem.—John Stockton, labourer, 22 Greenall-st., and George Stockton, labourer, 3 Clare-st., were charged with fighting in Fennel-st., on the 11th inst. John was bound over in £5 for six months, and George dismissed. STREET OBSTRUCTION.—Bernard Boyle and James Smith, were charged with allowing a horse and cart to stand in Winwick-st., on the 11th inst. and dismissed on payment of costs. A SLEEPING CARMAN.—Thomas Garvin, a cabman was charged with being asleep in charge of his horse and cab In Winwick-st., at 3 a.m., on the 10th inst. The defend- ant pleaded that in consequence of a wedding at Apple- ton he had been at work since six the previous morning and dropped off to sleep.—Alderman Francornb : There is generally a wedding or a funeral when there is a drunken do. I don't see why they should either begin life or end it with drinking.—The defendant was fined 55. STREET GAMING.—Joseph Hardman and George Fearnley, boys, for playing a game of chance for money on Sunday afternoon, were fined Is. each. TUESDAY.—Before Messrs. R. Garnett and E. J. Guest CHARGE OF THREATENING A MOTHER.—WiIIiAM Noon, married man, was charged with threatening his mother, Catherine Noon, on Saturday night.--lhe complainant said he came on the Thursday night from Wales, where his wife was, and slept one night at his mother's. On Saturday night he came in drunk, and pushed her down, and kicked the table over, and said he would see some- " ' • her.7-fle denied _

threatening her or assaulting the point of going back to Flintshire to his wife.—He was discharged on promising to be out of the town by noon and not to molest his mother. AN ARMY ABSENTEE—James Cope was charged with absenting himself without leave from the army reserve. He said he had been to America and been left behind there by the crew of the ship he went with. He thought he would have been back by the next quarter, but could not get back. He sent notice on the 28th of the last month by letter to the authorities.—He was fined 40s. and costs. DRUNK.—Catherine Brown, drunk in Bridge-st., the previous night, was sent to jail for a month with hard labour. ABSENTEES FROM SCECOOL.—It the instance of Mr. G. Riley, school attendance officer, the following persons were fined for not sending their children to school : Michael Brannaghan, labourer, Jolley's-yard, 2s. 6d., and Bridget Brannan, Buckley-court, and Samuel Hollo- well, railway man, 29, Lord Nelson-st., ss. each. _

- . WEDNESDAY.—Bef ore Alderman Wright, (chairman) and Mr. E. M. Crosfield. DRONE AND DISORDERLY.—Robert Downey, drunk and disorderly in the Market Place, the previous even- ing, who had been very abusive to Mr. Woods, jeweller, in his shop, was dismissed on promising to kave the town. THEFT OF TIMBER.—John Edwards, of Dial Court,who had surrendered that morning was charged under a war- rant with stealing, on the 29th of March, a quantity of timber, the property of Thos. Williams. He had stolen it from some new buildings in Garibaldi-st. He had had the chance offered him of sending the timber back, but would not. He was sent to prison fcr a month's hard labour. FHlDAY.—Before _Aldermen_ Harrison (chairman) and

Wright. and Dr. Gornall. FRAUDULENT ENLISTMENT. Joseph Blazmers, was charged with making a false answer on attestation OH enlistment in the militia. A month's imprisonment. OTHER ASSAULTS—Henry Dagnall, 4 Buckley's Court, and Thomas Lee, Edelsten's Yard, summoned each other on charges of assault, on the 17th inst. at Town End.— Lee said he had appeared in a case against Dagnall's uncle in that court, and Dagnall met him and demanded the is. he got as a witness, and on his refusing it struck him, and thedefendant's female cousin hit him with a key.—Dagnall was fined ss. and costs and Lee dismissed. A ROUGH CHARACTSR.—WiIIiam Ellis, labourer, last from St. Helens, was charged with being drunk and dis- orderly in Buttermarket-et., on Thursday night, and assaulting William Hawksley on the same occasion.— D.S. Monaghan, the complainant, and another witness proved the cases, and Monaghan produced a nunsber of keys and a screw driver of which Ellis refused to give any account.—Hawksley said he never saw defendant be- fore the time of the assault, and he came up to him, swore at him, and struck him twice, and witness, by using his stick, prevented him striking a third time.— The Chief Constable said the defendant was an old offender who never worked except in jail, and worse things than these produced had on occasions been found lon him.—He was sent to prison for a month's hard labour. CHARGE OF NON-MAINTENANCE.—The case of George Ball, file-cutter, 2, Gorsey-lane, which was adjourned four weeks previous and in which he was charged with non-compliance with an order for payment of £7 3s. arrears for the maintenance of his wife Catherine Ball, 4, Orford Avenue,was heard .—M r. Jenkins appeared for the defence.—The complainant admitted having been several times convicted of being drunk and the like.—The defend- ant said he had been laid up months with a broken leg, and it was impossible for him to pay the arrears and live.—She hail told him that she had 10s. a week from one son and 12s. a week from another.—The complainant said she had not an average a week coming in from the sons, and she had to keep them out of the money.—Alderman Harrison said nothing had been proved against the woman's morality.—She might have • been guilty of little freaks and getting drunk now and then.—Mr. Jenkins : l'sn't that immorality.— . Alderman Harrison : Not within the meaning—The deputy magistrates' clerk said the offences were all coin- ' mitted before the order was made.—The defendant in reply to Mr. Jenkins, said in consequence of the condi- tion of his foot he could only earn half lie formerly did. . In answer to the Bench he said the arrears only com- menced in Decomher last, when he was disabled.—The Bench reduced the order to ss. a. week, and half the ! arrears were struck off, two months being allowed to pay this.

_ SAD DEATH OF A LIBERAL M.P.

Mr. L. L. Dillwyn, ALP., for Swansea, died there on Sunday, after a few hours illness. The hon. member arrived in his constituency from London in the middle of last week, apparently in his usual health, to begin his political campaign. On Satur- day evening, whilst at a meeting of his election com- mittee he was sr ized with a fit, and had to be carried to the Royal Hotel. After a lapse of several hours he recovered consciousness, and on Sunday morning seemed to be progressing favourably. Shortly before noon a ' change for the worse took place, and he died soon after midday. The deceased member was born in Swansea, on May 19,1819, His death removes a well known and prominent figure from the House of Commons and Parliamentary circles, and he will be universally regretted. In 1838 Mr. Dillwyn married Elizabeth, the daughter and heiress of Sir Henry de la Beche, who died in 1866. He leaves a family, One of his sons being a member of the bar. In addition to being a deputy lieutenant and magistrate for the county of Glamorgan, Mr. Dilwyn was a lieutenant-colonel of the 3rd Glamor- ganshire Rifle Volunteers. The funeral of the late Mr. Dillwyn, M.P., took place on Thursday, near Swansea, in the presence of 2,000 spectators.

BY MUNCHATJSEN THE SEKUND ! We'n a chap in eawr village wo " stretches" Ez fast ez a Sammie Brid flies : An' he never feels gradely onless he's Dispensin' sum thunderin lies. An' lest yo shud think aw'm romancin', An' writhe wot's not strictly true; Wi' eaur Editor's sanction aw'll gie yo

• A-very fair sample or two. - - He wur oncet at a greyt match at cricket. Wen Alfred Mynn made a big hit, An' th' ball wur i'th air twenty minutes, An' then tumblet into a pit Wen they went fer that bail in the wayter, Thay fund an owd pike welly dead; He wur sttimmin'abeawt wheer it dropt in, An' wur stunn'd we the blow on his yed; Once agen, wen he played at Sent Helen, He wur bathe a very fast ball, Wich he hit o'er two fields an' sum heauses, An' it stuck in an owd chapel wall! On the very same day, he wur fieldin', An' on makiu' a savage throw in, He laid the poor Umpire stone deead, We a teirible blow on his chin! But the biggest o' aw his big doin's, Wuz performed wr a two-barreed gun; Wen be shot at a greyt drove o' shepsters, An' browt um aw deawn wi' a run Then it took him an' two o' his cronies Haul a day just to gether them brids ; An' be sent um to Manchester Market, An' bowd um fer Seventeen Quids ! . Aw cud work a wole wick on his explites, But aw think wot aw've wrote is enuff ; Still, befoor aw wind up these few verses, Ass mun gie him a weel-desarv'd puff. W'en another ez once won a medal, Per lyin', hut he's only raw; An' tho' good, fer a yeadith, he's not in it— Munchausen the Sekund byets aw I

ANOTHER CASE OF NEGLECT OF CHILDREN. DRINK TUE CAUSE AS USUAL.

- - At the Warrington Borough Police Court, on Wednesday, before Alderman Wright (chairman) and Mr. E. M. Crosfield, Harriet Travis was charged that F., he betwe6u the Ist of May and the 21st June did wilfully neglect her two children, Henry aged 9, and Annie aged 6. Mr. Buckton, solicitor, ap- peared for the prosecutichi on behalf of the Society for the Prevention of Cruelty, to, Children —Mr, Buckton stated that the prisoner had lodged with Mrs.Rylands in School Brow. She appeared to have been in the habit of drinking, and the ease was the effect of drink. She could stand so much that she was never a ctually in the condition ordinarily called drunk,still the effect had been that she had spent all the money she had in drink instead of on her family. The children had been going about ill-clad. filthy, and generally in a , neglected condition.—Mrs. Jane Edgar, wife of John Edgar, of 126, School Brow, deposed that on the sth inst., she went to the defendant's lodgings. There was a bird- cage, but no furniture there, and no fire or food. She took the children some meat and bread and butter. The little girl subsequently had food from her. The defend- ant's husband was a decent hard-working man.—Mrs. Jane Graham, 111, School Brew, gave similar evidence as to the 3rd of June. The children, she said, had been neglected during the past fertnight.—Martha Daniels, 91, School Brow, gave corroborative evidence.—Mrs. Rylands deposed to the defendant paying her 15s. a fortnight for her own board and that of the two children and anether child.. She had given her food to give to the children and the defendant had said with an oath that she would not.—Dr. Cannell said the girl on the Bth of June, was much emaciated and suffering from bronchitis. She had the appearance of being neglected, and the scanty clothing would aggravate her disease. There was danger of consumption developing. She was in a dangerous state.—Seth Travis, the defendant's hus- band deposed that lie earned 345. a week, and had given his wife his wages regularly. He went to live with his daughter because of the pawning of the children's clothes, and had to giv'e up his house 4-1 years since.—Alderman Wright (thechairman) : Are we to understand because yonr wife wasted the money?—Witness : There must be something of that, and her companions too.—He did not think the children had ever been neglected, they had had plenty of food, but if people pawned their clothes he could not help it. He could not cury the children in his pocket.—P.S. Chantler deposed to apprehending the defendant at a house in Batteraby-lane.—The defendant, who denied the charge, was fined 40s. and costs ; in default a month's hard labour, and the Bench repri- manded the husband for not Seeing that the children were properly looked after: She paid the amount.

div.head: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.
div.p: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.
CIIICIKET.

The Athletic News" has the following in its issue on ' Monday :—" Warrington defeated their friends from Sale very easily on Saturday, despite the fact that they were without S. M. Cresfield, their captain. The best score in the match was made by G. Clarke, who has always shown consistent form, but on this occasion he eclipsed his previous efforts by putting together the fine total of 106. Clarke is by no means a giddy youth, for lam lead to believe that he commenced playing cricket nearly thirty years ago, so that his vigorous display is all the more meritorious.

Speaking about Warrington, lam reminded of the fact that an enthusiast has sent me the following choice note. Perpend " Warringtonians in general were in a state of ecstacy over the success of Mr. S. M. Crosfield in the Nottingham match. When he makes his debut on the Warrington ground something extraordinary will happen, so say the gods."

I am very pleased to hear of the ecstasy with which the Warringrtonians are clothing themselves. If they put some on their feet it will serve somewhat to soften the torture in treading on'the petrified kidneys which adorn the pavements of the town. But if they demon- strated their delight before the conclusion of the Lan- cashire and Notts match, they can now adorn themselves with a glorious hump, for they were a bit too previous. I don't know how many times a man can make a debut, but I was under the impression that in most places the first appearance was quite enough. Perhaps they manage this sort of thing better in Warrington. When- ever the next elebut of S. M. Crosfield takes place, I hope someone will send me word of the "something extraor- dinary "that is going to happen. Perhaps the " gods " are going to kill the enterprising admirer who has sent me the above note. If so the gods be praised. They must love him, tor is it not written, " They whom the gods love die young." ? And he must be young, even though he be long.

The Lancashire Eleven are making the same sort of figure in this as they did in the early part of last season —that is, losing match after match and putting them- selves in an apparently hopeless position with regard to the championship. The defeat by Yorkshire has been followed by a still more severe reverse at the hands of Nottinghamshire. The team, however, usually improves as the season advances, and we hope to be able to give a better account of their performances when the Oxford University and Surrey matches have been played. Mr. liornby took a holiday instead of going to Nottingham, and we imagine says the " Manchester Guardian," we are expressing the general opinion in saying that his absence had in all probability nothing to do with the result. Mr. Sydney Croafield captained the team with excellent judgment, and played a splendid innings. On Friday night Lancashire seemed to have the advantage; but the bowling was weak on Saturday, and the Nottingham men, hitting with a degree of freedom which was very welcome to the so-called " crowd," fairly wore down Mold and Briggs, and achieved a bril- liant victory. Watson's bowling was of no use whatever in the match, and Mold was quite ineffective in the second innings.

The county bowling evidently needs strengthening; but where is the new man to be found ? Briggs works vary hard, and those who have looked askance at his comparative failure in batting would do well to re- member the amount of work lie is called upon to do as a bowler. Mold has been out of form so far, but we believe he will not be long in taking a higher place in the averages than he occupies at present. With regard to the batting, some speculation has been excited as to , the reason of Mr. Kemp's retention in the Eleven. The Rochdale amateur has been unlucky hitherto, but he is one of the men of whom it is never safe to predict that they will fail.

Yorkshire have assumed the lead in the race for championship honours. Last week they defeated Kent and Middlesex; and their record now shows only a single defeat and nine victories. They were beaten by the M.C.C., but they have defeated Cambridge Univer- sity, Essex, Staffordshire, Derbyshire, Leicestershire, Sussex, Lancashire, Kent, and Middlesex. Such a re- cord has given the gr,ratest satisfaction in the county. The victories over the first-class counties have been achieved by cricket worthy of the best traditions of Yorkshire. Tie new men are coming to the front rapidly ; but the veteran Ulyett is still almost un- approachable.

Gloucestershire has fallen a prey to Sussex, chiefly through the instrumentality of the " despised " lob. In Dr. E. M. Grace the western county has a dangerous slow bowler, but ne does not appear to have given his comrades much practice. Even the champion himself was " uneasy." In the first innings lie was caught off a slow ; and in the second Humphreys sent him a ball that fairly bowled him. Mr. George Brann was found in a hitting mood, and his 133 must be regarded as a very fine preininence. Sussex will be inspirited by this victory.

The Surrey and Middlesex match afforded Mr. Walter Read an opportunity of which he made good use, arfd the famous amatehr may now be regarded as having fairly regained his form. Abel also played extremely well, and Stoddart, for Middlesex, hit with splendid vigour. The Surrey executive have great reason to con- gratulate themselves on Lockwond's achievements both with the bat and ball this year.

Lancashire's fast bowler, Mold, has accomplished some notable feats with the ball in his career, but he was Awfully disappointed at Werneth, when he failed to capture the whole of the wickets. He only got nine of them, and then wasn't satisfied. In fact, so much was he put about that he said he would gladly have given a sovereign to have taken the other. We like a man who loves a lot, and Mold is built after our own heart. Some people might think that he couldn't do it, but as a matter of fact • Mold has the 1 papers signed, sealed, and delivered that on no less than three occasions he has struck terror in the hearts ot ten batters, and struck their wickets at the same time. References, we understand, can be made to Warrington, Uppingham Rovers, and Surrey. Club and Ground.

The four princiPal matches last week end furnished a cnincidence,inasmuch as in each case the side that went in second came off victorious. Surrey won by seven wickets, Cambridge University and Notts each by six wickets, and Yorkshire by four. In every instance the wicket held good to the end, and for once in a way the bat was master of the ball.

div.p: 6TII V.B. KING'S LIVERPOOL REGIMENT

The annual inspection of this Battalion took place at Sefton Park on Saturday, the inspecting officer being Col. Twentyman, commanding Bth and 40th Regimental Districts. The Newton detach- ment of the regiment under the command of Captain Norman McCorquodale, consisting of 1 officer, 5 sergeants, 14 drummers and buglers, and 114 rank and file, marched from their headquarters at South- worth-road and proceeded to Edgehill by the 4.20 express,and from thence to Sefton Park, when,hav- ing joined the headquarters,the whole were formed ' into line. After receiving /the inspecting officer with the customary "general salute." they pro- ceeded to "march past" in company and quarter column, during the performance of which Col. Twenty- man expressed his appreciation of the 'steadiness of the men, especially the rear companies (Newton detach- ment). Line having been reformed, the battalion was put through the manual firing and bayonet exercises which were well and smartly performed. Col. Wood then took thr regiment and having manceuvred into a
IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT.
HOUSE OF LORDS.—MoNnear. The Lord Chancellor took his seat on the woolsack at
• four o'clock. NEW PEEL—Lord Rockwood took his seat on his

elevation to the peerage. THE EVELYN V. HIIRLDERT CASE.—LOMI COLERIDGE initiated a short discussion on the Evelyn-Hurlbert case, In the course of which Lord HEascanu. said the rules placed s difficulty in the way of the Publis Prosecutor getting copies of impounded documents, but measures were being taken to prevent such an incident again ris-

ing. THR SHALL AGRICULTURAL HOLDINGS BILL.—On the report of amendments to this Bill, Lord Herschel' moved an amendment to make small holdings personalty of a holder dying intestate.—Lord Sausenay opposed the amendment, which was rejected by 83 to 21. MISCILLANSOUS.—The Drainage and Improvement of Land (Ireland) (No. 2) Bill was read a second time The Accumulations Bill passed through committee. The Poor-law Schools !Ireland) Bill was read a second time. The Isle of Man (Customs) Bill Was read a third time. The other orders of the day were disposed of, and "the House adjournedd, at ten minutes past seven o'clock. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—Mcummr.

• The Speaker took the chair at thrbe o'clock. OGYRRNMENT BUSINESS.-011 the motion of 'Mr. Gowning, it was agreed that for the remainder of the session the House should adjourn each day on the con- clusion of Government business. POST-OFFICE OFFICIALS AND THE ELECTIONS.—Mr. HOWELL called attention to the circular issued forbidd- ing post-office officials taking a prominent part in the forthcoming general election, or endeavouring to extract promises from candidates with reference to their duty and pay, and held that such a notice was violation of the Postmaster-General's official duties and position.— Sir J. Fergusson said it was customary on theY eve of a general election to issue such a circular, and that if members of the postal service were to take a leading part in the election it would lead to all sorts of abuse. MR. TATE'S OFFER.—Mr. GOSCEIEN, replying to Dr. Farquhartoa, said he could hold out no hope as tc a successful resumption with Mr. Tate of the negotia- tions respecting the establishment of a gallery of British art. Trim Dissourriow.—Mr. BALFOUR, in reply to hon. members, said the Archdeaconry of Cornwall Bill Would not be further proceeded with, and the prorogation and dissolution would in all probability take place on Tues- day, June 28th. IN COMMITTEBI—The House then went into committee on the East India revenue accounts, when the Hon. G. N. Curzon presented his yearly financial statement, and the usual resolutions were passed. The HOUSE) adjourned at ten o'clock. HOUSE OF LORDS.—TUESDAY. The Lord Chancellor took his seat on the wool-sack at a quarter past four o'clock. SMALL AGRICULTURAL HOLDINGS BILL.—On the motion to read this Bill a third time, Lord Denman moved that it be read a third time that day six months. His lordship protested against the Bill passing into law without suffi- cient consideration. The Marquis of SALISBURY drew attention to the fact that the noble lord's remarks were not relevant, Lord DENMAN Yoh wish to cloture me again, do you (sarcastically) ? lam very much obliged to you (warmly). I will not give Way in an hereditary house to the best man who ever sat in it. His lordship then resumed his seat without putting his motion. The Bill was read& third time and passed. IRISH NATIONAIe EDUCATION BILL.—Earl CADOGAN moved the second reading of this Bill, which came up from the House of Commons, and was read a first time on Friday.—The Marquis of WATERFORD, considering the measure a very liberal one, Warmly supported it.—Lord COURTOWN also supported the Bill, and said that in his opinion the conscience clause should be found in a measure dealing with national education in Ireland.— Lord Da VRSCI also suppOrted the Bill, which was read a second time, Bums ADVANCED.—The Military Lands (Consolidation) Bill, the Railway and Central Traffic Act, 1888, Amend- ment Bill, the Telegraph Bill, the Public Libraries Law Consolidation Bill, and the Land Commissioners (Ireland) Bill were read a second time. The House adjourned at ten minutes past eight. HOUSE OF CQMMONS.—TussnaT. _ . .

The Speaker took the chair at three o'clock. POST CARDS.—Sir J. FERGOSSON informed Mr. ffenniker Heaton that the boon of redirection conferred upon the public in respect to letters could not be extended to postcards. - MAILS TO AMERICA.—Sir J. FacciussoN, at Mr. Heaton's request gave the weight of mails despatched from this country during last year to the United States, and for the conveyance of which the British Government paid £98,300. BILLS ADVANCED.—A number of Bills were read a second time, amongst them being the British Columbia (Loan) Bill, the object of which is to guarantee a roan to the Government of British Columbia for the purpose of carrying out a scheme of crofter emigration, The Shop Hours Bill passed through Committee and was read a third time. The House adjourned at five o'clock. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—Wmasiosv.

The Speaker took the chair at a quarter past twelve, and a house was made at twenty-five minutes past. THE DISSOLUTION.—Mr. LABOUCHERE again asked whether arrangements could be made so as to include Saturday week in the legal days for pelting in the boroughs, but Mr, A. J. Balfour said he must adhere to his announcement that the dissolution would take place next Tuesday. SMALL HOLDINGS BILL.—The Lords' amendments to the Small Holdings Bill were considered. A division was taken on the amendment to omit clause 11,which clause provided that small holdings were to be considered as personalty and not realty, and the amendment was car. tied by 48 votes to 17. The remainder of the amend- ments were agreed to. On the House going into Com- mittee on the Fishery Board (Scotland) Bill, Dr. Clark moved to relate.; progress in order that amendments might be put on the paper by Scotch members, and Mr. Hunter supported the motion. Mr. A. J. BALFOUR,' in assenting to the proposal, said the respoesibility for de- feating the bill would rest on the hon. members. Pro- gress was then reported and the bill withdrawn, The British Columbia Loan (Scotch Crofters' Emigration) Bill passed through Committee, and the .House rose shortly after two 4 'cl HOUSE OF LORDS.—THURSDAY. • The Lord Chancellor took his seat on the woolsack at a quarter-past four o'clock. MISCELLANEOUS—Lord Connemara took the'oath and subscribed the roll on his elevation to the peerage. 'The Casual Wards Bill, which stood for second reading, was withdrawn. The National Education (Ireland) Bill passed through Committee, after discussion,and without amendment. The Public Works Loan Bill and a number of others were read a second time. Lord Brassey called attention to the difficulties which the North Borneo Co. had to encounter, and urged the desirability of North Borneo being converted into a Crown Colony. Lord Ithutsford replied that the question 0 Government in- terference was not ripe for consideration. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—THURSDAY. 'he Speaker took the chair at three o'clock. There were only four questions on the paper, all of them unimportant. THE GOVERNMENT AND SATURDAY POLLING. Mr. RITCHIE moved that at the conclusion of the busi- ness the House should adjourn until Monday. Mr. LABoucnEne opposed the motion. He understood that the House cf Lords would finish their business on Friday, therefore if there was a Saturday sitting instead of Monday the dissolution could be held onMondav, and the writs issued the same day in order that Saturday could be included in the permissible days on which the poll could be taken. Mr. RITCHIE, after remarking that this subject had already been several times discussed within the past few days, repeated the Ministerial objections to Saturday pollings, on the ground that they practically disqualified small shop-keepers and Jews,that experience had shown they did not increase the polls, and that working-mr had no difficulty in voting on ordinary days since ' polling hours had been extended till eight o'clock,. The British Columbia Loan Bill was read a th• and passed. After a short sitting, the House adjourned till Monda, THE PLEASIJEIi OF RATING k DRINKING. sins of companies in sucrcession to the front, when e. performed a portion of battalion drill. The weather, which was somewhat threatening All the afternoon, now gave signs of breaking down, and the inspection was brought to a close by Col. Twentyman addressing the battalion. He said that he was highly pleased at the ap- pearance and physique of the men,who,be thought,could do their drill well. He saw a great many things to ad- mire in the regiment, but requested that the officers and guides should pay more attention to their own particular duties. He felt bound to make these observations not in a spirit of fault-finding but solely for the good of the regiment. When these small matters were rectified, there would be nothing to complain of. He was happy to be able to make a favourablareport of the battalion to headquarters. The regiment thus marched to their headquarters at Everton-road, pro4ded by the lancer escort, which kept the ground. The strength on parade was 611 all ranks, a number which has not been reached on similar parades for many years. The naost noticeable features of this inspection were the very large proportion of men in the ranks, the-battalion being formed of 8 com- panies of 25 file each, the cyclist section, consisting of 1 officer ;And 23 men were particularly and worthily attractive of attention, and last, though not least, the small proportion of recruits in plain clothes. This of course to a certain extent accounts for the large num- bers in the ranks. These important points, with many others, give very striking evidence of the improvement in this battalion under the 'command of Lieutenant-Col. Wood, especially to those who knew the regiment a few years ago. There is but very little doubt that these improvements will continue until a very perfect state of discipline and efficiency is attained. The total strength of the battalion is now 698 all ranks.
