div.head: SERIOUS RAILWAY COLLISION AT WIN WICK JUNCTION.
div.p: SERIOUS RAILWAY COLLISION AT WIN WICK JUNCTION.

A collision of a serious character, but happily, unattended with personal injury, occurred at Win- wick Junction, about, 3.15. on Tuesday morning. The morning was rather foggy, and a light engine, proceeding in steam to the north, was stopped by signals in the loop. On the way from Warrington was a special fast goods for Liverpool, which had received "line clear " at Winwick Junction. As the goods entered the section, the signalman gave the light engine a signal to proceed, but it had not gone far before the fast goods came up and pitched into it at full speed. The impact caused the tender of the light engine to leave the rails, and for about 150 yards it ran in this position, tearing up the ballast and damaging the permanent way, until it reached the points, when it broke loose ifrom the engine and overturned, going through the fence on the side of the line. The tender was smashed, and the engine of the goods train received some damage to its buffers, but was able to proceed. The line was blocked for some time, but, owing to the very early hour, the traffic was not interfered with. The driver of the light engine was shaken, but he and the fireman, by jumping from the engine, es- caped serious injury.

div.head: CHARGE OF SEVERELY WOUNDING.
div.p: CHARGE OF SEVERELY WOUNDING.

Before tie Warrington borough magistrates, on Tuesday, Thomas savage a married man, aged 42, a labourer at Messrs. Rylands' wire works, and living at 40, Orferd-st., was charged with feloniously and maliciously wounding, about half-past six the pre- vious evening, James Owen, aged 29, a widower and his brother-in-law, also a labourer at Rylands's works, and living behind a provision shop which is at 33, School Brow.—The Chief Constable said the prisoner married the complainant's sister,and on the 10th of May the two men were working together at their place of employment, when the prisoner missed Owen from the works, and went to his (the prisoner's) house, and, as he (the prisoner) alleged discovered his wife and Owen in the house The prisoner came to the Police Station and com- plained. There was a great uproar in the neighbourhood. On Monday night, the prisoner went home, and something was amiss which caused a quarrel between him and his wife, and it got to blows on his part. The complainant was somewhere outside, and went to the:house, and theprisoner either struck him with a poker, or threw something at him, and severely fractured his skull, causing him to bleed very much, and P.C. Newey took him to the Infirmary, where he was at present, the doctors considering the case a very dan- gerous one. The prisoner on being apprehended denied striking Owen with a poker, but said he threw a plate at him and added "what business has he to come into my house ?" The prisoner had had drink, but was consi- dered sober, and the complainant was perfectly sober. Alexander Lomas, a boy, deposed to seeing the prisoner throw a plate at Owen and then go upstairs out of the way, and to Owen throwing half bricks through the window at him.—The Prisoner, at the Chief Constable's request, was remanded for a week, though it was stated that-Owen might be two or three weeks !.n the Infir- mary.

div.head: WARRINGTON CHURCH SOCIETY.
div.p: WARRINGTON CHURCH SOCIETY.

A meeting of this newly formed Society was held on Monday evening,at the Masonic Rooms Sankey- st. Mr. C. Sawkins Burgess presided. There was a moderate attendance. A letter of apology for non-attendance was read from the Rector of War- rington, in which he said that the proposed object of the society he believed to be an excellent one, and worthy of the support of all churchmen. The CHAIRMAN said they were met that night to in- augurate the Warrington Church Society. It would be in the recollection of all of them that sonic three weeks ago a conference of churchmen was held in that room, at which it was resolved to form a society, and at which, also, a provisional committee was appointed to make all the preliminary arrangements. That com- mittee has had several meetings and the chief result of its work had been the production of the rules of the society, which had been printed and circulated. A few members bad been enrolled, but no systematic or organ- ised attempt had been made to obtain members. Some persona had objected to join the society on the ground that there were so many societies, and that to join any more was to increase the number of meetings one had to attend .The provisional Committee had,however,carefully refrained from fixing regular meetings of the society, and only one compulsory meeting in the year had been fixed, and that was the annual general meeting. Allud- ing to the work the society proposed to undertake, he said that they would prof-Ably provide for a series of public meetings during the winter. He would like to express a hope that all who took an interest in the church's welfare would do all in their power to help the society in its work. Some had said they would not join at present, but would wait to see what the society was going to do. He would, however, point out, that in order to be successful in carrying out the scheme they had put before them, they required a large number of enthusiastic members. The subscription had been pur- posely fixed at the low sum of is. per annum, and there was nothing in their rules to exclude the membership of ladies. Referring to the criticism of a " Radical Churchman" published in some of the local newspapers, the Chairman denied that they were a set of Tories, and that their object was to promote the interests of the Tory party. Let him say once for all, that there was not a shadow of foundation for that statement. (Hear, hear.) Speaking for himself, if there had been the slightest pretext for such a statement, he would not have had anything to do with the formation or promotion of the society, and he knew he was speaking the feeling of the majority of those who were acting with him. (Hear, hear.) It was clearly under- stood amongst them that they were not to bean adjunct of any political party, and unless they were prepared to place the interests of the church before party objects they should absolutely fail in the object they had in view. The only safe course for them as churchmen was not to ally themselves with any political party. (Hear, hear.) One of the things of most urgent importance was to formulate questions to put to the Parliamentary candidates. They were on the eve of a great crisis. The issues at the comir g election were very grave, and it might be that in the next Parliament questions affect- ing the church might be brought up as ripe for settle- ment, and it appeared to him that there were at least two points upon which they should address questions to Parliamentary candidates—he referred to denomina- tional education and disendowment. (Hear, hear.) I They should have a clear declaration from their repre- sentative as to whether ho will oppose any measure which interfered with the management of their church schools. With regard to disendowment he did not think either political party were per- fectly safe on the subject They knew that one of them was practically pledged to disendownient of the church in Wales, and it passed his comprehension I how that could be lone without affecting the church in England. It seemed to him that both churches must stand or fall together. (Hear, hear.) He then moved that the following officers of the society be appointed : —President, the 'Rector o: Warrington ; hon. sec. Mr. Herbert Woods ; hon. treasurer, Mr. H. Dobson. The Rev. F. SLATER seconded this proposal,which was carried. Mr. R. DonsoN moved that the committee consist of the following :—Rev. Morley Stevenson, Rev. J. J. Langham, Messrs. C. S. Burgess, J. Coxon, J. D. Buck- ton, F. Appleton, J. Burgess, H. J. Westbrook, Edward Gibbon, John Hatton, and John Hesketh. Canon WEST, of Manchester. then gave an address to the meeting in which he strongly advised thatthe society should be careful in keeping itself free from and depend- ence upon any political party. The wanted to lift the Church out of political party attachments. Unless they were careful their organisation would get into the hands of a few, and those few of one party, who would speak in the name of the Church,and yet whose action might be repudiated by a majority of churchmen in the district. Speaking with regard to the three questions which had , been mentioned by the Rector at the previous meeting of denominational education, disendow- ment, and temperance. Canon West thought the two first-named should take precedence of the last-named. For his own part he could not give up his Churchman- ship for his teetotalism. He would sooner cut his right hand off than send a man to Parliament who was pledged to the disestablishment of the Church in Wales, simply because that man claimed to be a temperance candidate. (Applause.) Questions were invited by Canon West, but none were forthcoming. He then said he would ask the Chairman which question in his opinion ought to be the most im- portant--disendowment or temperance? The CHAIRMAN : Disendowment. (Applause.) A vote of thanks to CANON WEST, moved by Mr. JOHN WHITE, and seconded by the REV. MORLEY STEVENSON, and a similar vote of thanks to the Chair- man, brought the meeting to a close.

AN UPROARIOUS CRICKET MATCH.-NEWTON- LE-WILLOWS WIT El CHAMPION AND OAKLEY , VERSUS EARLESTOWN, WITH MILLER AND HARRISON.

Sir,—l have been, for the last 45 years, a lover of the game of cricket, and have taken part in many hard- fought battles; but I never witnessed such rowdy scenes as were enacted on the Newton ground last Saturday. Let me at once acquit the players on both sides of any part in the rowdyism ; but the action of the Earlestown portion of the spectators would not have been out of place at a bear baiting or a cock fight ; and was certainly not inferior in the matter of howling and hooting to the most brutal football match. There were many ladies on the field, who had to listen to disgusting language freely bandied about ; and the fielders were hailed with all kinds of epithets, as seemed right to these desecrators oh a manly game. In one particular part of the field, when a hall was struck in the crowd, they took care to kick it away, and so put the fielder to extra trouble in finding it ; this being a sample of the fairness of these models of modesty and fair play ! Betting, also, was a noisy element introduced ; and altogether it was a scene I hope never to witness again. The Newton Executive will no doubt be chary how they grant their ground again for such sorry exhibitions ; and these actions will come home to roost, when, as is by no means unlikely, the Earlestown Cricket Club is left severely alone by every respectable club.—Yours, &c., AN OLD STAGER AT CRICKET. Newton-le-W illows, 21, 6, 1892.

div.head: WORD FOR MR. BRUNYER.
div.p: A WORD FOR MR. BRUNYER.
" Look on this picture and on this."

Sir,—llistory shows that the liberties the working classes now enjoy have been obtained by the Liberal party and that the Tory party have ever been the up- holders of the rich to the disadvantage of the poor,of the peer against the plebeian, and who now under the guise of Unionist are playing their old game of bamboozling the electors with bogies of the most flimsy descriptiox, And working-men if they knew on which side their bread is buttered will put a large X opposite the name of John Tomlinson Brunner in the ballot box.

Taking the matter personally, Mr. Brunner has keen an excellent member of Parliament. He has attended to his duties most assiduously, has introduced Several claues into Acts of Parliament which have proved of the greatest nenefit, and he has shown that his promises are not like pie crusts 'made to be broken. His votes have always been in ac- cordance with his pledges, and those have ever been in favour of the people. Those in Northwich district should ever feel grateful to him for his work in connec- tion with the Subsidence Bill. In fact, there is no reason why the feelings of the electors should have changed ; I do not believe they have changed, and the coming election will show that the constituency is still Liberal to the core. Mr. Whiteley is continually asking where is the scheme of Home Rule? Can lie tell us where is the Tory programme ? From his recent speeches his would appear to be made up of an Eight Hours Bill for Miners, compensation to publicans, and Mr. Chamberlain's pre- cious State aid pensions of ss. a week. I don't want to ask too much at once, but will he support one man one vote, improved registration laws, a reform of the Land Laws, which will make the transfer of land easy and cheap, and which will give a tenant compensation for disturbance; an Allotments Act which will no of some use ; free education and popular control of the schools; and the abolition of perpetual pensions ; and last but not least, seeing the benefit would be so soon derived, will he give his influence to have the poll- ing day for the Northwich Division fixed for a Saturday, so that the Runcorn chemical workers who are now employed at Northwich and Lostock and others can come and vote without losing half a day, and so that the watermen will have a chance to vote at all. I have spoken to some shopkeepers both large and small and they state that Saturday is equally as good a day for them as any other.—Yours, &c., AN ELECTOR. Runcorn, June 23, 1892.

THE WARRINGTON CANDIDATES AND QUES- TIONS SUBMITTED BY THE AMALGAMATED SOCIETY OF RAILWAY SERVANTS. Sir,—As Branch Secretary to the above, I am glad although in duty bound, to tackle the chief objection which Mr. Dakin, and perhaps a few others have to the questions put by our Society. At the same time, I strongly object to his assumption, that because there are a large number of railway servants outside the Society, the majority of them are opposed to its action; vain assumption is no argument. Again,l object to the very suggestive manner in which Mr. Dakin singles out a particular company as a criterion. Fortunately, or unfortunately, exceptions do not govern arguments ; that being so, they are useless in our case. Now for the questions : No. 1. Mr. Eakin dismisses as impracticable " A school boy's objection certainly," and the result of vain logic, in drawing the inference that the practical railway men of our Society meant a hard and fast maximum limit. Such is misleading to the public, and a wrong construe- ticn of our Society's expectations. What our Society wants is a maximum limit with an enhanced rate of pay- ment for overtime. Then the companies will keep to the day's limit as near as it is possible, and thus administcr to the welfare of their servants, and the safety both of them and the public. . The report of the Select Committee goes a long way to prove that Mr. Dakin's theory of long hours is wrong ;

and for him to complain of men like myself advocating this principle, is hardly supported by the " logic " which he parades. The 11 hours day limit recom- mended by the Committee (it might just as well have been 10) will go a long way towards abolishing excessive hours of labour, which at present prevail on many railways. Everybody, "generally speaking," agree that alO h urs day is sufficient and reasonable. We feel, therefore, justified in asking for it ; and the very first outcome of it would be to obviate the very thing Mr. Robert Pierpoint and Mr. Dakin seem so afraid of. Out of work and short time cases would be less numerous, owing to the fairer division of labour, which would in- evitably follow upon its adoption. Question No, 4. In Mr. Dakin's objection to this ques- tion, he again joins issue with Mr. Robert Pierpoint, and between them they produce the finest bit of logic ever exhibited. Here it is in all its sweet simplicity "The adoption of self-acting coupling appliances," they say, would entail the dismissal of thousands of shunters. Now if the self-acting couplers could talk and marshall the traffic, then there might be some justification for such a statement. Why, sit, the greatest duffer on the railway, who knows anything about shunting, would come to a different " logical " conclusion from this. I say, as a practical railway-man, that it will make no difference to the employment of shunters; and you may depend upon it, that had there been the slightest possi- bility of such being the case, the Companies would have adopted the same lone ago. No, sir, the only advant- age intended from self-acting coupling appliances, is to minimise the danger of both shunters and breaksmen, which is very great both to life and limb, and is quite a sufficient reason to justify the questions being put. Question No. 5. As to this I contend that it is just as desirable for locomotive drivers to qualify for certifi- cates in the interests of the public, as it is for an en- gineer or captain on Board a ship. A " Loco" engine- man has to understand the rules of the road as well as the technicalities of his engine, and, seeing that they have lives entrusted to their care, it is only a logical conclusion to expect them to give a measure of qualifi- cations to satisfy the public in railway travelling, and thereby, add, by giving confidence to the Company's interest

The meeting in Widnes Drill Hall, last evening week, was the best held up to that time in support of Mr. Deacon's candidature. The huge building was crowded. Not only was the whole of the sitt- ing accommodation utilised, but there were many hundreds standing alongside the walls, and people were swarming right up to the platform, and the proceedings were characterised by an enthusiasm and" go" that appeared inspiring to the candidate and all concerned.

Mr. Deacon was in good form. He spoke for half- an-hour with an ease and confidence,and a declama- tory finish that marks him out as a coming plat- form orator. And what is more to the purpose, his matter was beyond criticism. He figuratively de- molished Mr. James White for his puerile personali- ties, at the previous Tory meeting, and he raised a perfect storm of cheering when he announced that no word of his should ever rankle in the breast of any of them after the contest was over.

The cause of Mr. White's ire was a yisit paid to Clapham to gather information about Mr. Gilliat's political career in that constituency, and as Mr. Deacon justly observed, they had a perfect right to critisice Mr. Gilliat's pubdc career and to lay his record before the electors if they thouglic neces- sary.

Mr. Gilliat's record,so far as 1. can glean ,is that of an unreasoning Tory, who has given a hl ind adher- lion to the Government in defiance of some of his election pledges. Those who are desirous of seeing reforms, political or social, carried out need not look to him forhelp if votes in the past are a guide.

Apropos of Home Rule, Mr. Deacon made a capital hit in reference to the religious persecution bogie that is at present being so assiduously paraded be- fore th• voters. He showed by a reference to his- tory that when the Protestants in this country were undergoing the direst persecution, and had to flee for their livs, the Catholics of Ireland received them and succoured them, and he asked were the descendants of such men, with better education and wider sympathies, likely to become faithless to their traditions,and oppress their Protestant fellow- countrymen? From the cheer that went up it would appear that the hundreds present were not afraid of the "bogie."

Question No. 6. It appears Mr. Dakiv is satisfied with contracting out of Liability Act, but it so happens that a great many are not, and his satisfaction is no argument. All it does is to obstruct the progress of those who suffer from it, viz., working-men off the railways as well as on. Can Mr. Dakin rest peaceable in his mind as an obstructionist to the welfare of his fellow men ? _

No. 7, and last, is the key to the whole lot ; and whether party capital is being made out of it or not,the sooner it becomes law the better will it be for working- men, whose interests will be best promoted by " paddl- ing their own canoe." . . . . .

when the public come to know the stringent conditions under which railway men are employed, it will be admitted by every right thinking person that we as a society are not asking too much nor anything that is unreasonable.

The Widnes Trades Council, which by the way also includes Ruacorn and district, have this week considered the replies pf the candidates to the questions sent out to them, and which were pub- lished in this journal last Saturday. The Council consider Mr. Gilliat's answers most unsatisfactory, and advise and urge the Trades Unionists in Widnes Division to vote for Mr. Deacon, who was highly favourable to the reforms indicated by the Coun- cil. In regard to the contest in the Northwich Division, the Trades Council consider both the re- plies of Mr. Brunner and Ar. Whiteley to be satis- factory, and they therefore, offer no advice to their members, who are allowed to exercise their own private judgment as to whom they should vote for.
In conclusion I beg to remind Mr. Dakin, it is better to be forward in a good cause than either to stand still or obstruct it. Yours truly, HORATIO OGDEN.
5, Colling,s-st., Warrington.

Mr. Brunner has spent a—v-ery busy week amongst his constituents this week. On Monday night he addressed meetings at Northwich and Wincham ; on Tuesday night he was again at Northwich and on Wednesday evening he was the principal speaker at an open air meeting at Moulton. Last night he was at Halton and Aston. At each place there has been a large and enthusiastic audience.

Runcorn Tempera•sce Federation appears to be an organisation of very slow growth. The stumbling block in the way last Tuesday was a proposition that concerted action on Temperance questions be taken at every Parlia- mentary Election. Of course there are Tory teetotallers and Unionist teetotalers, and it would appear Irma the fact that consideration of this important motion has been adjourned until after the General Election that their politics are stronger than their teetotalism, notwithstand- ing the protestations so frequently heard to the con- tary. If the Federation is to be of any practical use whatever, it must make felt its influence at every Parlia- mentary Election. The representatives, on Tuesday evening, did decide to interfere in the elections of local administrative bodies, which cannot help forwaid legis- lation on temperance, and then they stultify themselves thoroughly by refusing to take action in the only elections where their interference would be any practical benefit to their cause. Runcorn Board of Commissioners cannot pass Local Option nor the Board of Guardians Sunday Closing, and the other local body, the Burial Board Will see decently interred both teetotalers and beer drinkers with the utmost impartiality— on payment of the usual fees, but they can't pass a bill to cOMpOnta the publicans. But of course, it is of flee utmost importanc6 to take an active part in the election of representatives to those bodies ; and the election of an M.P. who would have a voice in saying "Ape" or " No " to temperance legislation is of an consequence whatever! Mr. James Tomkinson, the Liberal candidate for Eddisbury Division has wooed that constituency with a constancy and ardour that merits acceptance at the hands of the electors, and if prognostications prove true he will on this occasion be triumphant over his opponent, Mr. Tollernache. Mr. Tom kinson is trying a bold experi- ment, which it crowned with success may have many imitators in future. His election motto is " Trust in the people and no canvassing," and in addition there is. no show of hands asked for at his meetings.

A precedent for this course was furnished at the recent County Council elections by Mr. Roger Bate, of Tarporley. In that contest it was claimed for the Tory candidate that six-sevenths of the electors had promised to poll for him, and Mr. Bate was told it would be folly and mis-spent money to oppose him. Mr. llate's reply was that he would put his views before the electors, and they could vote for him or not, as their judgmeat dic- tated, and he would have no canvassing and no election machinery. His trust in the common sense and discrim- ination of the voters was proved well justified, as he won the seat by a substantial majority.

After this can " Scrutator " say " we lose £l5O the estimated cost of the poll for ever, fora mere sentimental fad ?" I could say much more on the letter in question, but must not trespass further on your valuable space. I trust that after the perusal of these statements, the rate- payers will see the economy in adopting the Triennial Elections, and by an outlay of £l5O save considerably more than tkat sum in six years. I am sir, Yours truly, H. E. HEYWOOD.

The Eddisbury Division comprises squiredom and parsondom in all its pristine glory, and the letters that have recently been sent to tenants by a great landowner show that there are grounds for not asking the voters to make an open declaration of their political faith. It is hoped and expected that Mr. Tomkinson's purity cam- paign will have as successful termination as Mr. Bate's.

The programme of the Liberal meetings for the com- ing week in the Northwich Division are published in the annmncement column. The chief meeting is ,at Run- corn on Tuesday night, where an attractive array of speakers is prornised,and Mr. Philip Speakman, C.C., for Runcorn North will occupy the position of Chairman.

"Let me make a nation's songs and I care not who makes the laws "was the saying of a famous man. Mr. W. Handley, the Liberal agent, who a year or two ago achieved some favour by his election songs, which have since been sung in all parts of England, contributes three to the sheet which apply to the present Northwich contest. The first entitled " Brunner's March to Vic- tory." sung to the tune of when " Johrmy comes march- ing home," commences WHEN Brunner's returned again we'll shout, Hurrah ! Hurrah ! And Whiteley's seat to th' right about, Hurrah ! Hurrah ! We'll show the Tories what we mean,

By Voting straight, and fighting keen; And we'll all feel gay, when Brunner's returned again. The third verse runs— when Whiteley to Blackburn goes again, Hurrah ! Hurrah He won't forget we Cheshire men, Hurrah ! Hurrah We've seen right tlito' the Tory plot, The Unionist cry is nought but rot, So we'll all feel gay,when Whiteley goes marching home. " Remember Brunner" sung to tile tune Of "Auld
Lang Syne," contains four verses of which I quote the following, Shall we desert our member? No ! None, better can we find ! He fought our battle long ago In the days of Auld Lang'Syne ! Chorus :
The third" Unfurl the Flag" (tune " Napoleon talks of war, boys "), concludes Lord Grosvenor came to woo us, but soon we sent him
back; Now Whiteley's come to boo us, to Brunner give the
sack. But Brunner is our member, to him we'll stick, that's plain ; He fought, and won before boys, and so he will again. And so he will, &c.
The sheet contains a number of other songs of more general application' including Mr. 11. B. Shores recent composition" The Old Brigade."

div.head: DR. HOUSTON'S ADDRESS.
div.p: DR. HOUSTON'S ADDRESS.

The address of Dr. Houston, the Liberal candidate for Warrington, will be found set forth in full in our adver- tising columns. He, first of all, points out that he came at the invitation of a large, influential, and representa- tive body of electors of Warrington to seek the high honour, and to undertake the serious duty, of serving the borough in Parliament. " I am," he says, "a Home Ruler; lam no Separatist. I ask for the sister country a local legislature for the management of her domestic affairs, subject to the supremacy of the imperial Parlia- ment." He is in favour of shortening the duration of Parliament, "One Man One Vote," the payment of members, the amendment of the registration laws, the disestablishment of the Welsh Church, the popu- lar control of the liquor traffic and Sunday closing, and of providing public schools for secondary and technical instruction in agriculture and other industries. He is in favour of the restoration of the land to the people, by means of allotments and compulsory sales, so as to give to labourers and others the opportunity of acquiring as much land as they can advantageously cultivate; and also of further improv- ing local government in the counties, by creating dis- trict and parish councils, with power to controrchari- ties, grant allotments, and take land compulsorily for public purposes. On the important subject of mining royalties, Dr. Houston says :—" I understand that the iron trade of Warrington has for a considerable time been in a more or less depr,!ssed condition, and, as a re- sult, the large number of men employed in this great industry have suffered severely. I believe that the present heavy burden of mining royalties is a most serious hindrance to successful competition with con- tinental manufacturers, and a constant danger to the future prosperity of this important trade. I am, there- fore, in favour of such re-adjustment of mining royal- ties and vrayleaves as will effectually and permanently remove all obstacles to the development of a business which is so vital to the prosperity of this borough, and which is so important a factor in the general trade of the United Kingdom." Other measures which Dr. Houston will support are the proper housing of the worging-classes, the taxation of ground rents for local administrative purposes, the ex- tension of the Factory Acts so as to do away with the sweating system, and the reducing, by all feasible means, the hours of labour. MR. LATHAM'S ADDRESS.

Mr. A. M. LATHAM, who is gallantly and ably uphold- ing the Liberal cause in the Knutsford Division, points out in his address, which is printed in our advertising columns, that having been born and bred in an agricul- tural district of Cheshire, he is fully conversa.nt with the wants both of the farmer and the agricultural labourer, and that he had not forgotten the lessons he learned in his boyhood from his father, the late Mr. G. W. Latham, formerly M.P. for Crewe. To the fa-mer he would give every security and freedom,and would encourage him in every possible way to make the best use of the land lie farms. He advocates the enactment of a fresh Agricultural Holdings Act, abolishing the present law of distress, and substituting some simple means of , obtaining compensation in place of the present costly method of arbitration. He would compensate the , farmer for all improvements, and secure him against the raising of his rent on such improvements. He holds that every labourer who wished for it should be able to obtain his allotment or small holding, and the means of getting the same should be simple, speedy, and sure. Rates should be equally divided between owner and occupier, and the ratepayers should be placed in a posi- tion to control the liquor traffic within their boundaries. Mr. Latham is also in favour of free and unsectarian education, and of" Trade Option " with regard to the hours of labour.

div.head: MR. NEILL'S ADDRESS.
div.p: MR. NEILL'S ADDRESS.

Mr. W. Neill, the Liberal candidate for Newton divi- sion, gives prominence in his address to Home Rule,and " speaking as an Ulster Protestant as well as an Eng- lishman by adoption" he believes that the integrity of the empire will be strengthened, and that prosperity and contentment will be promoted in Ireland by the establishment of a statutory Parliament in Dublin, em- powered to deal with purely Irish affairs. He is in com- plete sympathy with the leaders of the labour move- ment in their desire to obtain shorter hours of labour, and, in his opinion, the establishment of a special state department for labour matters would greatly promote industrial interests. The time has come, he thinks, when the whole question of the Poor Laws urgently requires reconsideration. Mr. Neill is in favour of placing the liquor traffic under popular control, and of the further extension of popular local government, including the establishments of Parish Councils. With regard to taxation, he urges that local rates should be more fairly distributed, and that no form of property should be allowed to escape, as is at present the case with ground rents and mining royalties. He is in favour of perfect religious as well as political freedom, and, whilst himself a member of the Estab- lished Church, he considers the demand of the vast majority in Wales for disestablishment of the Church in Wales as reasonable, and one which should be acceded to.

div.head: MR. DEACON'S ADDRESS.
div.p: MR. DEACON'S ADDRESS.

Mr. H. WADE DEACON, in his address to the electors of the Widnes divielen, given prominence to the fact Mat he has always lived in Widnes. If elected he will give a hearty support to Mr. Gladstone's Irish policy, for he believes that by granting Home Rule " we shall per- form an act of justice which will bring peace and happi- ness to that country." He is in favour of the disestab- lishment and disendowment of the Church in Wales, because they are desired by the Welsh people, and be- cause he believes it to be an intolerable injustice to maintain the Church of the minority against the will of the majority. As he earnestly desires to assist in ameli- orating the condition of labour, he is in favour of an extension of the Factory Acts, of the insertion .in all contracts issued by the Government of public bodies against "sweating," and the amendment of the Em- ployers' Liability Act, and of a reform of the Poor Laws. He will also support the Miners' Eight Hours Bill and give careful consideration to legislative proposals of a , similar nature. He is in hearty agreement with the prin- ciple of the direct veto, and he is in favour of Sunday . Closing and the transference of the licensing power to a ; properly elected representative body. In other parts of Ids address, Mr. Deacon speaks in supwat of an ex- tension of the system of national education,nt a thorough reform of the land laws, and of the creation of district and parish councils, endowed with compulsory powers of acquiring land for allotments and public purposes at fair prices. He will also support a reform of registra- tion laws; " One man one vote," payment of members of Parliament, and " mending or ending" the House of Lords.

CONSERVATIVE MEETING. A meeting of the supporters of Mr. Coningsby Disraeli, the Conservative candidate for the Altrincham Parlia- mentary Division, was held on Wednesday, evening, in the Girl's School, Sandy-lane, Lymm. There was a good attendance. Mr. Disraeli delivered #n address on several political topics, after which Mr. Underwood moved the following resolution :—" That this meeting heartily approves of the candidtture of Mr. Disraeli for the Altrincham Division, and pledges itself to use every legitimate offort to secure his return." The motion was seconded by Mr. George Warburton, and carried.
LONDON 'AND THE ULSTER QUESTION.

Ulstermen in London who are supporters of Home Rule dined at the Holborn Restaurant on Thursday night, Sir Charles Russell presiding. Subsequently speeches were delivered by the president, Sir Charles GavanDuffy,and by the Rev. S. Guinness Rogers, Pres- byterian and Unitarian mini3ters, -and other Protestant representatives. Sir Charles Russell expressed his con- viction that the Self-government of Ireland wouid be adequately safeguarded by the constitutional power of , veto, and by the rights of the lipperial Parliament. The 'Rev. 3, Guinness ROgers denourMd the description of a large number of Irishmen as our batural enemies, and powerfully, claimed for others the same freedom of con- science that he claimed for himself. The speech of Mr. Rogers was received with marked applause and cries of "Bravo."

div.head: LIBERAL MEETING AT HALTON LAST NIGHT.
div.p: LIBERAL MEETING AT HALTON LAST NIGHT.
SPEECH BY MR. BRUNNER.

Last night a meeting in support of the candida- ture of Mr. J, T. Brunner, M.P., was held in the Girls' Schoolroom at Halton. There was a good attendance of voters. Mr. R. Posnett, of Highfield Tannery, presided, and in opening the proceedings, said the Tories always claimed at their meetings that they were gathered together to support the unity and integrity of the empire. They (the Liberals) were there too witi that purpose. They believed that when the question of Home Rule was settled, the unity and integrity of the empire would not be touched in the slightest degree, but would be increased. The union of hearts would produce a truer union than they had now. They believed that Mr. Gladstone was the only man who could settle the Home Rule question, and during that election they would do all they could to strengthen the hands of Mr. Gladstone and his govern- ment, for he would be returned to power by a large majority. (Applause.) He characterised tha claim of one corner of Ulster to rule the majority of the people of Ire- land as arrant humbug, and Home Rule would be carried because it was a right, true, and just policy. (Applause.) Mr. Whiteley had recently said that they were such an ignorant lot in the Northwich Division that he had to repeat the same speech over and over again to drum it into them. Re could tell Mr. Whiteley they were not so , ignorant, and they did not want a Blackburn Rover to come and teach them. (Laughter and applause.) A Blackburn Rover was very well in Lancashire, but they were quite satisfied with Mr. Brunner, who had shown himself not a man of promises but of action, and who had done good deeds throughout the Division. (Applause.) Mr. Brunner, who had a cordial reception, said it had been circulated by a Unionist that he was a foreigner, and he had before had to explain that he was the son of a Swiss Father and a Mau' mother, his nurse was a Welsh woman, and he was born in Liver- pool. (Laughter.) All he had was bound up in that division in which they lived. When they prospered he prospered ; when they were happy he was happy, and therefore he was as thoroughly a Cheshire man as any man in that room. (Applause.) He had been asked to say a word about Free Education. The Bill which had been passed by the House of Com- mons did not free Lhe schools, but gave a grant of 103. a year per child in average attendance, which in many., places did not free the schools. The Tories claimed the credit for that Bill, but had the Liberals not voted for it it would n.t have been passed. (Applause.) The education the children got was not free in the sense that it was given to them, because it was paid for by the people out of the taxes. (Hear hear.) Before the Tories found that some measure of free education was absolutely inevitable they used to say that free education would pauperise the people, but no one need feel himself a pauper because he honestly paid for it out of his own pocket, (Applause,) ' The Chairman had referred to Ulster. Now, out of the 33 representatives that sat for the pro- vice of Ulster in the House of Commons during the last six years, seventeen had been Home Rulers and sixteen anti-Home Rulers. But that did not show the true rela- tion of the number of Catholics to Protestants, and if they were to give Ulster a separate representation,Ulster would immediately vote to join itself to the rest of Ireland, so that in the face of that fact they could not treat Ulster as if Ulster was entirely opposed to Home Rule. (Applause). Attempts would be made to per- suade them that if they granted Home Rule, the Catho- lics, being in a great majority, would oppress the rrotestaute. He pointed out that tho puhlio hnflioo in Catholic towns employed large numbers of officials and workmen who were Protestants, while in the towns where the latter were in a majority, very, very few Catholics were employed, and in Belfast, not one. (Applause). Ireland was too near for England to allow Ireland to oppress a Protestant,had they the will, which ho;did not believe. (Applause). It was necessary that the electors should know Mr. Whiteley's connection with the liquor trade. In February, Mr. Whiteley declared Om was quoting a conservative paper), that it would be his business in Northwich Division to defend the interests of the liquor trade. He asked them not to vote for a man who came to de- fend the liquor trade but vote for him—(Mr. Brunner), who was endeavouring honestly and openly to represent them all. (Loud ay plause). Alluding to the Smith Barry testimonial, Mr. Brunner said, circulars had been sent to tenants on Mr. Barry's estate, who were known to be Liberals, and the on.y inference was that if they did not subscribe he would be a marked man. (Hear, hear). He asked them to so vote at the election that pressure should not be put upon men to act contrary to their political convictions. (Loud applause). Mr. Looker proposed a resolution of confidence in Mr. Gladstene's leadershin.—Mr, B. Bniveton seconded the motion, which was carried by acclamation. Speeches were also delivered by Mr. Parker Lowe, M.A.8.C.L., and others.

LIBERAL MEETING AT ASTON. i public meeting was also held at Aston Board Sch•ol under the presidency of Mr. Thomas Rigby, and addresses were delivered by Mr. J. 'I. Brunner, Mr. Parker Lowe, M.A. (of the Eighty Club), and others. There was a capital attendance.

div.head: CROFT.
div.p: CROFT.

THE CROPS.—The crops generally are looking favour- able. Some of the farmers in the district are now cart- ing cabbages to the markets and will commence digging a few early potatoes this week or next. The fruit crop is a failure in this district.

ANNUAL SERMONS Al THE UNITARIAN CHAPEL.—The annual sermons on behalf of the Sunday School were preached in the Unitarian Chapel, Lady-lane, Croft, on Sunday afternoon and evening, by the Be'. A. W. Fos, 8.A., of Longsight, Manchester. There as a large con- gregation at each service. Appropriate hymns were sung by the Cairo-street Chapel choir, of Warrington, in which the congregation heartily joined and an anthem was sung at each service by the choir in a highly credit- ablemanner. The Rev. gentleman preached two excel- lent discourses, which were very attentively listened to and much appreciated. The collections amounted to £ll is. 9cl. Tea was provided for friends from a dis- tance. SUNDAY ScnooL TEA PARTY.—The annual tea party for the Sunday School scholars, teachers, choir, and friends in connection with the Unitarian Chapel, Lady- lane, Croft, was held on Monday afternoon. The scholars, &c., met at the Sunday School at two O'clock, and shortly after proceeded to a field (kindly lent by Mr. Thomas Welsby) where cricket and various games were engaged in until about four o'clock, when they returned to the school, and partook of an excellent tea. Afterwards play was again resumed in the fields, and racing, &c., took place. Nuts and sweets were also dis- tributed during the evening, the minister, the Rev. W. Mason, of Leigh, and others d Aug their utmost to pro- mote the children's enjoyment. A pleasant afternoon and evening were spent.

THE ROYAL BETROTHAL.

Clarence-house has been visited by many distinguished persons, who signed the visitors' book and left their congratulations on the betrothal of Prince Ferdinand of Roumania and Princess Marie of Edinburgh.

MR. GOSCHEN AND HOME RULE. Speaking in London yesterday afternoon, the CHAN- CELLOR of the EXCHEQUER said it could not be said a few weeks hence that the General Election had been fought on the question of Home Rule because Mr. Gladstone dictmot give even an outline of his scheme.

div.head: FATAL FRENCH DUEL.
div.p: A FATAL FRENCH DUEL.

„ - PARIS, FRIDAY, 1 A.M.—The duel which was rougnt yesterday morning between the Marquis de Mores and Captain Mayer has had a fatal termination, the captain, who sustained a serious wound in one of his lungs, hav- ing succumbed to his injury. The lateness of the hour at which the death took place has prevented the sensa- tion which the event will undoubtedly cause later on, and the arrest of the deceased's antagonist may be ex- pected.

div.head: DEATH OF THE EARL OF HARE WOOD.
div.p: DEATH OF THE EARL OF HARE WOOD.

The Earl of Harewood, who had been ill for some time past, died about four o'clock on Thursday morning, at Harewood, near Leeds. The late earl was Henry Thynne Lascelles, was fourth earl, and was born June 18th, 1824 succeeding to the title in 1857. He unsuccessfuly con- tested Yorkshire, West Riding, East Division, as a Con- servative in 1889. He married, in 1881, Lady Florence Katherine Bridgeman, daughter of the third Earl of Bradford.
DISASTROUS LANDSLIP. 30 PERSONS }KILLED AND INoURED.

A Reutei's telegram from Bologna reports that a disastrous landslip involving great loss of life, occurred yesterday morning at Monte Sasso, on the Bologno and Florence Railway. Several houses were buried with their occupants by the falling mass of earth, and the Mayor estimates the number of killed and injured at 30. The railway communication has been interrupted by the calamity.

MR. J. MORLEY AND IRISH PRO TECTION. Mr. John Morley, having been appealed to with regard to the statement made by a Northamptonshire shoe manufacturer that if the Irish got control of their own affairs, they would put a prohibitive tax upon the im- port of boots and shoes, which would mean a loss of £20,000 in East Northamptonshire alone, he has sent the following reply :—" 95, Elm-park Gardens. S.W., June 21. Dear Sir,—ln the Irish Home Rule Bill of 1886 the Irish legislative body would have had no power to impose an import duty on either boots or shoes, or anything else. The statement, therefore, to which you refer is entirely untrue.—Yours truly, JOHN MORLEY.' Mr. William Wood on Monday announced his resigna- tion of the Mayoralty of Wigan, giving his reason for doing se that he does not approve of the Conservative party's action with regard to the Eight Hours Ques- tion.

div.head: YESTERDAY'S PARLIAMENT HOUSE OF LORDS.
div.p: YESTERDAY'S PARLIAMENT HOUSE OF LORDS.
The House met at a quarter-past four.

THE SALVATION ARMY.—Lord STANLEY of Alderley moved the rejection of Eastbourne Improvement Bill on its third reading. The Lord CHANCELLOR said things had greatly improved in Eastbourne since the Bill had been before Parliament. The members of the Salvation and Skeleton armies had acted disgracefully in violat- ing the law. Both the police and the magistrates had acted with great forbearance. Bill read a third time and passed. WOMEN'S SUFFRAGE BILL.—Lord DENMAN moved the second reading of the Women's Suffrage Bill. Lord liaLtssurer on the grand that their lordships should not interfere with the constitution of the House of Commons The motion to read a second time was negatived.

div.p: THE SHIP CANAL.

Mr. Bushell; acting on behalt of tlio Manchester Ship Canal Co., applied to the Runcorn magistrates on Mon- day for a license to enable them to store 4,000 tons of mixed explosives at Weston.—Superintendent Atherton objected. The place, he said, was not adapted for that amount, which was more fit to be stored in a hulk in the river.—Mr. Bushell said they did not expect to store more than 2,000 tons, but the reason for askir.g for 4,000 was because they could only store ilb. of mixed explo- sives to one lb. of gunpowder.—Superintendent Ather- ton : If you get the license you would have the upper hand if anything occurred.—The Bench only granted a license to store 2,000 tons.

ACCIDENT TO AN EXCURSION TRAIN. On Thursday morning, a Bromyard and Worcester excursion tram to Warwick left the metals, near Pershore, cawing serious damage to the permanent way and temporarily disorganizing the traffic. The passen- gers continued their journey in a made up train.
STRANDING OF A PASSENGER STEAMER.

• During a dense fog which prevailed on the north-east coast ou Wednesday night, the passenger steamer Comet, returning from Salthurn to Newcastle with 184 passen- gers, got on the rocks at Seaham Harbour. A panic ensued on board, the women fainted and others rushed wildly about. Fortunately help arrived, and all were safely landed in boats. The passengers were sent home by a special train, except one female, who is so ill that he cannot be removed.

div.head: MURDER OF A DETECTIVE.
div.p: THE MURDER OF A DETECTIVE.

At the inquest held on Thursday at Charing Cross Hospital concerning the death of Detective Sergeant Joyce, who was shot a few days ago while attempting to arrest John Goodman, the Coroner's jury returned a verdict of wilful murder against the latter. Goodman, who had armed himself with a revolver, fired at three persons, and not only killed the detective, but seriously injured another man named Ruhman.

FIGHTING IN AFGHANISTAN. . PROGRESS OP THE REBELLION. SIMLA, Tnunswa.--Advices from Kandahar estimate the Afghan losses in the recent fighting with the rebel- lious Hazaras tit 250 regulars and 1,200 irregulars. It is added that the Ameer's soldiery are now dispirited, and that his levies are deserting in large numbers. ' THE NEW BISHOP OF SALFORD.
The Press Association's Manchester correspondent is informed that Father Henry Bowden, of the Brompton Oratory, will succeed Archbishop Vaughan as Bishop of Salford.
MR. GLADSTONE'S MANIFESTO.

Mr. Gladstone, in his address to the electors of Midlothian, says the electors must decide whether the three countries are henceforth to constitute in reality,as well as by statute and in name, a United Kingdom. Irish grievances had constituted the great burden of Parlia- ment, and the chief impediment to the prosecution of its arduous and complicated office. As regards Great Britain the proposal for which the Liberal party had untiredly contended during the last six years was the proposal to set both Parliament and Ireland tree—lreland for the management of her own domestic affairs by a local Legislature in close sympathy with Irish life, and Parliament for the work of overtaking the vast arrears of business, and supply- ing, with reasonable despatch, the varied legislative wants of England, Scotland, and Wales. As regards the government of Ireland by the now expiring Parliament, Mr. Gladstone contends that it has utterly failed in every respect ,save one. The Ministry bad enabled the Irish agriculturist to improve his condition by passinga., 1118 ct in 1887, the main provision of which it denounced n n 6 as unusual and dishonourable. Ireland was now calm and peaceful in her reliance upon the constituencies of Great Britain, and the sentiments which already pre- vailed between British and Irish peoples supplied a happy omen of the reciprocal affection which could not but follow the frank concession of Home Rule sheltered by imperial supremacy.. Mr. Gladstone then enumerates Liberal reforms which he promises to deal with in his election speeches.

A Chicago telegram on Tuesday states that the nomin- ation of Mr. Cleveland seems to be a certainty. Mr. H. M. Stanley, the African explorer, has issued hi address to the electors of North Lambeth, as a Liberal Unionist candidate.

PIaILIAMENTARY ELECTION, 1892. TO TUE ELECTORS OF THE BOROUGH OF WARRINGTON. HElsrarlVWEN.—For seven years past the voles of this great constituency has not been heard in the Oounoile of the Empire You have been practically disfranchised. It is time to put en end to this humiliating state of things- I came at the invitation of a large, influential, and repre- sentative body of Electors to seek the high honour, and to undertake the serious duty, of serving you in Parliament. Their choice has been ratified by thousands among you, whom have met in public assembly, and in private conference. My political opinions are by this time well-known to you. I 'Lave expounded them on the platform, hi meeting after tweeting, from one end of the constituency to the other. I am a Home Ruler; I ant no Separatist. I ask for the Sister Country a Local Legislature for the management of her 'domestic affairs, subject to the supremacy of the Imperial Parliament. I am in favour of shortening the duration of Parlia- ments, One Man One Vote, the Payment df Mem- bers, the Amendment of the Registration Laws by the appointment of responsible registration officers, the reduction of the qualifying period. the preservation of the right to vote notwithstanding change of residenee,and the securing to every duly qualifed citizen his fiallelectoral rights, I shall support whatever measures may be necessary to prevent the Honse of Lords being anylonger an obstacle in the way of remedial legislation. , lam in favour of the Disestablishment Of the Welsh Church. I am in favour of providing public schodis for Secondary and Technical Instruction,in agriculture and other industries. lam in favour of providing for the direct and Pepular Control of the Liqtsor Traffic, and of Sunday Closing. I am in favour of the Restoration of the Land to the ',People, by means of allotments ,and compulsory sales, so as to give to labourers and others the opportunity,of acquiring asanuch land as they can advantageously cultivate ; and I am in favour of further impro ring Local Government in the Coun- ties by creating District and Pariah,Councils, with 'power to control charities, grant allotments, and take land-compul- sorily for public purposes. By them measures vitality will be restored to our villages. and the sexcessive competition in the labour market, and thooverierowding of our towns, will be prevented. I am in favour of taking whatever steps are necessary to secure the proper Housing of the Working Classes. I am in favour of the Taxation of Ground Rents for local administrative purposes. I understand that the Iron Trade of Warrington has for a considerable time been dn a more or less depressed condition, and, as a result, thedargemuniber of men employed • in this great industry have .suffered severely. I believe that the present heavy burden of Mining Royalties is a ..most serious hindrance to successful competition with Continental manufacturers, and a constant danger to the 'future prosperity of this important trade. lam therefore in favour of such a readjustment •of Mining Royalties and Wayleaves as -will effectually and permanently remove all obstacles to the development of a business which Is so vital to the, prosperity of this Borough, and which is so important a factor in the general trade of the United Kingdom. Jam in favour of making the Sale and Transfer of Land cheap, simple, and easy; the Enfranchisement of Leaseholds ; and the protection of tenants from unjust exactions by their landlores. I am in favour of a Free Breakfast Table. lam in favour of establishing a juster system of Local and National Taxation, so as to distribute the burthen more equally. I ant in favour of extending the Factory Acts, so as to do away with the evils of the Sweating System ; I am in favour of reducing, by fill feasible means, the Hours of Labour to such a point as will allow the working-man reasonable leisure for recreation and Improvement; and I shall support any practicable system by which the industrious and well-con- ducted workmen shall, when broken down by age or infir- mity, be sewed from the ignominy and misery of workhoute charity. From the opinions above enunciated you can judge of the line of policy which I shall pursue in Parliament, if you honour me with your confidence. I therefore earnestly appeal to you to unite in securing my return by such a majority as will prove this borough to be, what It) molly is, a Liberal and Progressive constituency. I have the Honour to be, Gentlemen, Your Obedient and Faithful Servant. ARTHUR HOUSTON. Warrington, June 21, 1892.

PARLIAMENTARY ELECTION, 1892. 9"0 THE PARLIAMENTARY ELECTORS OF 1. THE RNUTSFORD DIVISION OF CHESHIRE. GENTLEMEN,—At the request of the Executive Council of the Liberal Association of this Division I have came forth to seek your suffrages on this-occasion in opposition to the Conservative Candidate. Though returned to power in 1886, on the distinct promise that Ireland should be governed with equal rights and privi- leges., the Conservative party at the very outset of this r4gime adopted the most stringent measures of coercion, in the administration of which they have violated every principle of justice and freedom and have only succeeded in intensify- ing that) hatred of English rule with which our fellow-country- men in Ireland are naturally inspired, and which can only be eradicated by such just and conciliatory measures as Mr. Gladstone has proposed. To Ireland I would give an Irish Parliament for the management of exclusively Irish affairs, and I consider that with suck a measure the ties which bind the two nations would be drawn closer,—agrarian crime in Ireland would disappear, and peace and prosperity would be established. The disestablishment of the Church in Wales is a reform that is immediately called for, and is one for which, if you honour me with your confidence, I would certainly vote. I am in femur of perfect religious equality. Born and bred in an Agricultural District of Cheshire. I atm!fully conversant with the wants both of the Farmer and of the Agricultural Labourer, and I have not forgotten the lessons I learned in my boyhood from my father, the late Mr. G. W. Latham, formerly H.P. for Crewe. To the Farmer I would give every security and freedom, and would enoeurage him in all possible ways to make the test use of the land he farms, and to increase wherever he van the yield per acre. This I consider the best remedy for the present agricultural depression. I advocate the enactment of a fresh Agricultural Holdings Act, largely amending that of 1883, abolishing the present law of distress, and substituting some simple means of ob- taining compensation in place of the present costly method of arbitration. I would also compensate the Farmer for all improvements, and, further give him ttecurity that his rent shall not be raised on account of such improvements. Every Labourer who wished for it should be able to obtain his allotment or small holding, and the means of getting the same should be simple, speedy, and sure. The control and management of local affairs, including .parochial charities, I would plate in the hands of parish or village and dist, ict councils elected by ballot by the parish- ioners, and to no man would I give more than one veto whetherin Parliamentary or local elections. Rates should be equally divided between owner ati.l OCC4- pier. My opinion with regard to the !Licensing laws is that the Ratepayers should be able to control the liquor trails within their boundaries, and to say how many, if any, licenses should be granted, and during what hours the houses holding these licenses should remain open. I would have all education free and unsectarian, and leave the management of the schools in the hands of the Ratepayers wherever there is any contribution of public money, how- ever small, there should be come form of representative con- trol. Though I have net yet seen any proposal for universally limiting the hours of laborer to (8) hours, which seems to be practicable, I am most strongly opposed to the hours of work being exoessive, or in any way injurious to the worker, and I am inclined to support any measure which embodied the principle of' Trade Option " as defined at the Trades' Union Congress of 1891, which would secure for the workman more leisure without endangering the prosperity of our commerce or unduly trenching on the liberty of the individual. I shall hope before the day of the pelt to address meetings in all parts of the constituency, and to elaborate my views on these and other questions on all of which it is impossible to touch in this address. It my views commend themselves to you I trust that you will vote for me fearlessly and without favour, disregarding all outside influences, and !remembering that the Ballot is absolutely secret and the, all statements to the contrary are false and lying. Should you consider me worthy of your support and return me as your member. it shall always be my endeavour in the future—as it has been lathe past—to strive to render the lot of the working-man more tolerable, and to give to the farmer more security and comfort in!his holding, and to promote all measures which will tend! te establish the welfare of the nation and the peace and prosperity of this' Empire on the sure and solid basis of a well-governed and contented people, I have the honour to remain, Gentlemen, 'Your most obedient Servant, ALEXANDER MERE LATHAM. 1, Temple Gardens, London, EC. June 18th, 1892.

NOTICE IS HEREEY GNIEN, that the next GENERAL QUARTER SESSIONS of the Peace for the COUNTY OF CHESTER, will be holden at the CASTLE OF CHESTER, in and for the said County, on ! MONDA, the 27th day of June instant, at Half-past Eleven ,o'clock in the Forenoon, when the Grand Jury will be empannelled. The hearing of all Appeals arising within the Hun- dreds of ,Broxton, Eddisbury, Diantwich and Wirral, forming the Chester District, and the trials of all pri- seners committed from such Hundreds will take place at such Sessions. The Grand and Petty Jury for the Chester District must be in attendance at the Castle of Chester, at the opening of the Court on MONDAY, the 27th day of June instant, at Half-past Eleven o'clock in the Forenoon. THE COURT will be Adjourned ty the Court House, Nether Knutsford,,on WEDNESDLY, the 29th day of June instant, at Eleven o'clock in the Forenoon, when another Grand Jury will be erepannelled. The hearing ..of all Appeals arrisisg within the Hundreds of Bucklow, Macclesfield, and Nerthwich, forming the Knutsford Tistrict, and the trials of all prisoners committed from the last-mentioned Hundreds will take place at such Ad- journed Sessins. The Grand and Petty Jury for the Kuutsforcl District must be in attendance at the Court House, Kuutsforcl, at the opening of the Court on WEB- NEW,3AY. the 29th day of lune instant, at Eleven o'clock in the Forenoon. REGINALD POTTS, Clerk of the Peace for the County of Chester. Chezter, 7th June, 1892.

PARLIAMENTARY ELECTION. 1892. T 0 THE ELECTORS OF THE NEWTON DIVISION OF SOUTH-WEST LANCASHIRE. GENTLEMEN, Having been selected by the Liberals of this Division to contest the seat as their candidate at this General Election, it is now my duty to lay before you on outline of my political principles. The most urgent question is now, as it was six years ago, that of the Government of Ireland. The Tories, after six years of power, having failed to devise any feasible scheme of Local Government for Ireland, it is clear that there is no middle course between what is called Home Rule and a con- tinuation of the system of Coercion under which Ireland has for so long been misgoverneal. And speaking as an Ulster Protestant as well as an Englishman by adoption. I believe that the integrity af this empire will be strengthened, and that prosperity and contentment will be promoted in Ireland, by the establishment of a Statutory Parliament in Dublin empowered to deal with purely Irish affairs, the control of all Imperial matters being retained by the Imperial Parlia- ment at Westminster. lam in complete sympathy with th leaders of the Labour Movement in their desire to obtain shorter hours of labour, to increase the opportun:ty for culture, and to gene rally Improve their position. The attainment of an Eight Hours Working Day I regard as an important step, and though I consider the enforcing of an universal Eight Hours Day by legislative enactment as impracticable, I believe that the legislature can legitimately and usefully interfere to limit hours in certain cases, as, for instance, the hours of labour of Miners and Railway Servants. Theestablishment of a special State Department, for labour matters, controlled by a responsible minister, would, in my opinion, greatly promote, industrial interests. The existing Poor Laws, however suitable they may have been in the past, have become antiquated, andare no longer in accord with popular requirements under altered conditions. They press harshly in sickness and old age upon deserving people, who through no fault of their own have been over- taken by poverty. I think the time has come when the whole question' urgently requires reconsideration. Much can, I think, be done to check poverty add misery by curtailment of the excessive consumption of alcoholic liquors, and the promotion of Temperance by all legitimate means. One of the first steps towards this end is, to my mind, the placing of the Liquor Traffic under popular control, both as to the granting of licences and the general regulation of Public- houses. I think that reconsideration and reform of the whole sub- ject of Incidence of Taxation, both Imperial and Local, is urgently demanded. Local Rates should be more fairly distributed, so that all sources, or possible sources, of income should bear their rela- tive share of Local Taxation ; and no form of Property should be allowed to escape, as is at present the case with Ground Rents and Mining Royalties. I consider the further extension of popular Local Govern- ment a matterof National importanc,?. and regard as essential the establishment of popularly-elected Parish Councils, with sufficiently wide powers for the control and administration of local affairs. The thorough reconsideration and reform of the Land Laws is, to my mind, of great importance. I think reform of the system of Registration and the abolition of the Plural Vote is essential to political equality. I am in favour of perfect Religious, as well as Political, Freedom, and while myself a member of the Established Church, I consider the demand of the vast majority in Wales for Disestablishment of the Church in Wales as reasonable, and one which should be acceded to. I look upon the House of Lords, as at presentconstituted, as opposed to the spirit of the age, and consider its reform as essential to the proper working of Democraac Government. On any other special topics I shall be happy to give my views 011 the platform. If you should do n e the honour of returning me as your representative at Westminster, whatever energy and ability I may have shall be spent in promoting the principles of Liberalism and the interests of this Constituency. I am, Gentlemen, Your obedient servant. W. NEILL.

HOW MINING ROYALIIES AFFECT WARRIN GTON WORKMEN, (From "The Roll Call.") The Royalties paid upon the Iron and Steel manu- factured in Warrington amount to nearly £50,000 per aunum. For every sovereign which the ironworker earn' as wages (for an employment so arduous and ex- haustive that the average life of the ironworker is only about 35 years), the owner of the Mine Royal- ties (who neither toils nor spins), receives six shillings and sixpence. The Royalties payable on the Continent only amount to as many pence per ton of finished iron as Warrington pays shillings. Not the iron trade alone, but every trade in the country suffers from these unjust and excessive dues. Workingmen, the Tory candidate has treated your requests for his opinion on this most vital sub- ject with silent contempt. If, therefore, you wish to put an end to a system which is throttling one of the most important and largest industries of our country, support the Liberals in their determination to bring the present condition of mining royaltiie into harmony with the necessities of the times.
